PURPOSE This Agreement sets out the framework for the sharing of Personal Data between the Parties as Data Controllers and defines the principles and procedures that the Parties shall adhere to and the responsibilities the Parties owe to each other. The Personal Data subject to this Agreement is listed within the Schedule. The sharing of Personal Data is necessary to support the Agreed Purposes as listed within the Schedule. It is recognised that there are significant benefits to the Parties of having access to the Shared Personal Data to achieve the Agreed Purposes. This Agreement is required to ensure that where Personal Data may be accessed, such access will at all times comply with the Data Protection Legislation. . COMPLIANCE The Parties agree that this Agreement formalises the lawful transfer of the Personal Data between the Parties and presents no new or additional privacy concerns. A data protection impact assessment has been conducted in respect of the Personal Data to be shared and the necessity of the sharing and this Agreement serves to address any residual privacy or information risks and documents the actions taken to identify, address and mitigate those risks wherever possible. The Parties shall not process the Personal Data in a way that is incompatible with the Agreed Purposes. As Data Controllers, the Parties remain responsible for ensuring that all uses of the Personal Data are in compliance with all applicable Data Protection Legislation. This Agreement must be formally approved and signed by the Parties before any Personal Data is shared by persons with authority to do so on behalf of their organisation. All Parties will ensure that the terms of this Agreement are known and understood by all Staff involved in the sharing of the Personal Data. Each Party is registered with the ICO has a valid Data Protection Registration Number with its national Data Protection Authority if required by the Enterprise Act which by the time that the data sharing is expected to commence, covers the intended data sharing pursuant to this Agreement. The Council’s ICO registration number is Z5948361 and the Provider’s ICO registration number is Z8583439. . PERSONAL DATA The Parties shall, in relation to any of the Personal Data processed in connection with its obligations under this Agreement: Process that Personal Data only in accordance with the Schedule, unless the Parties are required to do otherwise by Law, which should be notified to the other Parties (unless notification is prohibited by Law); not Process in an irrelevant or excessive way with regard to the Agreed Purposes; ensure they do not knowingly or negligently do or omit to do anything which places the Parties breach of the obligations under the Data Protection Legislation; ensure that they have in place Protective Measures to protect against: a) unauthorised or unlawful processing of Personal Data; b) accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, Personal Data, and such measures to be reviewed as appropriate to protect against a Data Loss Event having taken account of the: (i) nature of the data to be protected; (ii) harm that might result from a Data Loss Event; (iii) state of technological development; and (iv) cost of implementing any measures; ensure the Personal Data is kept and stored securely in accordance with Data Protection Legislation; ensure that: (i) the Staff do not process Personal Data except in accordance the Schedule; (ii) each Party takes all reasonable steps to ensure the reliability and integrity of any Staff who have access to the Personal Data and ensure that they: (A) are aware of and comply with the duties under this Agreement; (B) are subject to appropriate confidentiality undertakings; (C) are informed of the confidential nature of the Personal Data and do not publish, disclose or divulge any of the Personal Data to any third party unless permitted by this Agreement; and (D) have undergone adequate training in the use, care, protection and handling of the Personal Data; not transfer the Personal Data outside of the UK unless the prior written consent of all Parties has been obtained and the following conditions are fulfilled: a) the Parties have provided appropriate safeguards in relation to the transfer (whether in accordance with UK GDPR Article 46 or LED Article ); b) the Data Subject has enforceable rights and effective legal remedies; c) the Parties outside the UK comply with the obligations under the Data Protection Legislation by providing an adequate level of protection to any Personal Data that is transferred (or, if it is not so bound, uses its best endeavours to assist the Parties in meeting its obligations under the Data Protection Legislation); securely destroy or return the Personal Data (and any copies of it) to the Data Discloser upon termination or expiry of this Agreement unless the Parties are required by Law to retain the Personal Data; and as far as is reasonably practical, anonymise or pseudoanonymise all Personal Data contained in statistics, reports and summaries to minimise the amount of Personal Data shared. . FAIR, LAWFUL AND TRANSPARENT PROCESSING The Personal Data shall be shared in accordance with the Agreed Purposes on the basis of the legal grounds as stated in the Schedule. The Parties undertake to inform Data Subjects of the purposes for which it will process their Personal Data and provide all of the information that it must provide in accordance with applicable laws, to ensure that the Data Subjects understand how their Personal Data will be processed by the Data Controller. The Parties shall, in respect of the Personal Data, ensure that their privacy notices are clear and provide sufficient information to Data Subjects, in order for them to understand: what Personal Data the Parties are sharing; the circumstances in which it will be shared; the purposes for the sharing; either the identity with whom the Personal Data is shared or a description of the type of organisation that will receive the Personal Data unless an exemption to the transparency provisions applies. . DATA QUALITY The Data Discloser shall ensure that the Personal Data is accurate. Where either Party becomes aware of inaccuracies in the Personal Data, they will notify the other Party immediately. . DATA SUBJECTS' RIGHTS Data Subjects have the right to obtain certain information about the processing of their Personal Data through a Subject Access Request. Data Subjects may also request rectification, erasure or blocking of their Personal Data. The Parties shall maintain a record of Subject Access Requests, the decisions made and any information that was exchanged. Records must include copies of the request for information, details of the data accessed and shared and where relevant, notes of any meeting, correspondence or phone calls relating to the request, together with relevant dates. The Parties agree that the responsibility for complying with a Subject Access Request falls to Party receiving the Subject Access Request in respect of the Personal Data held by that Party. The Parties agree to provide reasonable and prompt assistance (within 5 business days of such a request for assistance) at their own expense as is necessary to each other to enable them to comply with Subject Access Requests and to respond to any other queries or complaints from Data Subjects. . DATA RETENTION AND DELETION The Data Receiver shall not retain or process Personal Data for longer than is necessary to carry out the Agreed Purposes. Notwithstanding Clause 8.1, the Parties shall continue to retain the Personal Data in accordance with any internal or statutory retention periods applicable in their organisations and/or industry. The Data Receiver shall ensure that any Personal Data is returned to the Data Discloser or destroyed in the following circumstances: (a) upon termination of the Agreement for whatever reason; (b) upon expiry of the Term (unless extended further in accordance the terms of this Agreement); and (c) once processing of the Personal Data is no longer necessary for the Agreed Purposes. . TRANSFERS For the purposes of this Clause, transfers of Personal Data shall mean any sharing of the Personal Data by the Data Receiver with a third party, and shall include, but is not limited to, the following: a) sharing of the Personal Data with any third party; b) publication of the Personal Data via any medium, including, but not limited to social media, websites, publically available communications. c) storing Personal Data on servers outside the UK; d) subcontracting the processing of Personal Data to data processors located outside the UK; e) granting third parties located outside the UK access rights to the Personal Data. The Data Receiver shall not share the Personal Data with a third party without the express written permission of the Data Discloser save as required by law or court order. Where Personal Data is to be shared under clause 9.2, the Data Receiver shall not disclose or transfer the Personal Data outside the UK without first ensuring that adequate and equivalent protections will be afforded to the Personal Data. . SECURITY AND TRAINING The Parties agree to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect the Personal Data in their possession against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, damage, alteration or disclosure, including but not limited to: a) ensuring IT equipment, including portable equipment is kept in lockable areas when unattended; b) not leaving portable equipment containing the Personal Data unattended; c) ensuring Staff use appropriate secure passwords for logging into systems or databases containing the Personal Data; d) ensuring that all IT equipment is protected by antivirus software, firewalls, passwords and suitable encryption devices; e) ensuring that any Special Category Personal Data is stored and transferred (including where stored or transferred on portable devices or removable media) using industry standard 256-bit AES encryption or suitable equivalent; f) limiting access to relevant databases and systems to those Staff who need to have access to the Personal Data, and ensuring that passwords are changed and updated regularly to prevent inappropriate access when individuals are no longer engaged by the Party; g) conducting regular threat assessment or penetration testing on systems; h) ensuring all Staff handling Personal Data have been made aware of their responsibilities with regards to handling of the Personal Data; and i) allowing for inspections and assessments to be undertaken by the other Party in respect of the security measures taken, or producing evidence of those measures if requested. . PERSONAL DATA BREACHES AND REPORTING PROCEDURES The Parties shall ensure they do not knowingly or negligently do or omit to do anything which places either Party in breach of the Data Protection Legislation. Each Party shall inform the other immediately if it: a) is in breach of the Protective Measures requirements; b) receives a request to rectify, block or erase the Personal Data; c) receives any complaint or communication relating to either Party's obligations under the Data Protection Legislation; d) receives any communication from the Information Commissioner or any other regulatory authority in connection with the Personal Data; e) receives a request from any third party for disclosure of the Personal Data where compliance with such request is required or purported to be required by Law; or f) becomes aware of a Data Loss Event, and without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours, shall notify the other Parties, by: (i) contacting the Data Protection Officer(s) as detailed within the Schedule; and (ii) informing them of the Data Loss Event, including in its notification: (A) a description of the Data Loss Event including where possible, the categories and approximate number of Data Subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of data records concerned; and (B) a description of the measures taken or proposes to take to address the Data Loss Event, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects. Following the notification of a Data Loss Event, the informing Party shall immediately assess the risks and consequences of the Data Loss Event and take measures, including: (i) to mitigate the possible adverse effects of the Data Loss Event; and (ii) to protect the data and the interests/safety of the Data Subject and/or Data Controller, and inform the other Parties as to the measures that it has taken. The informing Party’s obligation to notify shall include the provision of further information in phases, as details become available. . RESOLUTION OF DISPUTES WITH DATA SUBJECTS OR THE DATA Taking into account the nature of the processing, the Parties shall provide each other, at their own expense, with full assistance in relation to the Personal Data and the obligations under Data Protection Legislation and any complaint, communication or request made including by promptly providing (and in any event within 24 hours of being received): i. full details and copies of the complaint, communication or request; ii. such assistance as is reasonably requested to enable the Parties to comply with a Data Subject Access Request within the relevant timescales set out in the Data Protection Legislation; iii. assistance as required with respect to any request from the Information Commissioner’s Office, or any consultation by the Parties with the Information Commissioner's Office; iv. any Personal Data it holds in relation to a Data Subject (as appropriate) within the timescales required by the Council; and v. each other Party with any information requested in relation to the request. . RECORDS The Parties shall maintain complete and accurate records and information to demonstrate its compliance with Data Protection Legislation. The Parties may reasonably request information from each to satisfy itself that obligations under the Data Protection Legislation are being met in relation to the Personal Data. Sub-processing Before allowing any Sub-processor to process any Personal Data related to this Agreement, the Parties must: a) notify the other Parties in writing of the intended Sub-processor and processing; b) obtain the written consent of the Parties; c) enter into a written agreement with the Sub-processor which gives effect to the terms set out in this Condition such that they apply to the Sub-processor; and d) provide the Parties with such information regarding the Sub-processor as the Parties may reasonably require. Description Details Data Protection Officer contact Council details (for each Party) (a) Andrew Maughan (b) (c) C&I (a) Mahwish Noor (b) (c) Subject matter of the The PICT Service aims to empower and upskill frontline Neighbourhood processing Housing Officers (NHOs) in the Landlord Service to support their work with residents who may present with complex mental health difficulties (whether diagnosed or not), and challenging behaviours, particularly where these difficulties impact on their housing (e.g. ability to maintain their tenancy), and vice versa. Duration of the processing (for April 2021 until foreseeable each Controller’s activities) Nature and purposes of the PICT Staff offer consultation and training to NHOs, rather than usually processing working directly with residents (although PICT staff can attend occasional joint appointments with NHOs and residents to facilitate access to support services). PICT staff do not have their own ‘caseload’. PICT seeks to equip the existing workforce with the knowledge, skills and confidence to work effectively with residents presenting with multiple and complex mental health needs and challenging behaviours. The aim of the intervention is to support an effective approach to achieving positive outcomes for residents, and support the delivery of the primary task of the Landlord Services. The hope is also that the NHOs will also develop an increased sense of personal achievement and emotional resilience in their work. Information Sharing Agreement Rescue and Response project Purpose Specific Information Sharing Agreement Owner: Rescue and Response project, Brent Council Review Date: October 2019 This Information Sharing Agreement (ISA) defines the arrangements for processing data between disclosing data controllers and recipient data controllers and sits underneath the overarching Information Sharing Protocol (ISP) / Partnership Agreement. Definitions of terms used in this agreement shall have the same meaning as defined under the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA). . Parties to the agreement: Full name and address of the organisations or businesses (distinguish between disclosing organisation and recipient organisation) Disclosing organisation Recipient organisation Brent Council- Rescue and Response Brent Council- Rescue and Response project project Abianda Abianda St Giles Trust St Giles Trust Safer London Safer London All London Boroughs All London Boroughs The Children Society The Children Society . Why is the information being shared? Rescue and Response is a three-year MOPAC (Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime) funded project, running between 2019 and 2021, which will support young Londoners affected by cross-border county lines activity. The signatories to this ISA has responsibilities to share information under legislation, which includes preventing and detecting crime and/or safeguarding and supporting individuals. The sharing of information is necessary for the Rescue and Response project to develop and deliver a support service for young people who are vulnerable and caught up in county lines drug distribution networks across London, and identify and use enforcement against those exploiting young people. This will benefit the public and community by reducing crime and improving the potential outcomes of young people. Everyone who works with children has a responsibility for keeping them safe. No single practitioner or agency can have a full picture of a child’s needs and circumstances and, if children and families are to receive the right help at the right time, everyone who comes into contact with them has a role to play in identifying concerns, sharing information and taking prompt action. Sharing information is relevant for  Addressing the increase in number of Young people identified as being exploited/at risk of count lines exploitation  Increased engagement with services for the young people referred and engaged.  Better understanding of County Lines and peer and criminal networks associated.  Increased feelings of safety and reduced feelings of vulnerability of those young people engaged through the project.  Identification of a person’s associations to ascertain if they are linked to/at risk from a criminal network  Identification of a person’s aliases to clarify if they are linked to/at risk from a criminal network  Identification of a criminal network’s to identify young people that may be at risk from their criminal activity  The prevention of crime and disorder  The detection of Crime  The protection of vulnerable members of the community . Potential recipients, types of recipients and the circumstances they will have access (if information is shared further)? Disclosing organisations will share with other signatory boroughs and police any relevant information regarding the young person on a need to know basis. This will include intelligence to prevent further crimes and to safeguard children and young people. The main information sharing will take place between signatory agencies, with the Rescue & Response Project Team acting as the hub, and delivering support services. The hub will be a central control for sharing information about individuals. It will manage the sharing of information as referrals from and to other signatories. Disclosing organisations may share with other internal and external departments so the organisation can provide a more holistic service for their benefit. This will be under existing sharing frameworks within each organisation as data controllers. . What information being shared? Personal and special category personal data will be processed. The data items include:  criminal data  health data (mental health)  financial data (mainly benefits),  contact data  family data  local authority service data (education, children safeguarding, adult safeguarding). The data subjects will be victims/potential victims and alleged/convicted perpetrators, as well as individuals who are connected to those data subjects, such as family, witnesses and providers of support. The relationships or identity (i.e. victim or perpetrator) will be defined and flagged during processing. . What is the classification of the information to be shared according to the Government Security Classification Policy (GSCP)? The handling and access of the data shall comply with the requirements of this classification. Data will be classified as OFFICIAL A subset of data will be classified as OFFICIAL - SENSITIVE. This will be relevant for information that could have more damaging consequences for individuals if it were lost, stolen or published in the media. This subset of information shall still be managed within the ‘OFFICIAL’ classification tier, but attract additional measures (generally procedural or personnel) to reinforce the ‘need to know’. In such cases where there is a clear and justifiable requirement to reinforce the ‘need to know’, information assets will be conspicuously marked: This will be relevant for the following subset of data items:  criminal data  health data (mental health), and  local authority service data (education, children safeguarding, adult safeguarding). Please see appendix A- data sharing flow chart and data table. Parties may have implemented the GSCP differently and each is responsible for applying their classification schemes appropriately. . What is your legal justification for sharing? Has consent been gained if required? The lawful basis conditions under GDPR will be Article 6 (c) legal obligation and (e) public task, therefore (a) consent is not required. Furthermore, where  Care Act 2014 – relevant sections include s.1 and s.6 The R&R Project will also cover young people aged up to 25 years. The Care Act allows the sharing of adult information with care and support needs to keep them safe from abuse and neglect. It is aimed at people with care and support needs who may be in vulnerable circumstances and at risk of abuse or neglect. In these cases, local services must work together to spot those at risk and take steps to protect them. The Act aims to create a legal framework so key organisations and individuals with responsibility for Adult Safeguarding can agree on how they must work together and what roles they must play to keep adults at risk safe. There are additional duties in the Care and Support Statutory Guidance , which sits beneath Care Act.  Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 – relevant sections include those under Part 4, Part 5 and Part 9 This Act provides a framework to address criminal activity which falls under anti-social behaviour to provide better protection for victims and communities.  Crime & Disorder Act 1998– relevant sections include s.115 The Act makes provision for preventing crime and disorder, this gives power to disclose information to specified relevant authorities where the disclosure is necessary or expedient for the purposes of the Act. Statutory guidance:  Pan London Child and Adult Protection Procedures Provide statutory duties which allow organisations to process and share information to better safeguard vulnerable adults and children through a multi-agency approach.  Working Together to Safeguard Children 2018 This is statutory guidance that allows the sharing of adult data for the benefit of the child as well as the sharing of children’s data. It states that local authorities, working with partner organisations and agencies, have specific duties to safeguard and promote the welfare of all children in their area. Children may be vulnerable to neglect and abuse or exploitation from within their family and from individuals they come across in their day-today lives. These threats can take a variety of different forms, including: sexual, physical and emotional abuse; neglect; exploitation by criminal gangs and organised crime groups; trafficking; online abuse; sexual exploitation and the influences of extremism leading to radicalisation. Whatever the form of abuse or neglect, practitioners should put the needs of children first when determining what action to take. The actual disclosure/sharing of any personal data under this ISA must be conducted within the framework of other relevant legislation and guidance including:  General Data Protection Regulation 2016  Data Protection Act 2018  Human Rights Act 1998  Common Law Duty of Confidentiality  Caldicott Principles  The Freedom of Information Act 2000 . Redundant data is disposed of securely and using formal procedures and compliance with the standard guidelines . What are the procedures for dealing with a breach of the agreement – notifying and investigating breaches The Brent form will be used and sent to the other effected data controller and sent within 24 hours to relevant effected parties All signatories will maintain robust data breach detection, investigation and internal reporting procedures and follow the guidance of the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). If a signatory has a data breach (or suspects a data breach in another signatory organisation) which relates to the information being shared under this agreement, it will:  inform the parties affected by the breach as soon as there is awareness of a breach and Brent Rescue and Response Project Team immediately identifying any urgent remedial actions required that might affect other parties  liaise with the other parties as appropriate to take steps to establish the likelihood and severity of the resulting risk to affected data subjects including the risk of physical, material or non-material damage to individuals such as loss of control over their personal data or limitation of their rights, discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, unauthorised reversal of pseudonymisation, damage to reputation, loss of confidentiality of personal data protected by professional secrecy or any other significant economic or social disadvantage to the natural person concerned.  identify whether it is likely that there will be such a risk to data subject’s rights and freedoms, and notify all affected Parties  where the incident meets the criteria, notify the ICO (within 72 hours where feasible) and, where appropriate, inform those individuals affected without undue delay. In all cases the signatory will keep full written records of any data breach, its investigation, the remedial steps taken and the reasons for such steps. All parties affected by a data breach will share with other signatories a lessons learned analysis of the cause and effects of reportable data breaches and will share with all partners at the next R&R Strategic Governance Group. It is noted that each party, as data controller, is individually liable for any penalty imposed on it by the ICO and for any loss or damage recovered against it by whatever means by any person in connection with a data breach. Each party is also responsible for the actions of any data processors that they engage with in relation to a breach. . What date will the information be shared? Initial date must be later that the date of the signatures below and should give an indication of subsequent dates for regular sharing. During the 3-year duration of the project which is between 2018/2019 – /2021. The project is scheduled to end in March 2021. . Information Sharing Protocol Facilitating information sharing between Brent Council, Rescue and Response partners and all London Boroughs, in order to contribute to the identification of young people being exploited through County Lines, and the identification of risk to the young people linked to the Rescue and Response project Title & Version Purpose specific information sharing protocol between the various partners of the Brent Rescue and Response Project (Pan London) and all London Boroughs Author Brent Local Authority Organisation London Borough of Brent Summary/Purpose Joint Data Controller data sharing. There are various acts of parliament which provide the legal power to share information in the right circumstance. This protocol formalises how information will be shared between the various partners of the Rescue and Response Project and all London Boroughs. The project covers any young people who live in London and have been identified as being exploited through County Lines. Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk Inter-agency information sharing protocol Rescue and Response County Lines Project Version 1 – October 2018 Owner: Information Governance Group Review Date: October 2018 Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk Introduction This protocol is an agreement between the following parties to share personal information held on police and local authority databases on a regular basis. This document is not a legally binding document. It aims to provide the basis for an agreement between the agencies and other organisations engaged in the Rescue and Response project to facilitate and govern the efficient, effective and secure sharing of good quality information. It sets out: The principles underpinning information sharing The general purposes for information sharing The responsibilities and commitments of partners to this agreement The arrangements for monitoring and review This protocol aligns with all other protocols to which agencies may already be signatories and does not in any way supersede those existing agreements. It is not intended that this document be definitive or exhaustive, it is recognised that as policy develops and implementation arrangements mature, this protocol will need to be reviewed and amended in light of new information sharing requirements to ensure that it is ‘fit for purpose’. As this protocol aims to provide a set of guiding principles for information sharing within the context of the Rescue and Response project to which partners can sign up, its purpose is not to be specific. It is a key principle of this agreement that this protocol should be underpinned by a series of specific data sharing agreements that detail the specific data/information sharing requirements between agencies. Policy context The Rescue and Response project will develop and deliver a support service for young people who are vulnerable and caught up in county lines drug distribution networks across London. This issue brings together gangs, national policing strategy, CSE, trafficking, exploitation and vulnerability; underpinned by a complex range of social and structural disadvantage. The need has been identified but is so far only partly understood and sporadically mapped, with support models untested at any scale. This project will be the first county lines support service that operates at scale - pan London and for three years. The project includes both support providers and intelligence analysis working together. It is led by a coalition of London boroughs (Brent, Islington, Tower Hamlets and Lewisham) with support from Metropolitan Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk Police Service special commands and the all London boroughs and highly experienced London based gangs’ agencies. In order for the development of the Rescue and Response project to be successful, it is essential that all agencies and organisations engaged in its development and implementation are empowered and committed to share good quality and relevant information in a responsible and secure way. This agreement deals with the need to share personal information in order to identify young people from London who are being exploited through County Lines, to then monitor them, support them by referring to voluntary agencies, and possibly conduct enforcement action against those linked to County Lines. This work will take place as part of the Rescue and Response project. It seeks to fulfil the aims and ambitions outlined in the MOPAC Police and Crime Plan for multiple agencies to: work together to keep children and young people safe, prevent violence against women and girls, reduce reoffending and repeat victimisation as well as enabling the Community Safety Partnership to meet its Statutory Obligations. It is intended to focus partnership activity on identifying and supporting young people from London who are being exploited through county lines, as well as targeting those offenders who are linked to county lines exploitation. Information will be shared in order to make informed decisions about the young people referred to the Rescue and Response project and which agency will provide direct support to those young people. Partner agencies will pool their information together regarding the young people identified as being exploited. The list of young people identified and referred will be: shared with the London borough they reside in, or come from; identified for support either through the Rescue and Response project, or alternative borough based interventions; an assessment made as to their level of engagement with partners and the most appropriate agency provide support intervention. This exchange of information will continue as the young people are supported by the partners of this multi-agency scheme. This will be an ongoing process as young people’s risk increases, move geographically, and where relevant, come out of prison. This will mean that there will always be young people who are being considered for the project, move within the project and face removal from the project. Information shared through the course of a young person being identified and referred to the Rescue and Response project will allow the partnership to: (a) Gain a complete picture of a young person’s support needs, risks, and their engagement with support services, in order to inform choices about further support and or enforcement activity. (b) Increase in number of young people identified as being exploited across London Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk (c) Increased engagement with services for those young people referred and engaged. (d) Better understanding of County Lines and peer and criminal networks associated (e) Increase in number of Young People identified as being at risk of county lines exploitation (f) Increased knowledge of the risk for young people associated with county lines/criminal networks (g) Increased feelings of safety and reduced feelings of vulnerability (h) Monitor their ongoing progress and engagement with support services and the outcomes of any enforcement activity. (i) Ensure that partners have the most up to date information when dealing with young people identified and referred. (j) Ensure that partners have the most up to date information when risk assessing staff encounters with young people. (k) Ensure effective targeting of support services, intervention programmes and enforcement activity. The aims and objectives of the Rescue and Response Project is to provide effective support to young people from London being exploited through County Lines programme, and identify young people earlier, in order to:  Reduce crime  Safeguard young people earlier  Reduction in recorded criminal behaviour of the young people referred  Increase in number of Young People identified as being exploited  Increased engagement with services  Better understanding of the problem and networks  Increase in number of Young people identified as being at risk of county lines exploitation  Reduce reoffending,  Make safer communities,  Improve public confidence in the criminal justice system, The information sharing under this agreement will allow partners to provide the best range of services to the young people whilst addressing any continuing offending or safeguarding concerns. The relevance of the scope of the protocol should be considered as part of a regular monitoring and review process. Purposes for sharing information Under the terms of this agreement information may be shared for any purpose that supports the development of the Rescue and Response project and that has been agreed within a specific information sharing agreement. In general, information sharing will be required to support the development and operation of the Rescue and Response project. Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk Key principles: The Partner Organisations recognise that many services cannot be effectively delivered without the exchange of Personal Information across key public sector, private and voluntary organisations. In signing up to this Protocol the signatories agree and commit to the following principles: . This protocol aims to align with individual partner agency statutory, legal and common law duties. . This agreement is to be entered into alongside any existing protocols, procedures, policies and guidance to which the partner already adheres and does not supersede them. . This protocol will be underpinned by individual data sharing agreements that will govern data sharing transactions between partners. . Information will only be used for the purposes stated in this protocol, and as detailed in individual information sharing agreements. . Partner agencies comply with the requirements of the Data Protection Act and in particular the data protection principles. . Partner agencies support, endorse and promote the accurate, timely, secure and confidential sharing of information for the purposes stated in this protocol. . Where it is agreed that it is necessary to share personal information, it will be shared only on a ‘need to know’ basis and this will be detailed in the individual information sharing agreements. All other information will be statistical and aggregated. . Personal and sensitive information will only be shared under this agreement where there is a statutory power to do so and the conditions for processing as determined in the Data Protection Act 2018 can be met. . Agencies agree to ensure that data sharing takes place in accordance with their legal, statutory and common law duties and that responsibility for ensuring that they have adequate notifications, privacy notices, retention schedules, policies, procedures and guidance to do so remains with them. . Signatories agree to the roles and responsibilities set out in section 9 . All information shared shall be classified according to the Government Security Classifications Policy (GSCP). The handling and access of the data shall comply with the requirements of this classification. . In the event of a Security Incident, the responsible Partner Organisation should immediately inform the Governing Group and all other affected Partner Organisations (usually the disclosing Partner Organisation(s)) with as many details as known at that time and regularly update the relevant Partner Organisations and Governing Group thereafter, including any subsequent investigation report or remedial actions. Any affected Partner Organisation will Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk then pass on the information in accordance with incident reporting procedures within their own organisation if appropriate. . Partner Organisations will follow the decision tree at Annex C. . Information shared pursuant to this Protocol may not be shared with any other organisation not a signatory to this Protocol without prior consent of the relevant Partner Organisation and/or data subject. . Each Partner Organisation shall comply with individual rights as defined under the Data Protection Act 2018, Freedom of Information Act 2005 and the Human Rights Act 1998. . All information will be supplied in line with the relevant standards for information quality and security. The systems and technical measures used by each Partner Organisation for the sharing of personal information shall be specified in any information sharing agreement. . Each Partner Organisation shall minimise the use of paper in sharing and storing information. Information in transit shall be secure and encrypted. Use of removable storage devices shall be prohibited. Paper in transit shall only be undertaken if adequate safeguard are in place and the information is minimised. . Use of public WI-FI shall be prohibited. . If a Partner Organisation is aware of a material inaccuracy or omission in information that it shares under an Information Sharing Agreement, the Partner Organisation must inform the recipient of that inaccuracy or omission. . Each Partner Organisation will nominate a person as a key contact to deal with queries and requests for information under this Protocol. . Each Partner Organisation is responsible for putting into place effective procedures to address complaints about data sharing and subject access requests relating directly to this Protocol. Information about these procedures should be made available to data subjects. Any complaints about data sharing relating directly to this Protocol should be directed promptly to the Data Protection Officer or Information Governance Manager of the relevant Partner Organisation. Conclusion This protocol proposes a consistent approach to the sharing of information between partner agencies for the purposes of developing and implementing the Rescue and Response project. All partners need to be able to balance the conflicting demands between the need to share information with other agencies and the requirement to maintain confidentiality. These conflicting demands are acknowledged by this protocol which provides a basis for partners to be confident that where information is shared it will Version 1 - October 2018 www.brent.gov.uk be done in a consistent, responsible and secure way for the purpose of safeguarding young people involved with the Rescue and Response project. Information Sharing Procedure relating to the London Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker Between The Greater London Authority and London Borough of Camden . This is a purpose-specific Information Sharing Procedure made under the Overarching Information Sharing Protocol between the Greater London Authority (GLA) and London Borough of Camden. . This Procedure shall be entered into by the specific business units/legal entities within the GLA and London Borough of Camden that are responsible for the purpose specific activity to which the information sharing relates. . 1st April 2022 . GLA Private Rented Sector Programme Manager (Housing and Land), GLA Senior Projects Officer (Housing and Land), GLA Projects Officer (Housing and Land). . Primary contact: Operations Managers (Enforcement team and Rogue Landlord team) Secondary contact: Principal EHO (Enforcement team) Purpose . The Mayor has committed to creating a London Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker (RLAC) on the GLA website, containing details of landlords and letting agents who have acted unlawfully and thus undergone enforcement action by participating partners (London boroughs or the London Fire Brigade). . A limited range of details will be accessible to the public, and a wider range, which will include historic convictions and other enforcement activity, to participating partners and the GLA. The data sharing will be a one-way transfer of data relating to landlord and letting agent enforcement action from the participating partner to the GLA. . There are effectively three tiers of user rights to the RLAC. The first is open to the general public on the GLA website, the second is “read-only” access for participating partners to allow officers to view additional enforcement actions and historic convictions, and the third provides upload and editing rights for a small number of officers from the participating partner organisation. Benefits . The benefits of the RLAC can be outlined according to the following beneficiaries: . GLA It will enable the Mayor to send a clear message to landlords and letting agents acting unlawfully across London that successful enforcement actions for relevant offences will result in them being named publicly, making it harder for them to operate ‘under the radar’. . Participating partners It will support London boroughs and the London Fire Brigade in their enforcement efforts through information sharing and increased awareness amongst renters, landlords and letting agents of the work that boroughs are doing locally to crack down on criminal behaviour. . General public It will provide renters with a readily accessible means of checking whether a landlord or agent they are considering renting a property from has faced enforcement action for a housing related offence. It will seek to ensure the private rented housing market operates in a fairer and more transparent way, and that tenants are protected from exploitation by unscrupulous landlords and letting agents. The Report a Rogue Tool sits alongside the RLAC to make reporting a landlord or agent to their borough clearer and easier for tenants. Reliance on personal information . The sharing of limited personal data relating to enforcement action is necessary for the RLAC to achieve its stated aims. Wholly anonymised or pseudonymised data would not support London boroughs in their efforts to crack down on landlords and letting agents acting unlawfully, nor would it enable the public to check whether their landlord or agent has faced enforcement action. Categories of information . The following categories of data will be shared with the public for landlord entries: landlord name (and ‘also known as’ or associated names, for instance company names) home address of landlord – street name and first four digits of postcode only address of rental property(ies) associated with the offence name of enforcement authority criminal conviction offence date of conviction expiry date of conviction court where conviction took place value of fine conditional discharge offence date of conditional discharge expiry date of conditional discharge court where conditional discharge was awarded details of enforcement notices issued by London Fire Brigade details of prohibition notices issued by London Fire Brigade civil penalty notice offence date of civil penalty issue . The following categories of data will be shared with the public for letting agents: trading name ownership details (Ltd co, partnership, sole trader) names of principal officers registered office address other branches website membership of a trade body membership of a redress scheme address of rental property associated with the offence (where appropriate) name of enforcement authority criminal conviction offence date of conviction expiry date of conviction court where conviction took place value of fine conditional discharge offence date of conditional discharge expiry date of conditional discharge court where condition discharge was awarded trading standards civil penalty notice offence date of civil penalty issue details of expulsion from a redress scheme . As well as the information listed above, other enforcement activity taken against landlords and letting agents will be shared on the non-public part of the RLAC, including simple cautions. . A list of relevant offences can be found at Annex 2. This list may be subject to change in consultation with all participating partners, for example when legislation changes. . Records on the RLAC from the same landlord or letting agent will be linked to demonstrate repeat offending. This link will be displayed on the public and nonpublic part of the RLAC. Links between two or more records originating from a single partner can be authorised by the partner themselves. Links from two or more different participating partners will be suggested by the RLAC, based on records containing the same (or very similar) names and home address of landlord, or trading name and office address of letting agent. The participating partners will then agree amongst themselves whether they are satisfied that this is the same person or organisation and will then approve or deny the link based on the details of the record. All partners associated with the entries will need to approve the link in order for it go forward to publication. . Any data which relates to an identified or identifiable natural person, either on its own or in conjunction with any other data held by either party, constitutes personal data as defined under Article 4(1) of the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), . For the purpose of this project, a company acting as a landlord or letting agent will be treated in the same way as an individual. . Any data consisting of information as to the commission or alleged commission of any offence by the data subject or any proceedings for any offence committed or alleged to have been committed by the data subject, the disposal of such proceedings or the sentence of any court in such proceedings, constitutes ‘data relating to criminal convictions and offences’. The processing of personal data about criminal convictions or offences must have a lawful basis under Article 6 of UK GDPR and either legal authority or official authority for the processing under Article 10 of UK GDPR Source(s) of the information . The data will be sourced from databases or computer systems held by each London borough and the London Fire Brigade. Frequency . Uploads onto the RLAC will take place no longer than ten working days following the enforcement outcome, subject to notification by the borough’s legal department. . Inaccurate personal data will be corrected no later than five working days after the inaccuracy has been identified. Legal powers to share the information . London boroughs have a range of powers (contained in the Housing Acts and other legislation) relating to the attainment of housing standards in the private rented sector (including overcrowding, housing conditions, houses in multiple occupation and the selective licensing of private landlords). Failures by private landlords to attain minimum standards and compliance in these areas can be met by enforcement action by the boroughs and lead to criminal sanctions. A list of relevant offences can be found at Annex 2. . Local authorities also have a general power of competence, enabling them to do anything that an individual may do (Localism Act 2011). They also have a power to do anything which is calculated to facilitate, or is conducive or incidental to, the discharge of any of their functions (Local Government Act 1972). . Section 17 Crime and Disorder Act 1998 requires the London boroughs to exercise their various functions with due regard to the likely effect of the exercise of those functions on, and the need to do all that it reasonably can to prevent a) crime and disorder in their area (including anti-social and other behaviour adversely affecting the local environment); and b) the misuse of drugs, alcohol and other substances in their area; and c) re-offending in their area. . The participation of the London boroughs in the RLAC is consistent with, and incidental to, its various housing powers. Participation in a scheme to bring to the public’s attention the action taken to tackle poor standards in the private rented sector and the sanctions applied to landlords and agents acting unlawfully, will serve to raise awareness, act as a deterrent and contribute to the improvement of housing conditions in the private rented sector. It thus demonstrates that regard has been paid to the need to prevent crime, disorder and behaviour adversely affecting the local environment. . The RLAC initiative falls within the Mayor’s power in section 30 of the Greater London Authority Act 1999 (the ‘GLA Act’) to act on behalf of the GLA to do anything which he considers will further the promotion of economic and social development in Greater London. Inclusion of Housing and Planning Act Civil Penalties on the RLAC . The Housing and Planning Act (‘HPA’) 2016 introduced civil penalties of up to £30,000 for certain specified housing offences under the Housing Act 2004 and breaches of banning orders under the HPA. These civil penalties are designed to be an alternative to prosecution. . Various boroughs have instructed the GLA to upload HPA civil penalties and trading standards civil penalties of £500 or more to the public tier of the RLAC. These boroughs are listed in the RLAC policies and procedures document which can be found on the Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker website at: www.london.gov.uk/rogue-landlord-checker. The boroughs in question will continue to use their own discretion to decide which cases should be uploaded to the RLAC, in line with their own policies and procedures. General Data Protection Regulation Statutory data processing conditions . Processing of personal data under this scheme must adhere to the ‘principles relating to processing personal data’ under Article 5 of UK GDPR. The first of these principles provides that personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner. . The processing of personal data is only considered to be lawful if a legal basis under Article 6(1) applies. The processing of data relating to criminal convictions and offences must meet the requirement in Article 10 of UK GDPR. Article 6 legal basis . The following legal basis under Article 6(1) applies to the processing of personal data: (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller . Section 8(c) of the 2018 Act prescribes that Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR – processing of personal data that is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of the controller’s official authority – includes processing of personal data that is necessary for the exercise of a function conferred on a person by an enactment or rule of law. Section 8(c) of the 2018 Act has been considered to apply by virtue of the legislation detailed in paragraphs 23 to 27 of this procedure. . Processing of data is considered to be necessary to help ensure that the private rented housing market operates in a fairer and more transparent way, and that tenants are protected from exploitation by unscrupulous landlords and letting agents. . Reliance on Article 6(1)(e) involves a test of necessity which requires a balance to be struck between the objectives of the Checker and the impact on those whose information is disclosed. Subject to the protections afforded by representations procedure in Annex 1, and by committing not to publicise spent convictions, the parties agree that processing will not amount to an unreasonable or unwarranted interference. Article 10 considerations . The processing of data relating to criminal convictions and offences meets the requirement under Article 10 of UK GDPR by virtue of the conditions listed in parts , 2 or 3 of Schedule 1 of the 2018 Act. The processing of data relating to criminal convictions and offences for the Checker will comply with paragraph 6(2)(a) of Schedule 1 of the 2018 Act: processing.. is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest… and the exercise of a function conferred on a person by an enactment or rule of law. The legislation detailed in paragraphs 23 to 27 of this procedure describes the applicable enactments. . The processing of data relating to criminal convictions and offences in this manner is considered to be a matter of substantial public interest for the following reasons a) London’s private rented sector is an important part of the London housing market, and the number of private renters continues to rise. At the same time, there is no easy way for tenants to find out about offences committed by a prospective landlord or agent so that they can make an informed choice. Addressing this information gap in relation to renting property in London is deemed to be matter of public interest. b) The processing allows London Boroughs and the London Fire Brigade to share information in order to deliver more targeted enforcement activity and to assist in cross-borough enforcement against rogue landlords and letting agents. c) Given the importance of the private rented sector within London’s housing market, the proposed processing contributes to meeting that interest, in a very significant way, not in a marginal or trivial way. There is a rational connection between the processing and the relevant substantial public interest. d) The processing directly meets the information gap explained above in relation to the London private rented sector. Law enforcement processing . To the extent that the processing of personal data under this scheme is by a competent authority for law enforcement purposes (as defined in section 31 of the Act), the processing meets the requirements of the six data protection principles in section 34 of the 2018 Act. In relation to the requirements of section of the 2018 Act, the processing is lawful since it is necessary for the performance of a task carried out for law enforcement purposes by a competent authority. Compatibility with original purpose for which personal data was captured . Data regarding enforcement action taken against landlords and agents is collected as part of the Fire Brigade and London boroughs’ work to protect tenants and improve conditions in the private rented sector. The RLAC is therefore compatible with this purpose in that its principle objectives are to empower tenants to check their landlord or agent’s history and deter unlawful practice in the sector. Fair processing requirements . To support compliance with the first data processing principles under Article 5(1)(a) of UK GDPR and meet the aforementioned conditions under schedules 2 and 3 of the DPA requirements of Articles 13 and 14 of UK GDPR – the provision of ‘fair processing’ information to data subjects - the GLA will write to the landlord or agent on behalf of London Borough of Camden. prior to his/her data being displayed on the RLAC. The GLA will send this letter within two working days of the entry being added to the RLAC holding area. . This will notify the data subject (landlord or letting agent) about the data which will be processed on behalf the borough or Fire Brigade and manner in which it will be processed. The letter will detail the categories of data (from paragraphs 11 – 13) which will be ultimately made accessible to the public, in addition to the data processed on the non-public part of the RLAC. . This notification will also set out timescales for the processing of their information and inform the data subject or agent of their right to make representations against the processing of their personal data in the manner described and update any inaccurate or incorrect data. . The representation process (see Annex 1) will cover the assessment of any complaints made by the data subject and submissions concerning inaccurate or incorrect data. This will ensure that the rights of the data subject are considered at all times and balanced against the legitimate interests and legal obligations that facilitate the processing of their personal data in this manner. . The GLA is required to keep clear and auditable records of the notification and representation processes on behalf of London Borough of Camden. to ensure fair processing of any personal data on behalf of the borough and demonstrate compliance with the appropriate data processing conditions outlined above. . The above procedure does not override a data subject’s right at any time to exercise their right to rectification (Article 16 of UK GDPR), to erasure (Article 17 of UK GDPR), to restriction of processing (Article 18 of UK GDPR) or to object (Article 21 of UK GDPR). If the GLA is in receipt of any such notice they shall pass this to the borough or Fire Brigade immediately upon receipt. Data Controller status of the receiving party . London Borough of Camden is the controller of all the personal data covered by this Procedure and is responsible for ensuring it is processed fairly and lawfully and in accordance with the principles of UK GDPR and the 2018 Act. . On receipt of any personal data under this Procedure, the GLA shall become a processor of that data and will only process that personal data in accordance with this Information Sharing Procedure and the Data Processing Agreement at Annex to this Procedure and for no other purposes. The GLA will at all times ensure that any of its staff with access to the RLAC are trained in the applicable data protection law in force at that time. The GLA will ensure that appropriate technical and organisational measures shall be taken against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of or damage to personal or sensitive personal data on the RLAC when exercising its functions as data processor. . Although the GLA is registered as a controller in its own right for projects outside of the scope of this agreement, the London Borough of Camden shall remain the controller in respect of the data for this project and continue to process the data for their own purposes. Human Rights Act 1998 . Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights prescribes that everyone has a right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence. There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety or the economic wellbeing of the country, for the prevention of disorder or crime, for the protection of health or morals or for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. . The sharing of personal data under this Procedure will comply with Article 8 as it is: In pursuit of a legitimate aim: The Mayor of London has a general power to do anything that will promote economic and social development, and environmental improvement in London. The Rogue landlord and agent Checker would be one way of achieving this by seeking to ensure the private rented housing market operates in a fairer and more transparent way, and that tenants are protected from exploitation by unscrupulous landlords and letting agents. Proportionate: In each case, the information shared will be proportionate for the purpose - the minimum information necessary for the purpose will be transferred and no more. Appropriate and necessary to a democratic society: Promoting social development, making London’s communities a better place to live, and protecting tenants from criminal landlords and letting agents are all activities appropriate to a democratic society. Each individual will have the opportunity to correct any inaccuracy prior to publication and to explain whether there is a reason why it would not be in the public interest to disclose their convictions (see Annex 1). Common law Duty of Confidentiality . In this case, there are no circumstances that would create an expectation of confidentiality on the part of any individuals whose data is shared between the partners for the agreed purposes. Crime and Disorder Act 1998 . Section 17 of the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 has been considered and without prejudice to any other obligation imposed on it, the RLAC is compatible with its various functions with due regard to the likely effect of exercising those functions to do all that it reasonably can to prevent, crime and disorder in its area (including antisocial and other behaviour adversely affecting the local environment). . The use of the RLAC will provide valuable intelligence to boroughs in regulating and investigating landlords operating across borough boundaries. Landlords acting unlawfully are directly linked to high levels of anti-social behaviour, poor property management and enviro-crimes in the private rented sector; the RLAC will protect tenants and prospective tenants from these landlords thus preventing further crime and disorder. . Information subject to this sharing agreement will be shared via the RLAC whereby both London Borough of Camden and the GLA will have mutual access to information once entered on to the system, subject to the appropriate access controls. . London Borough of Camden will input existing convictions into an excel spreadsheet containing mandatory fields and optional fields. This document will then be uploaded as a CSV file onto the RLAC. Following upload onto the RLAC, the entries will remain in the holding area whilst the GLA notifies the data subject (see Annex for details on the holding area and notification). Subsequent entries will be added using a manual entry online form. Access to the information shared . RLAC users on the non-public tier will have one of three types of access: superusers, viewing and editing, or viewing-only. a) Super-users will be able to view all published information held on each entry, upload new entries, edit existing entries, make decisions regarding representations, and manage the viewing-only and viewing and editing users for their borough. There will be two super-users per borough. b) Viewing and editing users will be able to log into the RLAC and view all published information held on each entry. They will be able to add new entries to the RLAC and edit existing entries. c) Viewing-only users will be able to log into the RLAC and view all published information held on each entry. This user type will be given to most enforcement officers at each borough. . At the GLA, the following roles will have super-user access: Private Rented Sector Manager, Housing and Land Directorate Senior Projects Officer, Housing and Land Directorate Project Officer, Housing and Land Directorate . At London Borough of Camden the following officers (job roles) will require superuser access: . Operations Manager . Principal EHO . User accounts for London Borough of Camden employees will be created, deleted and managed by the super-user. Each user will have one account, and there will be strictly no sharing of log ins. User accounts of all type must be kept up to date, for example when officers resign the account should be deleted promptly. Regular or routine onward disclosures by the recipient of the Information . The GLA is in ongoing discussions with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) about the development of a national criminal landlord database as provided for by the Housing and Planning Act 2016. The MHCLG database will request from boroughs a very similar set of data to that which is to be included in the RLAC. . If agreement is secured from MHCLG, London Borough of Camden in principle authorises the GLA to act as an intermediary between the two systems, effectively passing on the data from the London RLAC to the national database, on behalf of the data controller (London Borough of Camden). The GLA will pass on any data which is eligible under the conditions for the database set out in the Housing and Planning Act 2016. Further engagement with all boroughs concerned would need to be undertaken and written agreement obtained prior to any data being transferred. Unplanned or ad hoc onward disclosures of the Information . There will be no unplanned disclosure without prior consent from the relevant data controller. Each participating partner will only be required to notify the original source of the Information where a secondary disclosure has been made to a third party for a purpose unconnected to those provided for in this Information Sharing Procedure. Retention period(s) . Personal data will only be retained for the minimum length of time necessary to achieve the specific aims of each function of the RLAC. First tier public view a) Civil penalties of £500 or more will remain publicly viewable for up to 12 months after the enforcement action date. Prior to 1 July 2021, the enforcement action date was taken as the date that the final civil penalty notice was served. Information as to how the enforcement action date is currently calculated may be found by referring to the RLAC policies and procedures document which can be found on the Rogue Landlord and Agent Checker website at: www.london.gov.uk/rogue-landlord-checker. b) Criminal convictions will remain accessible to the public until the date at which the conviction becomes spent. The vast majority of landlord and letting agent convictions will result in a fine, meaning that the conviction becomes spent after months. c) In rare cases, a prosecution may result in a custodial sentence, meaning the conviction will last longer than 12 months in line with the provisions of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012. Each new entry on the RLAC will be set to a default removal data of 12 months following the date of conviction. It will be possible for the data controller to override this in instances of a custodial sentence. d) Enforcement and prohibition notices from the London Fire Brigade will have a retention period of three years, mirroring the retention policy for the London Fire Brigade website. e) The London Borough of Camden can reduce the retention period for their entries if this is considered appropriate. Second tier borough view f) Entries will remain accessible to the user groups specified in section 53 for a maximum of ten years, at which point they will be automatically deleted from the RLAC. This retention period is considered to be appropriate because it reflects the period over which the information remains relevant and useful to the boroughs for enforcement purposes. The RLAC will default the deletion date to ten years, but London Borough of Camden is able to override this if they feel a shorter retention period is appropriate. In no circumstances can the retention period exceed the maximum set out in this procedure for each entry. Secure storage and destruction of the information . Further to the arrangements discussed elsewhere in this Information Sharing Procedure, and those specified in the Data Processing Agreement at Annex 3, the user guide developed to cover use of the shared RLAC will detail specific access controls, process or other security measure that will be implemented to protect the information held on the RLAC and the integrity of those systems in accordance with the guidance issued by the Information Commissioner’s Office. . From April 2022 data will not be transferred outside the United Kingdom at any point and the RLAC will reside on servers based in the UK. . Access to the non-public RLAC will be restricted by IP address. Only IP address from participating partners (the GLA, London Fire Brigade and London boroughs) will be given access. . All data will be encrypted in transit. In the instance where a spreadsheet is used for transfer, only a CSV file will be used. . The RLAC will be penetration tested annually by the GLA, and results will be shared with London Borough of Camden. . All passwords for the RLAC will comply with NCSC latest guidelines. . All user access and actions on the RLAC will be logged for auditing purposes. Notification and rectification of errors in the information . Information shared by London Borough of Camden is subject to procedures and validations to ensure data quality at the point it is originally input/entered into its own systems. . On becoming aware of incorrect data, London Borough of Camden will correct their record on the RLAC as soon as possible and no later than five working days after becoming aware of that error. . The GLA, as the receiving authority and data processor, will not amend any personal data provided by London Borough of Camden without explicit instruction from London Borough of Camden, as the data controller. . Annex 1 to this procedure details the representations process whereby a landlord or agent can request rectification of any inaccuracies. Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FoIA) . The GLA and London Borough of Camden are both public authorities for the purposes of the FoIA. This means that any information held by either the GLA or London Borough of Camden, is accessible by the public on written request, subject to certain limited exemptions. . The GLA and London Borough of Camden shall demonstrate a commitment to openness and transparency regarding information sharing arrangements in accordance with this Procedure and the Overarching Information Sharing Protocol between both parties, subject to any limitations posed by security or confidentiality requirements. . In the event that an information access request is received relating to information covered by this procedure, both parties agree to notify one another within five working days following receipt of the request and to consult with the other in line with the Code of Practice as implemented by section 45 of FoIA. . For the purposes of information held on the shared RLAC, information is only considered to be “held for the purposes of FoIA” by the party which was responsible for the original record being entered on to the shared RLAC – read-only access to information entered on to the RLAC by another public authority does not constitute “information held” for the purposes of FoIA. . Any non-public personal data considered in response to a Freedom of Information Act request should be anonymised and withheld as appropriate under section 40(2) of that Act. Subject Access Requests (SAR) . Article 15 of UK GDPR provides the right to an individual to request access to personal data of which they are the subject. This also includes the right to be told the purposes for which their data is being processed and with whom their data is being shared. . London Borough of Camden is the controller of all the personal data covered by this Procedure and is responsible for handling and considering any Subject Access Request made in relation to any personal data for which they are the controller. . If the GLA receives a Subject Access Request that relates solely to the personal data held on the RLAC, the GLA will notify the London Borough of Camden (as the controller of that personal data) within five working days of receiving such a request, and promptly notify the data subject making the request that they should re-submit their SAR to London Borough of Camden. . On receipt of any SAR, London Borough of Camden will notify the GLA within five working days if the request covers any data or information processed by the GLA on behalf of London Borough of Camden which cannot otherwise be accessed via the RLAC. . The GLA must provide London Borough of Camden with any information or data which is subject to a SAR that is processed on behalf of London Borough of Camden as soon as possible and no later than ten working days following receipt of an instruction from the London Borough of Camden. . The GLA will remain a controller in its own right for other information and personal data processed outside of this agreement and the Data Processing Agreement at Annex 3. This agreement will not affect the ability of the GLA to process its own personal data for its own purposes in line with the GLA’s obligations and legal requirements. . The obligation for the GLA (as a processor) to provide London Borough of Camden (as a controller) with personal data processed on their behalf under the terms of this agreement does not extend to include any other personal data that might be held by the GLA for its own purposes outside of this agreement in a situation where the GLA also holds different personal data on the same data subject for a different purpose. . This Procedure does not require adherence to any other conditions. London Borough of Camden and the GLA agree to inform the other party should any new applicable conditions arise. . Examples of loss or unauthorised disclosure may include: Accidental loss or damage to Information Damage or loss of information by means of malicious software/hacking Deliberate or knowing disclosure of Information to a person not entitled to receive it. . The designated points of contact are responsible for notifying the other party in the event of loss or unauthorised disclosures of data within 24 hours of the event. . The designated points of contact will also be responsible for notifying other relevant internal departments. In the case of London Borough of Camden, this will be the Data Protection Officer at and the GLA it will be the GLA Data Protection Officer. . This Information Sharing Procedure will be reviewed as and when changes to information sharing activities arise, or where revised legislation or national guidance necessitates a review or every two years as necessary. . Both the GLA and London Borough of Camden reserve the right to review the Procedure at any time in order to respond to any serious incidents related to the data transfer in this project. . This procedure shall only be varied or amended with the written agreement of both parties. . This Procedure may be terminated in the following situations: a) Immediately in the event of a serious breach of the terms of the Overarching Information Sharing Protocol or of this Procedure; or b) By one month’s notice by either party. . Upon termination of the agreement, all records will be destroyed from the RLAC by the GLA and the landlord or agents concerned will be notified. Upon termination, London Borough of Camden’s access to the RLAC will be revoked. The GLA remains the owner of the RLAC but has no claim over the data belonging to the former participating partner. This Procedure is signed on behalf of: Greater London Authority
