Appendix C: Applicable legislation Note that all legislation can be found at www.legislation.gov.uk Legislation Main purpose of Legislation Counter-Terrorism and Section 26 of the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015 (the Act) places Security Act 2015 and a duty on certain bodies (“specified authorities” listed in Schedule 6 to the Counter Terrorism and Act), in the exercise of their functions, to have “due regard to the need to Border Security Act 2019 prevent people from being drawn into terrorism”. (Prevent Duty Guidance for England and Wales 2015). Section 36 provides for processing of personal data necessary for the purposes of the various Channel duties set out in the Act, the purpose being to put in place a local panel to carry out assessments and provide support for persons vulnerable to being drawn into terrorism. Section 38 (amended by CTBSA2019) requires Channel partners to co-operate with the local authority and the police in providing any relevant information to the panel so that they can effectively carry out their functions to determine whether an individual is vulnerable to being drawn into terrorism. Section 20 CTBSA 2019 amends the 2015 act to enable Police and Local authority to refer individuals for assessment by the panel if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the individual is vulnerable to being drawn into terrorism. The Localism Act 2011 General powers for Local Government to act as in any manner they believe suitable for the purposes of promoting economic, social and environmental well-being within their boundaries. Gives a legal basis under Section 8 of the DPA for this use. However, as a general power it can be challenged, and an additional legal basis is preferred. The Education Act 2002 The Education Act 2002 puts a duty on schools to exercise their functions with a view to safeguarding and promoting the welfare of children. Prevent is covered by the Education Act 2002, even though schools and colleges are subject to the Prevent duty under Section 26 of the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015. ‘Keeping Children Safe in Education’ (KCSIE) which is statutory guidance from the Department for Education issued under Section 175 of the Education Act 2002. KCSIE clearly states: protecting children from the risk of radicalisation ‘should be a part of a schools’ or colleges’ safeguarding approach’. It also says: ‘The Prevent duty should be seen as part of schools’ and colleges’ Legislation Main purpose of Legislation wider safeguarding obligations’. Gives a legal basis under Section 8 of the DPA for this use. The Children Act 2004 The Children Act 2004, as amended places duties on the police, clinical commissioning groups and the local authority to make arrangements to work together, and with other partners locally, to safeguard and promote the welfare of all children in their area. Provides a general safeguarding and welfare power giving a legal basis under Section 8 of the DPA. The Criminal Justice Act This act amended a wide range of provisions in the PACE act and provided new regulations on offence management, disclosure and trials. The regulation clarifies the process and procedure for police and their legal basis for use. The Police and Criminal This act makes the specific provision for the secretary of state to issue Evidence Act 1984 codes of practice to police with statutory effects. It provides the basis for many of the police actions in respect of matters relating to safeguarding and other matters, and as such provides their legal basis for use. The Children & Social Safeguarding partners, as defined under the Children Act 2004 (and Work Act 2017 amended by the Children and Social Work Act, 2017), have a statutory duty to work with relevant appropriate agencies within their locality to safeguard and protect children. The Mental Capacity Act Where the capacity of an individual to make a specific decision is brought into question, the Mental Capacity Act 2005 provides safeguards within a statutory framework to protect the rights of those who may not be able to make their own decisions. The Crime and Disorder s115 provides agencies and professionals with a permissive power (but not Act 1998 a legal duty) to disclose personal information lawfully where necessary or expedient for any provision of the Act, to a Chief Officer of Police, a Police Authority, Local Authorities, Probation Provider or Health Authority (or to a person acting on behalf of any of these bodies), even if they do not otherwise have a power to do so. Also places a duty on councils to formulate a strategy to reduce crime and disorder in their area and to work with police authorities to do this. Legislation Main purpose of Legislation Section 14 Offender Disclosure for Offender Management Purposes, Section 14 sets out the Management Act 2007 powers of certain bodies to share data for specified purposes which include (Disclosure for Offender • The probation purposes Management Purposes The performance of the functions relating to prisons or prisoners (inc young offender institutions and secure training centres, together with those persons detained within them); Any other purpose connected with the management of offenders (including the development or assessment of policies relating to matters connected with the management of offenders). The Care Act 2014 The Care Act 2014 is covered under the Channel Duty Guidance and stipulates local authorities are required to have Safeguarding Adults Boards in their area. These boards provide strategic leadership to the work of the local authority and partner agencies on the development of policy and practice in relation to safeguarding adults at risk. Appendix D: Information Sharing Checklist The following questions must be considered when deciding whether to share information. ● Whose information is this? ● Is there a lawful basis to share the information? Justify the purpose and identify relevant legislation that applies. ● Can information be pseudonymised or anonymised ahead of sharing? ● How have individuals been informed that the information will be shared eg via a privacy notice? Will they have the expectation that their information will be shared? Consider whether notifying the individual of the sharing may place someone at risk or prejudice a police or safeguarding investigation. ● Have any requests not to share been received and considered? ● How much information is it necessary to share in this situation? ● Is the information accurate and up to date? Has the difference between fact and opinion been stated? ● Is access to the information limited to only those who need it? Is it being given to the right person? ● Is the information being shared in a secure way? ● Has the decision to share or not share, and the rationale for the decision, been recorded?
Information Sharing Agreement In relation to: Noise Insulation Works data relating to residents in the London Borough of Camden administrative area. This individual Agreement is made between: High Speed Two (HS2) Limited (Company No. 06791686) registered office at Two Snowhill, Snow Hill Queensway, Birmingham B4 6GA (“HS2”) and The Mayor and Burgesses of the London Borough of Camden of Town Hall, Judd Street, London WC1H 9LP (“the Council”) Introduction Background This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement will share data. HS2 is undertaking, as part of the High Speed Two Project, Noise Insulation works on properties in the London Borough of Camden (LBC) administrative area. It has been identified that a limited data share between HS2 and LBC would be beneficial to ensure a collaborative approach to completion of these works. This agreement is in relation to noise insulation (NI). The parties to this Agreement are registered Data Controllers under the Data Protection Act. Both parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ensuring data quality. storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including for managing data subject rights & complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality, and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ, and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Purpose for the sharing The data sharing will allow the Sender (HS2) to provide assurance to the Recipient (LBC) regarding completion of Noise Insulation works to Camden owned properties provisionally, thereby improving project outcomes. Information relating to the individual outcomes in relation to the NI outcomes is held by contractors CSJV and more recently SCS and MDJV, because they are responsible for undertaking the installations. Although Camden has its own data from conversations with residents. HS2 and Camden have agreed to bring the data that both parties hold together and that Camden will conduct an engagement exercise with its residents later this year to close out the NI programme. As a result, HS2 is sharing the data it has accumulated whilst conducting the NI programme, with Camden. This includes the handover packs and its database (NI Master Tracker which is updated and provided to Camden on a monthly basis), including correspondence and consents/refusals. Specifically BORIS Reports or the agreed equivalent documentation are issued with a handover pack or linked to them in relation to installs. Whilst the majority of the handover packs relate to the actual installation of NI fixtures, resident acceptance/sign off or decline letter etc. there may be DPA rights based on communications between CSjv and the resident of properties where Camden are not the landlord/freeholder, hence this agreement. However, cooperation via this DSA is necessary because Camden officers need the full information concerning an individual and their circumstances to be available to them. Works carried out should be transparent, auditable and recorded in a format easy to access for all relevant parties as set out in the recommendations as part of the Golden Thread of information in the Hackitt report. Redacted information would make it difficult to understand the handover packs and mean that we start capturing the information from scratch. This will improve project outcomes by ensuring that everyone eligible for NI has been contacted, that the installs have been safely fitted in accordance with Camden and fire safety requirements and any associated risk are identified and mitigated. Other benefits include: a) Up to date information allowing a faster follow up and closing of the project b) A record of quality assurance to indemnify Camden as a landlord. c) Allows for further analysis and learning from the past evidence e.g. uncontactable residents d) gives confidence in the transparency of the NI process This Agreement has been developed to: a) Define the specific purposes for which the signatory agencies have agreed to share information:-. i. To indemnify Camden and satisfy fire/ safety liabilities: The handover packs will include a form of Boris report or a link to such, for every Camden owned property that has noise insulation installed, for all the fixtures. The report will clearly evidence in the handover packs that all works and fire stopping has been carried out in accordance with the requirements of a 3rd party accredited company e.g. Exova BM TRADA Q-Mark Fire Stopping Installation Scheme1. The Boris report will also include the before and after installation photos and clearly show warning labels confirming the fire stopping and for these not to be disturbed. ii. In order to assist Camden when residents dispute NI information, HS2 is to provide background evidence of contact with Camden residents via its officers and contractors. In addition, a record of resident decision making in relation to NI installation such as signed copies of letters refusing NI etc. This will facilitate informed conversations between Camden and its residents. iii. The data relating to all 3 fixtures (secondary glazing, mechanical ventilation and solar blinds or film) would be inputted and their individual status noted. This information will also serve to indemnify Camden against claims for compensation/prosecution if the fixtures fail or cause accident/incident/ fire spread and satisfy the legal requirements and regulations placed on Camden. The data should evidence that “all works carried out should not worsen fire safety conditions or prejudice LBC under the Regulatory reform Fire Safety Order (Article 10 Principles of Prevention). b) Set out how the parties will meet their data protection obligations as it will: The Exova BM TRADA Q-Mark fire stopping installation scheme is designed to allow installers to demonstrate that they are competent to assemble and install fire stopping products and ensure that installations have been conducted appropriately in accordance with UKAS (or equivalent nationally accredited body which is covered by the ILAC agreement) accredited test evidence and/or the manufacturer’s instructions and / or the manufacturer’s scope of certification. i) Outline the Personal and Special Category Data to be shared. ii) Set out the lawful basis conditions under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared. iii) Stipulate the roles and procedure that will support the processing. iv) Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. v) Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and agency-specific security requirements. c) Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. Legal Requirements HS2 has been designated by the Secretary of State to be the ‘nominated undertaker’, a function conferred on HS2 under the s.45 High Speed Rail (London - West Midlands) Act and s.41 High Speed Rail (West Midlands - Crewe) Act 2021. Lawful Basis For personal data the legal basis is UK GDPR Article 6(1)(e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller Use of this article requires that the Data Protection Act section 8 be satisfied. This is met by the High Speed Rail (London - West Midlands) Act 2017 and High Speed Rail (West Midlands - Crewe) Act 2021 for HS2 and the Localism Act 2011 for the Council. For special category data the legal basis is UK GDPR Article 9(2)(g): The processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest, on the basis of domestic law which shall be proportionate to the aim pursued, respect the essence of the right to data protection and provide for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject. The DPA 2018 Schedule 1, Part 2 condition met is para. 6 (statutory purposes). The processing is in the substantial public interest and necessary for the purposes of a function conferred on a person by enactment or rule of law. This sharing can be considered to be necessary for the purposes of constructing the railway, a function which has been conferred on HS2 under the High Speed Rail (London - West Midlands) Act 2017 and High Speed Rail (West Midlands - Crewe) Act 2021. In order to undertake these functions, HS2 must work in partnership with relevant stakeholders in order to achieve the required outcomes. This partnership working includes the limited sharing of personal data where required and necessary to achieve specific objectives. The requirement is met by the Localism Act 2011 for the Council. Length of agreement and review The HS2 Programme Lead or delegated authority will monitor and review the data being shared from time to time. This agreement will commence at midnight on the date hereof. This agreement will remain in place until all relevant work on the Project has been completed within the LBC area or until 01/01/2030, whichever is the sooner, or until terminated by either party upon one month’s written notice, save in the event of a data breach where either party shall be entitled to terminate in writing upon no notice. A review of this information sharing agreement will take place after an initial six months and yearly thereafter, unless otherwise agreed by the organisations’ Data Protection Officers. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, the scope has not slipped, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. The terms of this agreement remain binding on any information shared and retained throughout its lifecycle, irrespective of whether the party remains a current signatory to this agreement. Information will be shared on a strict need to know basis only and the data will only be processed by staff in order for them to perform their duties in accordance with one or more of the defined purposes. Under no circumstances should personal data be processed in any way that is unsecure or left unattended or in such a way that it could get into a 3rd parties’ hands. It is the responsibility of the sender to ensure that the method is secure and that they have the correct contact details for the receiver. Recipients and other organisations that the information may be shared with Contractors and partners of HS2 Limited: SCS and SCSJV – Skansa Costain Strasburg & Skansa Costain Strasburg Joint Venture MDJV – Mace Dragados Joint Venture CSJV – Costain Skansa Joint Venture Sub-contractors/ Installers: Selectaglaze Granada Everest Adept Exterior Plas London Borough of Camden Data Quality Each partner is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and relevance of the personal data that it processes and shares and must have clear processes in place for managing data quality. Any party learning of the inaccuracy of personal data is responsible for informing the parties with whom that data has been shared. The data will be quality checked at regular intervals no greater than every 3 months. Retention and destruction Noise insulation works information should be securely deleted after a period of five years following the works being finalised and closed in accordance with each organisation’s procedures. Information must not be retained for longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was obtained. Disposal or deletion of personal data once it is no longer required, must be done securely with appropriate safeguards, in accordance with that organisation’s disposal policies. Data subject rights Where a data subject approaches the Recipient or the Sender, seeking to exercise their rights under data protection legislation, the recipient organisation will respond in accordance with relevant legislation. The Recipient agrees to notify the Sender of the receipt of any such approach relating to information falling with the scope of this agreement and permit HS2 to make comment regarding possible disclosure. Where a data subject approaches a Contractor, the Contractor agrees to pass that request to HS2’s data protection team ) within how long? Organisations agree that they will adhere to the transparency requirements of the UKGDPR and will issue appropriate privacy notices, which inform the data subject that the information will be shared with the parties under this agreement. Data Security All parties agree and confirm that they have appropriate technical and organisational measures in place to protect the information under this agreement against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, personal data in a manner appropriate to its sensitivity. All personal data held by partner organisations electronically will be stored in a secure network area with password protected entry and appropriate back-up functionality. The systems will be auditable so that it is possible for any auditor to establish who has accessed the system. All laptops, computers, and any other portable devices will be encrypted. Any individual no longer required to have access will promptly have such access revoked by the line manager and Human Resources related to the relevant employer. Information shared via a secured file will be protected by a strong password (i.e., consisting of no few than 8 characters and including a combination of numbers, symbols and, upper and lower case characters). Outside UK processing Parties are responsible for ensuring that if information is processed or shared outside the UK, that appropriate safeguards are in place and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. These are for example, a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies, binding corporate rules, and/or standard data protection contractual clauses. Data breaches/incidents All parties must have a clear policy and procedure regarding the reporting and handling of data protection breaches or data loss incidents. This must include assessing the level of risk to the data subject(s), as well as to make a decision on notifying the ICO within the statutory time frame of 72 hours. This complies with Articles 33 and 34 of UK GDPR. If the incident may impact the processing of another party to this agreement, all relevant parties should be informed and appropriate coordination of the incident must take place. The decision to report the incident will lie with the data controller(s) of the information concerned. The parties agree to provide all reasonable and necessary assistance at their own expense to each other to facilitate the handling of any personal data breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. It is confirmed that security breaches (including misuse or unauthorised disclosure) are covered by the partner’s internal disciplinary procedures. If misuse is found there should be a mechanism to facilitate an investigation, including initiating criminal proceedings where necessary. General Obligations Obligations to an individual party The Recipient agrees that it will not share information falling under the scope of this agreement with any other organisation without first seeking the prior written consent of the Sender, unless required to do so by law. Review of Agreement The agreement will be reviewed on an annual basis starting from the date of the agreement comes into force or following a data breach or incident involving data falling under the scope of this agreement. Failure to comply with the terms of this agreement may result in immediate termination of the sharing of data. This agreement will remain in force irrespective of whether the agreement has been officially reviewed until a notice of termination is served. Freedom of Information and Transparency The Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Environmental Information Regulations 2004 gives all individuals the right to access official information held by the council. The council will seek opinion from HS2 where there is concern about information being released and any impact it is likely to have. The final decision to disclose or not will lie with the Council. In order to ensure that the Council is able to respond within the statutory deadline, any request for assistance or information made to HS2 under FOI/EIR should be made promptly, and any opinion provided to the Council within 10 working days. The Council will proactively publish this document, with personal data redacted. (A) The Parties wish to enter into a data sharing framework agreement to create a framework of terms and conditions that will apply on each and every occasion one Party wishes to transfer Shared Personal Data to the other Party. (B) This is a free-standing Agreement that does not incorporate commercial business terms established by the Parties under separate commercial arrangements. (C) The terms and conditions of this Agreement will govern the relationship between the Parties in respect of Shared Personal Data and provide a mechanism whereby the Parties may enter into data sharing arrangements in response to a public heath incident or event in relation to communicable disease and other risks to public health through the execution of a Data Sharing Addendum (DSA). (D) This Agreement including associated DSAs will ensure all Parties can carry out their statutory functions in line with Regulation 3 of The Health Service (Control of Patient Information) Regulations 2002 in a lawful, auditable and transparent manner. (E) The Data Receiver agrees to use the Personal Data within the EEA on the terms set out in this Agreement. . Interpretation The following definitions and rules of interpretation apply in this Agreement. Definitions: Agreed Purpose: has the meaning given to it in clause 2 of this Agreement and as set out in each fully executed Data Sharing Addendum (DSA). Agreement: this data sharing framework agreement, which is a free-standing document that does not incorporate commercial business terms established by the Parties under separate commercial arrangements. Business Day: a day other than a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday in the UK when banks in London are open for business. Commencement Date: the date when the Agreement has been signed by all of the Parties. Data Sharing Addendum or DSA: the Data Sharing Addendum agreed between the Parties in accordance with Clause 2 (Purpose) for the Agreed Purpose, containing detailed information about the type of Personal Data to be shared, the Agreed Purpose for sharing and using the Personal Data, any special conditions for use or reuse of the Shared Personal Data and the related matters listed in the template DSA set out in Schedule 2. Data Sharing Code: The Information Commissioner's Data Sharing Code of Practice issued in September 2021, as updated or amended from time to time. Data Protection Legislation: all applicable data protection and privacy legislation in force from time to time in the UK including the General Data Protection Regulation as enacted into English law by the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and as amended by the Data Protection Act 2018 and Privacy and Electronic Communications (Amendments etc) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (UK GDPR); the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA ); the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations 2003and any other legislation and regulatory requirements in force from time to time which apply to a Party relating to the use of Personal Data (including, without limitation, the privacy of electronic communications) and the guidance and codes of practice issued by the Supervisory Authority. EEA: The European Economic Area as established via the Agreement on the European Economic Area, an international agreement which enables the extension of the European Union's single market to member states of the European Free Trade Association. Personal Data Breach: a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to the Shared Personal Data. Shared Personal Data: the Personal Data and Special Categories of Personal data to be shared between the Parties pursuant to a fully executed DSA under the terms of this Agreement and detailed within each fully executed DSA. Special Categories of Personal Data: the categories of Personal Data set out in Article 9(1) of the UK GDPR. Subject Access Request: the exercise by a Data Subject of his or her rights under Article 15 of the UK GDPR and the DPA 2018. Supervisory Authority: the relevant data protection authority in the territories where the Parties to this Agreement are established. Term: the period commencing on the Commencement Date and ending on termination of this Agreement under clause 13.2 or clause 13.5. Controller, Processor, Data Subject and Personal Data, Processing and "appropriate technical and organisational measures" shall have the meanings given to them in the Data Protection Legislation. Clause, schedule and paragraph headings shall not affect the interpretation of this Agreement. The schedules form part of this Agreement and shall have effect as if set out in full in the body of this Agreement. Any reference to this Agreement includes the schedules. Unless the context otherwise, requires, words in the singular shall include the plural and in the plural shall include the singular. A reference to a company shall include any company, corporation or other body corporate, wherever and however incorporated or established. A reference to a statute or statutory provision shall include all subordinate legislation made from time to time under that statute or statutory provision. References to clauses and schedules are to the clauses and schedules of this Agreement and references to paragraphs are to paragraphs of the relevant Schedule. Any words following the terms including, include, in particular or for example or any similar phrase shall be construed as illustrative and shall not limit the generality of the related general words. In the case of any ambiguity between any provision contained in the body of this Agreement and any provision contained in the DSA, schedules or appendices, the provision in the body of this Agreement shall take precedence. Unless the context otherwise requires, any reference to European Union law that is directly applicable or directly effective in the UK at any time is a reference to it as it applies England from time to time. A reference to writing or written includes email. Unless the context otherwise requires the reference to one gender shall include a reference to the other genders. . Purpose This Agreement sets out the framework for the sharing of Personal Data when one Controller (the Data Discloser) discloses Personal Data to another Controller (the Data Receiver). It defines the principles and procedures that the Parties shall adhere to and the responsibilities the Parties owe to each other. The Parties consider this data sharing necessary to fulfil their statutory duties in relation to public health and communicable disease surveillance. Each time the Data Receiver is engaged to receive Shared Personal Data, a DSA shall be completed. The Parties shall assist each other to discuss and agree each DSA and both Data Receiver and Data Discloser shall sign the DSA once it has been agreed. Upon the execution of each DSA the terms and conditions agreed in the DSA shall be incorporated into this Agreement and shall not form a separate contract to it. The Parties shall not process Shared Personal Data in a way that is incompatible with the purposes described in this Clause 2 and the DSA (Agreed Purpose). Each Party shall appoint a single point of contact (SPoC) and delegated deputy who will work together to reach an agreement with regards to any issues arising from the data sharing and to actively improve the effectiveness of the data sharing initiative. The points of contact for each of the Parties are: (a) , Head of Information Governance & Privacy, UKHSA (b) , Public Health Intelligence Lead, London Borough of Camden . Compliance with the Data Protection Legislation Each Party must ensure compliance with the Data Protection Legislation at all times during the Term of this Agreement. Each Party has such valid registrations and paid such fees as are required by its Supervisory Authority which, by the time that the data sharing is expected to commence, covers the intended data sharing pursuant to this Agreement, unless an exemption applies. . Shared Personal Data Further detail on the Shared Personal Data will be detailed in each fully executed DSA, together with any access and processing restrictions as agreed and established by the Parties. The Shared Personal Data must not be irrelevant or excessive with regard to the Agreed Purpose. . Lawful, fair and transparent processing Each Party shall ensure that it processes the Shared Personal Data fairly and lawfully during the Term of this Agreement. Each Party shall ensure that it has legitimate grounds under the Data Protection Legislation for the processing of Shared Personal Data. Each Party agrees that the legitimate grounds under the Data Protection Legislation for the processing of Shared Personal Data are: (a) UK GDPR Article 6(1)(e) – the processing is necessary for the performance of the Parties’ official tasks carried out in the public interest. (b) UK GDPR Article 9(2)(i) – the processing is necessary for reasons of public interest in the area of public health. (c) Data Protection Act 2018 – Schedule 1, Part 1 (3) – ‘Public Health’ . Data quality The Data Discloser shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that the Shared Personal Data are accurate. Shared Personal Data must be limited to the Personal Data described in each associated fully executed DSA to this Agreement. . Data Subjects' rights The Parties each agree to provide such assistance as is reasonably required to enable the other Party to comply with requests from Data Subjects to exercise their rights under the Data Protection Legislation within the time limits imposed by the Data Protection Legislation. The SPoC for each Party is responsible for maintaining a record of individual requests for information, the decisions made and any information that was exchanged. Records must include copies of the request for information, details of the data accessed and shared and where relevant, notes of any meeting, correspondence or phone calls relating to the request. The SPoC for each Party are detailed in clause 2.5. . Data retention and deletion The Data Receiver shall not retain or process Shared Personal Data for longer than is necessary to carry out the Agreed Purpose. Notwithstanding clause 8.1, the Parties shall continue to retain Shared Personal Data in accordance with any statutory or professional retention periods applicable in their respective areas of work and profession. The Data Receiver shall ensure that any Shared Personal Data are returned to the Data Discloser or destroyed in accordance with the agreed Deletion Procedure set out in Schedule 4 in the following circumstances: (a) on termination or expiry of the Agreement; (b) on expiry of the Term of the DSA; (c) once processing of the Shared Personal Data is no longer necessary for the purposes it was originally shared for, as set out in clause 2.3 and each DSA. Following the deletion of Shared Personal Data in accordance with clause 8.3, the Data Receiver shall notify the Data Discloser that the Shared Personal Data in question has been deleted in accordance with the Deletion Procedure set out in Schedule 4 to this Agreement. . Transfers For the purposes of this clause, transfers of Personal Data shall mean any sharing of Personal Data by the Data Receiver with a third party, and shall include, but is not limited to, the following: (a) subcontracting the processing of Shared Personal Data; (b) granting a third party controller access to the Shared Personal Data. (c) third parties commissioned by either Party to share Personal Data as part of the Purpose. If the Data Receiver appoints a third party Processor to process the Shared Personal Data it shall comply with Article 28 and Article 30 of the UK GDPR and shall remain liable to the Data Discloser for the acts and/or omissions of the Processor. The Data Receiver shall not disclose or transfer Shared Personal Data outside the EEA. . Security and training The Data Discloser shall only provide the Shared Personal Data to the Data Receiver by using secure methods as agreed and set out in Schedule 3. The Parties undertake to have in place throughout the Term appropriate technical and organisational security measures to: (a) prevent: (i) unauthorised or unlawful processing of the Shared Personal Data; and (ii) the accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, the Shared Personal Data; (b) ensure a level of security appropriate to: (i) the harm that might result from such unauthorised or unlawful processing or accidental loss, destruction or damage; and (ii) the nature of the Shared Personal Data to be protected. The level of technical and organisational measures agreed by the Parties as appropriate as at the Commencement Date having regard to the state of technological development and the cost of implementing such measures is set out in Schedule 3. The Parties shall keep such security measures under review and shall carry out such updates as they agree are appropriate throughout the Term. It is the responsibility of each Party to ensure that its staff members are appropriately trained to handle and process the Shared Personal Data in accordance with the technical and organisational security measures set out in Schedule 3 and the Data Protection Legislation, and have entered into confidentiality agreements relating to the processing of Personal Data. The level, content and regularity of training referred to in clause 10.3 shall be proportionate to the staff members' role, responsibility and frequency with respect to their handling and processing of the Shared Personal Data. . Personal data breaches and reporting procedures The Parties shall each comply with its obligation to report a Personal Data Breach to the appropriate Supervisory Authority and (where applicable) Data Subjects under Article 33 of the UK GDPR and shall each inform the other Party of any Personal Data Breach involving data shared under this Agreement irrespective of whether there is a requirement to notify any Supervisory Authority or Data Subject(s). The Parties agree to notify each other and provide reasonable assistance as is necessary to each other to facilitate the handling of any Personal Data Breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. . Review of Agreement months, having consideration to the aims and purposes set out in clause 2. The Parties shall continue, amend or terminate the Agreement depending on the outcome of this review. The review of the effectiveness of this Agreement will involve: (a) assessing whether the purposes for which the Shared Personal Data is being processed are still the ones listed in clause 2 of this Agreement; (b) assessing whether the legal framework governing data quality, retention, and Data Subjects' rights are being complied with; and (c) assessing whether personal data breaches involving the Shared Personal Data have been handled in accordance with this Agreement and the applicable legal framework. Each Party reserves its rights to inspect the other Parties arrangements for the processing of Shared Personal Data and to terminate the Agreement where it considers that the other Party is not processing the Shared Personal Data in accordance with this Agreement. . Term and Termination This Agreement shall take effect on the Commencement Date and shall continue in full force and effect unless it is terminated under clause 13.2 or clause 13.5. Any Party may terminate this Agreement during its Term by giving written notice to the other Parties in accordance with clause 28. Such termination shall be effective on the expiry of all DSAs entered into before the date on which the notice is served, unless otherwise agreed to by the Parties in writing. If any Party exercises the option to terminate under clause 13.2 and all DSAs have expired, this Agreement will terminate with immediate effect and no new DSAs shall be entered into. If this Agreement is entered into after the Parties have begun sharing Personal Data with each other, it shall apply retrospectively to the Processing of such Personal Data from the date on which such sharing began. The Data Discloser may suspend or terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by giving written notice to the other Parties in accordance with clause 28 if: (a) the Data Receiver is in material breach of this Agreement and/or any Data Sharing Addendum, and that breach cannot be remedied; (b) the Data Receiver is in material breach of this Agreement and/or any Data Sharing Addendum which can be remedied but the Data Receiver fails to do so within 30 days starting on the day after receipt of written notice from the SPoC; (c) in respect of Shared Personal Data, the Data Receiver no longer has the legal basis to Process such Shared Personal Data; (d) it becomes unlawful for the Data Receiver to perform all or any of its obligations under this Agreement; or (e) there is a change to the Data Protection Legislation which materially affects the Data Discloser’s powers to provide Personal Data to the Data Receiver. On termination of this Agreement under clause 13.5, all existing DSAs shall terminate automatically. The Parties shall not enter into any further DSAs after the date on which notice to terminate is served under clauses 13.2 or 13.5. . Resolution of disputes with Data Subjects or the Supervisory Authority In the event of a dispute or claim brought by a Data Subject or the Supervisory Authority concerning the processing of Shared Personal Data against one or more Parties, the Parties will inform each other about any such disputes or claims, and will cooperate with a view to settling them amicably in a timely fashion. The Parties agree to respond to any generally available non-binding mediation procedure initiated by a Data Subject or by the Supervisory Authority. If they do participate in the proceedings, the Parties may elect to do so remotely (such as by telephone or other electronic means). The Parties also agree to consider participating in any other arbitration, mediation or other dispute resolution proceedings developed for data protection disputes. Each Party shall abide by a decision of a competent court of the Data Discloser's country of establishment or of the Supervisory Authority. . Warranties Each Party warrants and undertakes that it will: (a) Process the Shared Personal Data in compliance with the Data Protection Legislation; (b) Make available on request to the Data Subjects who are third party beneficiaries a copy of this Agreement, unless the Agreement contains confidential information; (c) Respond within a reasonable time and as far as reasonably possible to enquiries from the relevant Supervisory Authority in relation to the Shared Personal Data; (d) Provide appropriate privacy information to Data Subjects, which includes details of the data sharing pursuant to this Agreement. (e) Respond to requests by Data Subjects to exercise their rights in accordance with the Data Protection Legislation; (f) Where applicable, maintain registration with all relevant Supervisory Authorities to process all Shared Personal Data for the Agreed Purpose; and (g) Take all appropriate steps to ensure compliance with the security measures set out in clause 10 above. The Data Discloser warrants and undertakes that it is entitled to provide the Shared Personal Data to the Data Receiver and it will take all reasonable steps to ensure that the Shared Personal Data are accurate. The Data Receiver warrants and undertakes that it will not disclose or transfer Shared Personal Data outside the EEA. Each Party warrants and undertakes that it has full capacity and authority to enter into and to perform its own obligations under this Agreement. Except as expressly stated in this Agreement, all warranties, conditions and terms, whether express or implied by statute, common law or otherwise are hereby excluded to the extent permitted by law. . Allocation of cost Each Party shall perform its obligations under this Agreement at its own cost. . Schedule 1 Key legislative provisions and authoritative guidance The UK Data Protection Legislation The Health Service (Control of Patient Information) Regulations 2002 Schedule 3 Appropriate technical and organisational security measures . Without prejudice to the Parties’ other obligations in respect of information security, the Parties shall: having regard to the state of technological development, provide a level of security (including appropriate technical and organisational measures) appropriate to: the harm that might result from unauthorised or unlawful processing of Shared Personal Data or accidental loss, destruction or damage of such Shared Personal Data; and the nature of the Shared Personal Data. ensure that access to the Shared Personal Data is limited to those personnel who need access to the Shared Personal Data to meet the Parties obligations under this Agreement; take reasonable steps to ensure the reliability of the Parties personnel who have access to the Shared Personal Data. inform the other Party as soon as reasonably practicable of any particular risk to the security of the Shared Personal Data of which it becomes aware, and of the categories of Data and individuals which may be affected; The Parties shall implement and maintain security standards, facilities, controls and procedures appropriate to the nature of the Shared Personal Data held by it and the harm that would be caused by its loss or disclosure including a comprehensive and up-to-date data protection policy. The Parties shall ensure that all their personnel who have access to the Shared Personal Data shall comply with the obligations upon them contained in the data protection policy. Each Party shall ensure: that it has properly configured access rights for its personnel including a well-defined joiners and leavers process to ensure access rights to the Shared Personal Data are properly managed; that it has proper controls in place to make sure that complex alphanumeric passwords are required for access to the Shared Personal Data and that training is provided in relation to the need to keep such passwords secure; it has in place procedures to identify wrongful use of Shared Personal Data, including the monitoring of wrongful access to Shard Personal Data; suitable and effective authentication processes are established and used to protect Shared Personal Data; Shared Personal Data is backed up on a regular basis and that all back up data is subject to such vigorous security procedures as are necessary in order to protect data integrity, such security measures being commensurate to the nature of the data. The Parties shall take particular care when transporting backup data and other personal information and shall ensure such backup data and other personal information is transported in a safe and secure manner; Shared Personal Data transferred electronically is encrypted; information stored on laptops or other portable media is encrypted and that the Parties maintains an accurate, up to date asset register, including all such portable media used to process the Shared Personal Data; that suitable physical security measures are established commensurate to the harm that could result from the unlawful disclosure of the Shared Personal Data. Such physical security measures shall be as identified in the Parties data protection policy; without prejudice to the Parties obligations in relation to the disposal of the Shared Personal Data, all Shared Personal Data which is disposed of must be disposed of pursuant to the Parties policy for the disposal of data identified in the data protection policy, including the disposal of assets containing personal data, a copy of which policy shall be provided, on request, to the other Party; the Parties establishes and maintains adequate data security compliance policies and audits its use of personal data in compliance with its data security policies on a regular basis and in any event annually; and All data transfers will be via access to systems managed and maintained by the Data Discloser or via a secure data transfer mechanism. Any and all electronic transfers will be encrypted with decryption passwords communicated by alternative method to data transfer. Introduction to the Sharing This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement, listed in Appendix A, will share information about young people. By signing this Agreement, the named agencies agree to accept the conditions set out in this document, according to their statutory and professional responsibilities, and agree to adhere to the procedures described. This Agreement has been developed to: ● Define the specific purposes for which the signatory agencies have agreed to share information. ● Outline the Personal, Special Category and Criminal Data to be shared. ● Set out the lawful basis condition under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared, including reference to the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Common Law Duty of Confidentiality. ● Stipulate the roles and procedure that will support the processing/sharing of information between agencies. ● Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. ● Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure that compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and agency-specific security requirements. ● Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. ● To illustrate the flow of information from referral through processing and outcome. Parties to this agreement cannot amend or add appendices unless agreed as part of a formal review. It is expected that each party will have procedures, processes and policies sitting underneath this agreement, for their respective organisations. These will, for example, describe the specific processes for secure transfer of data. . Ownership of this agreement This agreement was drafted by a working group of representatives of the local authorities and London Councils. These professionals were specialists in information governance and law. The local authority representatives worked under the banner of the Information Governance for London Group (IGfL), to draft one agreement that would work for all boroughs across London. The aim is to reduce the number of versions of sharing agreements that historically differed between boroughs, partly to reduce the burden on pan-London organisations, that must have agreements with multiple boroughs. IGfL, a group of information and security professionals at London boroughs, assisted with co-ordination of this agreement, but the responsibilities within it, and compliance with data protection legislation, remain with the listed data controllers. . Responsibilities of parties involved The parties are registered Data Controllers under the Data Protection Act. Signatories are identified as those who have signed this agreement on the platform on which this agreement is hosted (expected to be the Information Sharing Gateway). A list of expected types of signatories is at Appendix A. All parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: ●having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ●ensuring data quality. ●storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. ●having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including for managing data subject rights & complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ●ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. ●undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. ●having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Organisations and their staff must consult the organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian if they are unsure at any point in the processing and sharing of personal data. . Confidentiality and vetting Each Partner must ensure that there are appropriate written contracts or agreements with employees, agency staff, volunteers etc. These must include requirements to ensure compliance with policies which include confidentiality. Each Partner must ensure that suitable vetting has taken place. . Assessment and review A review of this information sharing agreement will take place at the end of the pilot phase, as part of the decision on whether to move into the efficacy phase of the project. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, there has been no scope creep, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. Changes in legislation and developments in the areas of public sector data sharing will be considered as and when they arise, as will any changes to the signatory parties. The working group who drafted this agreement strongly recommend that a working group approach is used for any reviews, as this was a successful way to achieve pan-London and cross-specialism consensus to one sharing agreement. . Termination of agreement In the event of termination of this agreement each party may continue to hold information originating from other parties for which they are data controller. . Outside of this agreement This DSA only covers the data collected in the LA LYPS Workbook. The IFS and Anna Freud Centre have DPIAs that cover other aspects of the LYPS. . Purpose and Benefits Purpose The London Young People Study (LYPS) is a pan-London project being run by the London Violence Reduction Unit and the Association of London Directors of Children's Services, funded by the Youth Endowment Fund (YEF). The program trains workers delivering services to young people (e.g. social workers, youth justice workers, teachers) to deliver high-intensity cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) informed support to young people aged 11-17, across the 32 London boroughs. This support, and the work to make it available, is branded ‘Your Choice’. The programme creates two groups; one where selected young people receive the CBT on top of normal interventions and support; and one with the majority in a control group where only normal interventions are delivered. Through the LYPS, Your Choice is being evaluated in London in order to determine whether the program is effective, and therefore whether it should receive funding to scale-up across the capital and nationwide. The proposed data sharing is in support of this evaluation and is a requirement of the YEF funding. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) and the Anna Freud Centre (AFC) are managing the evaluation and will gather additional data from the young people directly, and from the DfE. We wish to process the data in order to evaluate the Your Choice program. We wish to do this for two reasons: ● Firstly, because youth violence is a serious issue affecting Londoners. Last year 5,864 were victims of the most serious violence and almost one per week was killed1. ● Secondly because there is a lack of evidence today about what works to reduce this violence, and this lack of evidence is preventing us from mobilizing resources and from designing the best services to reduce the problem and its impact. MOPAC (2021) ‘Understanding serious violence amongst young people in London’. Accessible at This is a priority for London’s Directors of Children’s Services and the Mayor – not least because of its intersection with other priority issues including poverty, racial inequality, and health inequalities. The output of the study will be answers to the questions . Are young people who receive this service more or less likely to experience serious violence than those who do not receive it? . Are the young people who receive this more or less likely to experience (positive or negative) criminal justice and education outcomes than those who do not? . What known factors (e.g. demographics, service organisation) modify these outcomes; . What is the cost per outcome when they are delivered through Your Choice and how does this compare to alternatives? . Benefits The benefits of this DSA are to achieve a more comprehensive, joined up and efficient method for councils to deliver the evaluation to which they have jointly committed. The benefits of the sharing are to allow a London-wide evaluation of the efficacy of the CBT provided to young people taking part in the programme. If the evaluation shows that the program is effective, then we can deliver better services to vulnerable young Londoners, with the aim of reducing youth violence and improving outcomes for young people. There is very little research available about this cohort of young people and little to inform public policy on the best way to improve the outcomes for young people. This is why the Youth Endowment Fund, Violence Reduction Unit and Home Office (the sponsors of the LYPS) are so interested in this study and why the legacy of the research is such an integral part of the programme. With so many young people dying as a result of youth violence it is in the public interest that new treatments and research be carried out on what may or may not work to reduce or prevent this tragic loss of life. If it can be shown that the Your Choice programme can improve the outcomes of young people, it may be rolled out across England and Wales so that it has benefits for the whole country. The DSA will: ● Cover the sharing of information for the purposes of the LYPS. ● Remove barriers to effective information sharing. ● Sets parameters for sharing personal data and clearly identifies the responsibilities of organisations. ● Identify the correct lawful basis to share personal information. ● Enables authorities to share data for the LYPS. ● Raises awareness amongst all agencies of the key issues relating to information sharing and gives confidence in the process of sharing information with others. ● Greater efficiencies in processes and resources. ● Preventing crime. ● Effectively dealing with public safety . Principles of information sharing Effective information sharing is a vital element of delivering the LYPS. Organisations can hold different pieces of information which need to be placed together to enable a thorough evaluation to be made. To share information, a lawful basis for doing so must be identified. This may come from legislation or from statutory guidance. The sharing of personal data must comply with both the GDPR Principles and the Caldicott Principles, listed at Appendix B. Together, those principles lead to a series of questions and considerations to be answered before sharing takes place. These are listed as an Information Sharing Checklist in Appendix D: Information Sharing Checklist. . Lawful Basis Local authorities have two main legislative drivers that cover the work of the Your Choice Programme. The Children’s Act 1989, section 17, imposes a duty on local authorities to “safeguard and promote the welfare of children in need in their area”. Additionally, the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act , section 8(3)c, imposes a duty on local authorities and others to “prepare and implement a strategy for exercising their functions to prevent and reduce serious violence in the area”. It is considered a part of the local authority’s public task (Article 6 (1)(e) to engage in this programme. Whilst the delivery of the CBT to young people is considered processing for health and social care purposes (Article 9 (2)(h), for sharing the data for research purposes the condition is substantial public interest (Article 9 (2)(g). The evaluation carried out by IFS is considered research in the area of public authority social care duties; evaluation of the Your Choice programme as a randomised control trial. In that regard the research is primarily scientific in nature and involves controlling for all the individual characteristics of the cohort that may affect the efficacy of the Your Choice treatment element of the study. As stated earlier, there is very little research available about this cohort of young people and little to inform public policy on the best way to improve the outcomes for the young people. This is why the Youth Endowment Fund, Violence Reduction Unit and Home Office (the sponsors of the LYPS) are so interested in this study and why the legacy of the research is such an integral part of the programme. With so many young people dying as a result of youth violence it is in the public interest that new ‘treatments’ and research be carried out on what may or may not work to reduce or prevent this tragic loss of life. If it can be shown that the ‘Your Choice’ treatment can improve the outcomes of young people, it may be rolled out across England and Wales so that it has benefits for the whole country. The IFS processing of data is covered by Article 6(1)(e) public task and Article 9(2)(j). Some personal data relating to criminal allegations and convictions is expected to be shared where it is relevant to the issues the young person raises during the programme or the evaluation of the programme. When processing special category data, a condition from Sch 1 Pt 1, or Sch 1 Pt 2 of the DPA 2018 must be identified. For processing data relating to criminal convictions and offences Article 10 of the UK GDPR applies, and a condition from the DPA 2018 Sch 1 Pt 3 must be identified. The conditions relevant to the parties sharing data under this agreement are: Article 6 conditions Article 9 conditions c) legal obligation f) necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims or whenever courts are acting in their judicial capacity e) performance of a task carried out in g) substantial public interest ● ● the public interest f) purposes of the legitimate interests h) purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the ● ● assessment of the working capacity of the employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment or the management of health or social care systems and services i) public interest in the area of public health, such as protecting against serious cross-border threats to health or ensuring high standards of quality and safety of health care and of medicinal products or medical devices j) archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or ● historical research purposes or statistical purposes Article 9(2) (b) (h) (i) (j) - Sch 1 Pt 1 Employment, social security and social Public health protection Health or social care ● Research Article 9(2) (g) - Sch 1 Pt 2 Statutory & government purposes Administration of justice Equality of opportunity or treatment Racial/ethnic diversity at snr mgmt Preventing or detecting unlawful acts Protecting the public against dishonesty Regulatory for unlawful acts and dishonesty Terrorist financing or money laundering Preventing fraud Support for individuals with disability or medical condition ● Safeguarding of children and individuals at risk Safeguarding economic well-being Criminal data - Sch 1 Pt 3 Legal claims Judicial acts Consideration of the lawful basis conditions will take place as part of the review at the end of the pilot. . Consent The parties will often work collaboratively with data subjects and aim for agreement with them on the actions to be taken. However, it is recognised that this is different to using consent (Article 6 (a)) or explicit consent (Article 9 (a)) as the lawful basis conditions used for processing under this agreement. Consent is not generally the lawful basis the public sector organisations use for processing information shared under this agreement. In the LYPS Your Choice Programme the young people eligible to take part in the study are asked for informed consent to be included. That consent is an ethical consideration to meet the requirement of the researchers’ organisations for conducting this randomised controlled trial and is not considered to be the lawful basis for personal data processing. Whether in the CBT group or the control group, a young person cannot take part in the programme without having their personal data included in the evaluation. If a young person chooses to leave the programme once it has begun, any data already collected with be included in the evaluation, unless the young person requests that their data be removed from the evaluation. This is part of the informed consent for the trial, and not consent as lawful basis. Once the evaluation phase has begun data cannot be deleted. . Proportionality and necessity Proportionality This study will impact upon the privacy of up to 4,000 young people and 1,000 staff. The privacy impact has been extensively mitigated through the programme’s design and balanced against the potential benefits outlined. We believe that the potential benefit of saving young Londoners’ lives is clearly worth the processing, and that the question is therefore the extent to which we can reduce processing to the absolute minimum required to achieve this end.
