Introduction to the Sharing This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement, listed in Appendix A, will share personal data about Children to enable the London Resettlement Partnership to be monitored and delivered. By signing this Agreement, the named agencies agree to accept the conditions set out in this document, according to their statutory and professional responsibilities, and agree to adhere to the procedures described. This Agreement has been developed to: ● Define the specific purposes for which the signatory agencies have agreed to share information. ● Outline the Personal, Special Category and Criminal Data to be shared. ● Set out the lawful basis conditions under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared, including reference to the Human Rights Act 1998 ● Stipulate the roles and procedures that will support the processing/sharing of information between agencies. ● Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. ● Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure that compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and agency-specific security requirements. ● Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. ● To illustrate the flow of information from referral through processing and outcome. Parties to this agreement cannot amend or add appendices unless agreed as part of a formal review. It is expected that each party will have procedures, processes and policies sitting underneath this agreement, for their respective organisations. These will, for example, describe the specific processes for secure transfer of data. . Partner / Parties For simplicity, the Partner Organisation will be referred to as ‘Partner’, ‘Partner Organisation’ or ‘Partner Agency’ in this agreement. . Responsibilities of parties involved The parties are registered Data Controllers under the Data Protection Act. A list of type of signatories is at Appendix A. All parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: ● having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ● ensuring data quality. ● storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. ● having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including for managing data subject rights and complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ● ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality, and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. ● undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ, and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. ● having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Organisations and their staff must consult the organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian if they are unsure at any point in the processing and sharing of personal data. . Confidentiality and vetting Each Partner must ensure that there are appropriate written contracts or agreements with employees, agency staff, volunteers etc. These must include requirements to ensure compliance with policies which include confidentiality. Each Partner must ensure that suitable vetting has taken place. This may be through standard employee checks and DBS checks. . Assessment and review A review of this information sharing agreement will take place yearly, unless otherwise agreed by the organisations’ Data Protection Officers. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, the scope has not slipped, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. Changes in legislation and developments in the areas of public sector data sharing will be considered as and when they arise, as will any changes to the signatory parties. . Termination of agreement In the event of termination of this agreement each party may continue to hold information originating from other parties for which they are Data Controller. . Purpose and Benefits . Purpose This agreement covers the sharing of information by and between the listed parties for the purpose of sharing data on all children remanded and sentenced to youth custody from London. This will allow the project to run and be evaluated as part of the London Resettlement Partnership. Camden is the lead authority for the London Resettlement Partnership and is required to collate data as part of the monitoring and evaluation process of the Youth Justice Board pathfinder. MOPAC is the evaluator for this project, and London Borough of Camden, as lead council, will share data received from the Boroughs under this DSA with MOPAC. Camden has a DSA with MOPAC which covers the necessary data protection and security matters including secure transfer and storage, retention and data subject rights etc for this data. Spark Inside have been commissioned to support children with 1:1 life coaching. Youth Justice Services will be contacted by Spark Inside if children are eligible for this service. Camden as the lead council have a contract with Spark Inside and have undertaken all necessary due diligence processes including secure sharing of information and data storage. Aggregate data from all local authorities will be shared with key stakeholders within the London Resettlement Partnership via quarterly reports. Individual local authorities will not be identified within this report. The overall aim of the project is to work with partners to improve resettlement outcomes for children and reduce reoffending. The project focuses on a number of aims in order to achieve this, including: Defining constructive resettlement principles and ascertain how this can work in practice in developing an enhanced constructive resettlement offer. Identifying clear pathways to Release on Temporary Licence (ROTL) (to include ROTL clinics) Improving education, training and employment outcomes Developing a pan London accommodation protocol Working with NHS England and partners to define ways of securing continuity of health pathways from custody to community Addressing the disproportionality of black, Asian and mixed ethnicity children and its impact on pathways to resettlement. Supporting local practice networks of resettlement case workers to define improvements and raise strategic issues Developing a body of effective practice and materials for dissemination nationally to YOTs and other agencies. Case level data will be collected for every child that is remanded or sentenced to youth custody from London. The case level data collated will include all data relevant to the resettlement journey of the child including offence data, health information, accommodation, education and interventions (see appendix B for a full list). In addition, up to 16 Asset Plus assessments will be required for the evaluation of the pathfinder. These will be randomly selected from across the 32 Boroughs. Asset Plus is an assessment, planning interventions framework, developed by the YJB and used by youth justice services in the assessment and planning for children. Appendix C outlines the data collated through the Asset Plus assessment. . Benefits The sharing will allow partners to better deliver their statutory services and will allow more effective use of resources, giving more joined up working which increases efficiency. London will benefit as the data will provide a benchmark for the resettlement of children in the youth justice system, highlight areas for improvement and showcase areas of best practice. The public will benefit from this approach, as services will be delivered in a more streamlined way that utilises the information shared to provide better tailored and appropriate services. Based on the above objectives for the London Resettlement Partnership data sharing will enable London to identify challenges and successes at a case level, and to use aggregate data to set benchmarks and track progress to realise the following benefits: Fewer children returning to custody A reduction in reoffending rates Improved accommodation outcomes for children released from custody Improved education, training, and employment outcomes Improved pathways for health between custody and community Increased use of release on temporary licence to address resettlement needs A drive to address disproportionality, hence more suitable outcomes for BAME children and support for staff Funding directed to the right services across London to address the needs of children in the youth justice system An evidence base to drive changes with policy, practice and legislation Improved partnership working across the youth justice sector. The benefits of this DSA are to: ● Cover the sharing of information for all London boroughs to Camden as the host local authority ● Sets parameters for sharing personal data and clearly identifies the responsibilities of organisations. ● Identify the correct lawful basis to share personal information. ● Ensure information is shared whenever there is a requirement to do so. ● Enables authorities to share data on performance, quality assurance, learning and impact analysis. Wider societal benefits are expected to be: ● Improved outcomes and decreased pressure on services can lead to long-term fiscal savings for reinvestment in services ● Reduced reoffending rates for children leaving custody ● Safer communities and fewer victims ● More children and young people positively contributing to society . Lawful Basis The sharing of information must comply with the law relating to confidentiality, data protection and human rights. Having a legitimate purpose for sharing information is an important part of meeting those legal requirements. This is a complex area and each Partner must take their own decisions and seek advice from their organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian. Articles 6, 9 and 10 of the UK GDPR set out the acceptable conditions for the processing and sharing of personal, special category, and criminal data. The conditions relevant in the UK GDPR to data processed under this agreement are below. Personal data: Article 6(1) (c) legal duty and 6(1)(e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest . The Crime and Disorder Act 1998 gives each LA in England & Wales has the responsibility to formulate a strategy to reduce crime and disorder in their area and to work with police authorities to do this. Section 115 of the Act gives partners the power to share information for the purpose of reducing crime and disorder. Schedule 9 (5) of the Police and Justice Act strengthens this by introducing a new duty on the same agencies. The Children Act 1989 Under S.47 of the Children’s Act 1989, a Local Authority has a duty to investigate when informed that a child in their area is in police protection or the subject of a protection order. The Children Act 2004, as amended by the Children and Social Work Act 2017, places duties on key agencies in a local area. Specifically, the police, clinical commissioning groups and the local authority are under a duty to make arrangements to work together, and with other partners locally, to safeguard and promote the welfare of all children in their area. The Statutory Guidance - Working Together to Safeguard Children (2018) and Information Sharing – Advice to Practitioners providing safeguarding services to Children, Young People, Parents, and Carers (July 2018) emphasise the need to share appropriately. Special Category Data: Art 9(g) Reasons of substantial public interest (with a basis in law) and (h) Health or social care (with a basis in law). For art 9(g) the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 conditions are para 6 6 (Statutory and government purposes) and para 18 (Safeguarding of children and of individuals at risk) with the underlying law being that identified in art 6 above; and for art 9(h) the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1 condition is (2)(2)(e) Health or social care purposes, the provision of social care. The underlying law is the same as for art 6. Criminal Offence Data: the processing complies with Art 10, the art 6 condition is as noted above and the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 conditions are as noted above. . Consent The parties will work collaboratively with data subjects and aim for agreement with them on the actions to be taken. However, it is recognised that this is different to using consent (Article 6 (a)) or explicit consent (Article 9 (a)) as the lawful basis conditions used for processing under this agreement. Consent is not the lawful basis the public sector organisations use for processing information shared under this agreement. It is noted that where consent is not the lawful basis for processing, consent does not need to be sought to share, and thus the concept of “overriding consent” is a misconception. It is possible that the other parties, such as voluntary groups, may use consent as a lawful basis for some personal data processing. Each party is responsible for managing consent where they use consent as the lawful basis condition. . Proportionality and necessity Proportionality, data minimisation, necessity and not being excessive are factors to be taken into consideration when deciding whether to share personal information. In making the decision, employees must weigh up what might happen as a result of the information being shared against what might happen if it is not, and apply their professional judgement. It is for this reason professionals must ensure they comply with Article 5(1)(c) and share the adequate and relevant information, and limit that information to what is necessary for the achieving of the DSA aims. In this case there will be data forms agreed between the parties to ensure that only the correct agreed as necessary data is shared. . Freedom of Information The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives all individuals the right to access official information held by a public authority (the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 also allow access to data. For ease of drafting, FOI is used to cover both legislation). Limited exemptions may apply and all public authorities must ensure they have recognised procedures in place for administering requests of this nature. All requests for FOI will be directed through the relevant organisations’ FOI processes. Each party will seek advice/opinion from the other parties where there is concern about that information being released and any impact it is likely to have. The final decision to disclose or not will lie with the party who received the request as the legal duty lies with them. In order to ensure that the authority in receipt of the FOIA request is able to respond within the statutory deadline, any request for assistance or information made to partner authorities should be made and processed within two working days, and any data exchange completed within seven working days. It is encouraged that all parties proactively publish this document. It may also be disclosed to the public under FOI. . Individuals Organisations processing personal data are required to begin with the ethos of Data Protection by Design and Default (also known as Privacy by Design (PbD)). This means that we must consider and uphold the privacy of an individual’s data before we begin and throughout the processing taking place. Each party agrees that they have undertaken a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment), where they feel the processing meets the legislative criteria for a DPIA. . Right to be informed – Privacy notices Where personal data is created or received by one of the parties, they are responsible, as required by law, for making the data subject(s) aware within a reasonable time frame that the organisation holds the data, what they will do with it, how long they will keep it, and who they will share it with (such as under this DSA). This is normally done through a privacy notice, whether written or verbal. Organisations agree that they will adhere to the transparency requirements of the UK GDPR and will issue appropriate notices which inform the data subject that the information will be shared with the parties under this agreement. . Data subject rights requests and complaints Each organisation must have in place appropriate policies and processes to handle data subject requests made in line with data protection law, to ensure they are responded to within deadline and in an appropriate manner. Requests include; right of access, right to rectification, right to erasure, right to restrict processing, right to data portability, right to object and rights related to automated decision making including profiling. If an individual successfully requests the erasure or limitation of use of their data (right to erasure, right to rectification, right to restrict processing, right to object), the party that has been informed by the data subject will communicate this to the other parties where relevant and appropriate. In each case each party is responsible for securely disposing of such information or limiting its processing. Each party must have clear, fair and objective complaint procedures. Any complaints from individuals how their data is being processed or shared will be handled under the policy and processes of the organisation concerned. . Data subjects The data subjects will be all 10-17 year old children who enter custody (males and females, remanded and sentenced) from all London Boroughs. Some children may turn 18 whilst they are being monitored as part of the London Resettlement Partnership, these young adults will remain in scope. The data subjects are vulnerable. Parties to this agreement are in positions of power over data subjects and data subjects have little or no control over why and how their data is processed. . Data . The data to be shared Data that will be shared includes: ● Name, address and contact details inc phone and email ● Age/date of birth ● Gender ● Ethnicity ● Criminal offence data including type of offence, gravity scores reoffending and breach data ● Special Educational Needs and Disabilities ● Physical or mental health or condition (to allow risk assessments to be made and necessary actions taken) ● Accommodation information ● Education, training and employment information ● Interventions Please refer to Appendix B for a full list. . Storing and handling information securely Information must be stored and shared lawfully and securely. Special category data may need a higher level of security. The employee/organisation sharing the information must choose the most appropriate secure method of transfer and be responsible for its safe delivery. Electronic records: Organisations may have different electronic methods for storing and sharing information securely. Some have local restrictions which block access to information shared using specific tools. Parties must make sure the chosen method is suitably secure and that access is only provided to those who need it, and only to the data needed. Unencrypted email (i.e. sent in plain text over the public internet) must not be used to share information under this DSA. Sharing methods that may be appropriate include: ● Email encryption tools where the email and attachments are encrypted from named sender to named recipient (e.g. Microsoft 365 Message Encryption; Egress Protect) ● Encryption via Transport Layer Security (TLS) where the email and attachments are encrypted in transit over the internet. Both the sender and recipient email domains must have TLS enabled. This can be checked using ● Secure corporately managed data repository and sharing platforms (e.g. MS Teams; Google Docs) ● Secure group email services (e.g. CJSM: ● Secure File Transfer Protocols ● Virtual Private Networks The above are examples, get advice from your organisation’s information security or IT teams on secure methods of sharing available at your organisation and document these in the organisation’s process documents. Phone/virtual meetings/face-to-face meetings: Information may be shared over the phone, in a virtual meeting, or at face to face meetings. Meeting attendance and distribution of content, e.g. meeting minutes or recordings, must be limited to those with a need to know. Sharing by telephone should be avoided unless the requirement is urgent and email is not practicable. Individuals should be aware of their surroundings and the presence of other individuals or voice recognition or ‘Internet of Things’ devices (e.g. virtual assistant apps like Alexa, Cortana, SIRI) to ensure they aren’t overheard by those that should not have access to the information discussed. Paper records: Printed paper records must always be kept to a minimum and kept secure whether in the office, home or during transit. Organisations must adopt an appropriate policy surrounding the use and transfer of paper records. Appropriate security methods must be applied when storing or disposing of paper records. . Access controls and security All parties will ensure that they have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place to guard against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, personal data. All personal data held by partner organisations electronically will be stored in a secure network area with password protected entry and appropriate back-up functionality. The systems will be auditable so that it is possible for any auditor to establish who has accessed the system. All laptops, computers, and any other portable devices will be encrypted. Any individual no longer required to have access will promptly have such access revoked by the line manager and Human Resources related to the relevant employer. There is an expectation that partner organisations will either be working toward ISO 27001, the International Standard for Information Security Management, or a similar standard of security such as NHS Digital’s Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSP ) and Cyber Essentials or Cyber Essentials Plus. . Outside UK processing There is no intention to shared data outside the UK. Parties are responsible for ensuring that if information is processed or shared outside the UK, that appropriate safeguards are in place and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. These are for example, a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies, binding corporate rules, and/or standard data protection contractual clauses. . Data quality Each partner is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and relevance of the personal data that it processes and shares and must have clear processes in place for managing data quality. Any party learning of the inaccuracy of personal data is responsible for informing the parties with whom that data has been shared. . Data breaches/incidents All parties must have a clear policy and procedure regarding the reporting and handling of data protection breaches or data loss incidents. This must include assessing the level of risk to the data subject(s), as well as to make a decision on notifying the ICO within the statutory time frame of 72 hours. This complies with Articles 33 and 34 of UK GDPR. If the incident may impact the processing of another party to this agreement, all relevant parties should be informed and appropriate coordination of the incident must take place. The decision to report the incident will lie with the data controller(s) of the information concerned. The parties agree to provide all reasonable and necessary assistance at their own expense to each other to facilitate the handling of any personal data breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. It is confirmed that security breaches (including misuse or unauthorised disclosure) are covered by the partner’s internal disciplinary procedures. If misuse is found there should be a mechanism to facilitate an investigation, including initiating criminal proceedings where necessary. . Retention and Disposal Organisations are required by data protection legislation to document processing activities for personal data, such as what personal data is held, where it came from and with whom it has been shared. This Record of Processing Activity (ROPA) must include the retention period for the data. Information must not be retained for longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was obtained. Disposal or deletion of personal data once it is no longer required, must be done securely with appropriate safeguards, in accordance with that organisation’s disposal policies. . Appendix C: Asset Plus Contents Section 1: Core Record Summarises information from the rest of the framework and the wider case management system, including: personal information parent/carer details current and previous offending or anti-social behaviour risk of harm, serious risk of harm and risk to the young person record of contact with other services details of the young person’s personal circumstances summary of key actions from the intervention plan Section 2: Information Gathering Collects information to explain the young person’s situation or behaviour, including: Personal, Family and Social Factors living arrangements and environmental factors parenting, family and relationships young person development learning, Education, training and employment Offending/anti-social Behaviour current offending patterns and attitudes other behaviours of concern Foundations for Change resilience, goals and attitudes opportunities engagement and participation factors affecting desistance Self-assessment questionnaires for young person and parents/carers Section 3: Explanations and Conclusions Practitioners will pull together and analyse elements of the Information Gathering section to make judgements about the young person in four main areas: . explaining offending behaviour patterns and trends based on the young person’s individual context . considering potential future behaviour, its likelihood and impact . use 1 and 2 alongside an indicative rating of reoffending to determine the likelihood of reoffending rating and Risk of Serious Harm rating . making a professional judgement about the likelihood and impact of adverse outcomes in relation to the young person’s safety and well-being Section 4: Pathways and Planning Supports practitioners to identify outcomes and plans that link to risks and positive factors identified in the Explanations and Conclusions section: outlines judgements made in the assessment alongside an indicative Scaled Approach Intervention Level frames the young person’s intervention plan around what can or needs to be done to deliver 5 key outcomes: repairing the harm (Restorative Justice) not reoffending not hurting others goals and life opportunities safety and well-being outlines targets and actions that will seek to deliver the intended outcomes highlights areas where there is a need for referral and gives consideration to engagement, risk, safety management and changing circumstances

Energy Bills Support Scheme Alternative Funding Data Sharing Agreement Between: The Secretary of State for the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy (“BEIS”) and a local authority, as defined in the Energy Prices Act , and more particularly listed in Annex A to the Grant Determination Letter (each an “Authority”) In this Agreement the following words and phrases will have the following meanings: “BEIS” means the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy “Partners” means parties to this Agreement, namely the Secretary of State for Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy and an Authority “DPA” means the Data Protection Act 2018 “DSA” means this Data Sharing Agreement FoIA means the Freedom of Information Act 2000 FOISA means the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 Guidance means the guidance for local authorities in Great Britain relating to the operation of the Energy Bills Support Scheme Alternative Funding (“Energy Bills Support Scheme Alternative Funding Guidance for local authorities in Great Britain”) UK GDPR means UK General Data Protection Regulation “Controller” “Personal Data Breach” “Processor” “Data Subject” have the meanings set out in Article 4 of the UK GDPR “Processing” “Personal Data” “Special Category data” . This DSA sets out the data sharing arrangements between the “Partners”, that is BEIS and an Authority, in relation to the delivery of the Energy Bills Support Scheme Alternative Funding to domestic energy consumers in Great Britain (“Scheme”). . The Scheme is intended to facilitate the £400 payment of support for domestic energy consumers in Great Britain that would otherwise not receive that support through the Energy Bills Support Scheme due to the absence of a domestic electricity supply. Once domestic energy consumers have applied to receive support and their application has gone through internal verification, eligible applicants' details will be shared with local authorities (for England, Scotland and Wales). . This DSA envisages a two-way Personal Data transfer, in that BEIS will be sharing Personal Data, as contained in the applications made to BEIS by the applicants, with an Authority, and an Authority will be sharing Personal Data back with BEIS in respect of reporting connected with the monitoring, fraud prevention and effectiveness of the Scheme. . The legal bases for BEIS for Processing the relevant Personal Data, including Special Category Data, include (i) the performance of a task carried out in the public interest under Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR, and (ii) the substantial public interest under Article (2)(g) of UK GDPR, more particularly in the context of the exercise of governmental functions, preventing or detecting unlawful acts, regulatory requirements relating to unlawful acts and dishonesty, and preventing fraud, as set out in Part 2 of Schedule 1 to the DPA. In particular, this Processing is necessary for the administration, delivery, reporting, monitoring, evaluation of the Scheme, as well as in connection with fraud prevention, and pre- and post- payment assurance and financial management activities to be undertaken in connection with the Scheme. . It is acknowledged and agreed that the Personal Data will be stored within a secure database within Salesforce, and it will be accessed via a secure system with restricted, on a “need to know” only basis, access by an Authority only for the purposes set out in

Consideration Parties (1) THE MAYOR AND BURGESSES OF THE LONDON BOROUGH OF CAMDEN of Town Hall, Judd Street, London WC1H 9JE (“the Council”); and (2) Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) whose registered office is at 169 Union Street, Southwark, London SE1 0LL. (“Provider”). Each referred to as a “Party” and together the “Parties”. A. The following agreement between the Parties reflects the arrangements that they have agreed to put in place between LB Camden, on behalf of the London Resettlement Partnership (LRP) and the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) who are evaluating the LRP Pathfinder. B. The Parties are data controllers and this Agreement explains the purposes for which the Personal Data may be used. C. As such, the Parties agree to share the Personal Data with each other on the terms set out in this Agreement. . INTERPRETATION Definitions “Agreed Purposes” shall mean the agreed purposes for sharing the Personal Data, as detailed in the Schedule; “Controller” shall have the same meaning as set out in the DPA 2018/UK GDPR and for the purposes of this Agreement both Parties shall be Controllers as further detailed in the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Data Discloser” shall mean the Party that discloses data to the other Party to this Agreement; “Data Loss Event” shall mean any event that results, or may result, in unauthorised access to Personal Data held by the Contractor under this Agreement, and/or actual or potential loss and/or destruction of Personal Data in breach of this Agreement, including any Personal Data Breach; “DPA 2018” shall mean the Data Protection Act 2018; “Data Protection Impact Assessment” shall mean an assessment by the Controller of the impact of the envisaged processing on the protection of Personal Data; “Data Protection Legislation” shall have the meaning ascribed to it by Data Protection Act 2018 section 3(9): “Data Protection Officer” shall have the same meaning as set out in the DPA 2018/UK GDPR and for the purposes of this Agreement shall be identified in the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Data Subject” shall have the same meaning as set out in the DPA 2018/UK GDPR and for the purposes of this Agreement shall be identified in the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Data Subject Access Request” shall mean a request made by, or on behalf of, a Data Subject in accordance with rights granted pursuant to the Data Protection Legislation to access their Personal Data; “UK GDPR” shall mean the UK implemented General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679); “ICO” shall mean the Information Commissioner's Office in the United Kingdom; “Law” shall mean any law, subordinate legislation within the meaning of Section 21(1) of the Interpretation Act 1978, bye-law, regulation, order, regulatory policy, mandatory guidance or code of practice, judgment of a relevant court of law, or directives or requirements with which the Contractor is bound to comply; “Personal Data” shall have the same meaning as set out in Section 3(2) of the Data Protection Act 2018 and for the purposes of this Contract shall be identified in the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Personal Data Breach” shall have the same meaning as set out in the UK GDPR and includes but is not limited to the exposure or potential or possible exposure of data including but not limited to Personal Data to any third parties to the Contract or those who have neither a contractual nor statutory right of access to the data including any circumstances in which such exposure or possible exposure would constitute a breach of the provisions of the Data Protection Legislation; “Process” has the meaning given to it under the Data Protection Legislation and for the purposes of this Agreement, the processing activities taking place are described in the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Processor” shall have the same meaning as set out in the DPA 2018/UK GDPR; “Protective Measures” shall mean the appropriate technical and organisational measures which may include: pseudonymising and encrypting Personal Data, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems and services, ensuring that availability of and access to Personal Data can be restored in a timely manner after an incident, and regularly assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of the such measures adopted by it; “Schedule” means the Schedule of Processing, Personal Data and Data Subjects; “Staff” shall mean all directors, officers, employees, agents, consultants and contractors of the Contractor and/or of any Sub-processor engaged in the performance of its obligations under this Agreement; “Sub-processor” shall mean any third party appointed to process Personal Data on behalf of the Contractor related to this Agreement. “Term” shall mean the duration of this Agreement as detailed in the Schedule. . PURPOSE This Agreement sets out the framework for the sharing of Personal Data between the Parties as Data Controllers and defines the principles and procedures that the Parties shall adhere to and the responsibilities the Parties owe to each other. The Personal Data subject to this Agreement is listed within the Schedule. The sharing of Personal Data is necessary to support the Agreed Purposes as listed within the Schedule. It is recognised that there are significant benefits to the Parties of having access to the Shared Personal Data to achieve the Agreed Purposes. This Agreement is required to ensure that where Personal Data may be accessed, such access will at all times comply with the Data Protection Legislation. . COMPLIANCE The Parties agree that this Agreement formalises the lawful transfer of the Personal Data between the Parties and presents no new or additional privacy concerns. A data protection impact assessment has been conducted in respect of the Personal Data to be shared and the necessity of the sharing and this Agreement serves to address any residual privacy or information risks and documents the actions taken to identify, address and mitigate those risks wherever possible. The Parties shall not process the Personal Data in a way that is incompatible with the Agreed Purposes. As Data Controllers, the Parties remain responsible for ensuring that all uses of the Personal Data are in compliance with all applicable Data Protection Legislation. This Agreement must be formally approved and signed by the Parties before any Personal Data is shared by persons with authority to do so on behalf of their organisation. All Parties will ensure that the terms of this Agreement are known and understood by all Staff involved in the sharing of the Personal Data. Each Party is registered with the ICO has a valid Data Protection Registration Number with its national Data Protection Authority if required by the Enterprise Act which by the time that the data sharing is expected to commence, covers the intended data sharing pursuant to this Agreement. The Council’s ICO registration number is Z5948361 and the Provider’s ICO registration number is Z2972789. . PERSONAL DATA The Parties shall, in relation to any of the Personal Data processed in connection with its obligations under this Agreement: Process that Personal Data only in accordance with the Schedule, unless the Parties are required to do otherwise by Law, which should be notified to the other Parties (unless notification is prohibited by Law); not Process in an irrelevant or excessive way with regard to the Agreed Purposes; ensure they do not knowingly or negligently do or omit to do anything which places the Parties breach of the obligations under the Data Protection Legislation; ensure that they have in place Protective Measures to protect against: a) unauthorised or unlawful processing of Personal Data; b) accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, Personal Data, and such measures to be reviewed as appropriate to protect against a Data Loss Event having taken account of the: (i) nature of the data to be protected; (ii) harm that might result from a Data Loss Event; (iii) state of technological development; and (iv) cost of implementing any measures; ensure the Personal Data is kept and stored securely in accordance with Data Protection Legislation; ensure that: (i) the Staff do not process Personal Data except in accordance the Schedule; (ii) each Party takes all reasonable steps to ensure the reliability and integrity of any Staff who have access to the Personal Data and ensure that they: (A) are aware of and comply with the duties under this Agreement; (B) are subject to appropriate confidentiality undertakings; (C) are informed of the confidential nature of the Personal Data and do not publish, disclose or divulge any of the Personal Data to any third party unless permitted by this Agreement; and (D) have undergone adequate training in the use, care, protection and handling of the Personal Data; not transfer the Personal Data outside of the UK unless the prior written consent of all Parties has been obtained and the following conditions are fulfilled: a) the Parties have provided appropriate safeguards in relation to the transfer (whether in accordance with UK GDPR Article 46 or LED Article ); b) the Data Subject has enforceable rights and effective legal remedies; c) the Parties outside the UK comply with the obligations under the Data Protection Legislation by providing an adequate level of protection to any Personal Data that is transferred (or, if it is not so bound, uses its best endeavours to assist the Parties in meeting its obligations under the Data Protection Legislation); securely destroy or return the Personal Data (and any copies of it) to the Data Discloser upon termination or expiry of this Agreement unless the Parties are required by Law to retain the Personal Data; and as far as is reasonably practical, anonymise or pseudonymise all Personal Data contained in statistics, reports and summaries to minimise the amount of Personal Data shared. . FAIR, LAWFUL AND TRANSPARENT PROCESSING The Personal Data shall be shared in accordance with the Agreed Purposes on the basis of the legal grounds as stated in the Schedule. The Parties undertake to inform Data Subjects of the purposes for which it will process their Personal Data and provide all of the information that it must provide in accordance with applicable laws, to ensure that the Data Subjects understand how their Personal Data will be processed by the Data Controller. The Parties shall, in respect of the Personal Data, ensure that their privacy notices are clear and provide sufficient information to Data Subjects, in order for them to understand: what Personal Data the Parties are sharing; the circumstances in which it will be shared; the purposes for the sharing; either the identity with whom the Personal Data is shared or a description of the type of organisation that will receive the Personal Data unless an exemption to the transparency provisions applies. . DATA QUALITY The Data Discloser shall ensure that the Personal Data is accurate. Where either Party becomes aware of inaccuracies in the Personal Data, they will notify the other Party immediately. . DATA SUBJECTS' RIGHTS Data Subjects have the right to obtain certain information about the processing of their Personal Data through a Subject Access Request. Data Subjects may also request rectification, erasure or blocking of their Personal Data. The Parties shall maintain a record of Subject Access Requests, the decisions made and any information that was exchanged. Records must include copies of the request for information, details of the data accessed and shared and where relevant, notes of any meeting, correspondence or phone calls relating to the request, together with relevant dates. falls to Party receiving the Subject Access Request in respect of the Personal Data held by that Party. The Parties agree to provide reasonable and prompt assistance (within 5 business days of such a request for assistance) at their own expense as is necessary to each other to enable them to comply with Subject Access Requests and to respond to any other queries or complaints from Data Subjects. . DATA RETENTION AND DELETION The Data Receiver shall not retain or process Personal Data for longer than is necessary to carry out the Agreed Purposes. Notwithstanding Clause 8.1, the Parties shall continue to retain the Personal Data in accordance with any internal or statutory retention periods applicable in their organisations and/or industry. The Data Receiver shall ensure that any Personal Data is returned to the Data Discloser or destroyed in the following circumstances: (a) upon termination of the Agreement for whatever reason; (b) upon expiry of the Term (unless extended further in accordance the terms of this Agreement); and (c) once processing of the Personal Data is no longer necessary for the Agreed Purposes. . TRANSFERS For the purposes of this Clause, transfers of Personal Data shall mean any sharing of the Personal Data by the Data Receiver with a third party, and shall include, but is not limited to, the following: a) sharing of the Personal Data with any third party; b) publication of the Personal Data via any medium, including, but not limited to social media, websites, publicly available communications. c) storing Personal Data on servers outside the UK; d) subcontracting the processing of Personal Data to data processors located outside the UK; e) granting third parties located outside the UK access rights to the Personal Data. The Data Receiver shall not share the Personal Data with a third party without the express written permission of the Data Discloser save as required by law or court order. Where Personal Data is to be shared under clause 9.2, the Data Receiver shall not disclose or transfer the Personal Data outside the UK without first ensuring that adequate and equivalent protections will be afforded to the Personal Data. . SECURITY AND TRAINING The Parties agree to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect the Personal Data in their possession against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, damage, alteration or disclosure, including but not limited to: a) ensuring IT equipment, including portable equipment is kept in lockable areas when unattended; b) not leaving portable equipment containing the Personal Data unattended; c) ensuring Staff use appropriate secure passwords for logging into systems or databases containing the Personal Data; d) ensuring that all IT equipment is protected by antivirus software, firewalls, passwords and suitable encryption devices; e) ensuring that any Special Category Personal Data is stored and transferred (including where stored or transferred on portable devices or removable media) using industry standard 256-bit AES encryption or suitable equivalent; f) limiting access to relevant databases and systems to those Staff who need to have access to the Personal Data, and ensuring that passwords are changed and updated regularly to prevent inappropriate access when individuals are no longer engaged by the Party; g) conducting regular threat assessment or penetration testing on systems; h) ensuring all Staff handling Personal Data have been made aware of their responsibilities with regards to handling of the Personal Data; and i) allowing for inspections and assessments to be undertaken by the other Party in respect of the security measures taken, or producing evidence of those measures if requested. . PERSONAL DATA BREACHES AND REPORTING PROCEDURES The Parties shall ensure they do not knowingly or negligently do or omit to do anything which places either Party in breach of the Data Protection Legislation. Each Party shall inform the other immediately if it: a) is in breach of the Protective Measures requirements; b) receives a request to rectify, block or erase the Personal Data; c) receives any complaint or communication relating to either Party's obligations under the Data Protection Legislation; d) receives any communication from the Information Commissioner or any other regulatory authority in connection with the Personal Data; e) receives a request from any third party for disclosure of the Personal Data where compliance with such request is required or purported to be required by Law; or f) becomes aware of a Data Loss Event, and without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours, shall notify the other Parties, by: (i) contacting the Data Protection Officer(s) as detailed within the Schedule; and (ii) informing them of the Data Loss Event, including in its notification: (A) a description of the Data Loss Event including where possible, the categories and approximate number of Data Subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of data records concerned; and (B) a description of the measures taken or proposes to take to address the Data Loss Event, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects. Following the notification of a Data Loss Event, the informing Party shall immediately assess the risks and consequences of the Data Loss Event and take measures, including: (i) to mitigate the possible adverse effects of the Data Loss Event; and (ii) to protect the data and the interests/safety of the Data Subject and/or Data Controller, and inform the other Parties as to the measures that it has taken. The informing Party’s obligation to notify shall include the provision of further information in phases, as details become available. . RESOLUTION OF DISPUTES WITH DATA SUBJECTS OR THE DATA Taking into account the nature of the processing, the Parties shall provide each other, at their own expense, with full assistance in relation to the Personal Data and the obligations under Data Protection Legislation and any complaint, communication or request made including by promptly providing (and in any event within 24 hours of being received): i. full details and copies of the complaint, communication or request; ii. such assistance as is reasonably requested to enable the Parties to comply with a Data Subject Access Request within the relevant timescales set out in the Data Protection Legislation; iii. assistance as required with respect to any request from the Information Commissioner’s Office, or any consultation by the Parties with the Information Commissioner's Office; iv. any Personal Data it holds in relation to a Data Subject (as appropriate) within the timescales required by the Council; and v. each other Party with any information requested in relation to the request. . RECORDS The Parties shall maintain complete and accurate records and information to demonstrate its compliance with Data Protection Legislation. The Parties may reasonably request information from each to satisfy itself that obligations under the Data Protection Legislation are being met in relation to the Personal Data. Sub-processing Before allowing any Sub-processor to process any Personal Data related to this Agreement, the Parties must: a) notify the other Parties in writing of the intended Sub-processor and processing; b) obtain the written consent of the Parties; c) enter into a written agreement with the Sub-processor which gives effect to the terms set out in this Condition such that they apply to the Sub-processor; and d) provide the Parties with such information regarding the Sub-processor as the Parties may reasonably require. The appointing Party shall remain fully liable for all acts or omissions of any Subprocessor. . WARRANTIES Each Party warrants and undertakes that it will: (a) Process the Personal Data in compliance with all applicable laws, enactments, regulations, orders, standards and other similar instruments that apply; (b) respond to Subject Access Requests in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and in accordance with the DPA 2018/UK GDPR; (c) make available upon request to the Data Subjects a copy of this Agreement, unless the Agreement contains confidential information; (d) respond within a reasonable time and as far as reasonably possible to enquiries from the relevant Data Protection Authority in relation to the Personal Data; (e) where applicable, maintain registration with all relevant Data Protection Authorities to process the Personal Data for the Agreed Purpose; and (f) take all appropriate steps to ensure compliance with the security measures set out in Clause 10. The Data Discloser shall ensure that the Personal Data is accurate. The Parties agree to take account of any guidance issued by the Information Commissioner’s Office. The Council may on not less than 30 Working Days’ notice to the Parties to amend this Agreement to ensure that it complies with any guidance. Each Party shall be responsible for their own costs incurred in complying with this Agreement. . TERM AND TERMINATION the Schedule. The Agreement shall automatically terminate on expiry of the Term unless, following a review of the terms of the Agreement, the Parties agree to extend the Agreement. Any such renewal shall be in writing signed by an authorised signatory of all Parties and the Parties shall seek to agree any such renewal at least 2 months in advance of the expiry of the Term. The provisions of this Agreement shall apply during the continuance of the Agreement and indefinitely after its expiry or termination. . ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES Each Party shall nominate a single point of contact within their organisation who may be contacted in respect of queries or complaints regarding DPA 2018/UK GDPR and/or compliance under the terms of this Agreement, as detailed within the Schedule. . THIRD PARTY RIGHTS No one other than a Party to this Agreement shall have any right to enforce any of its terms. . VARIATION No variation of this Agreement shall be effective unless it is in writing and signed by the Parties (or their authorised representatives). . WAIVER No failure or delay by a Party to exercise any right or remedy provided under this Agreement or by law shall constitute a waiver of that or any other right or remedy, nor shall it prevent or restrict the further exercise of that or any other right or remedy. No single or partial exercise of such right or remedy shall prevent or restrict the further exercise of that or any other right or remedy. . SEVERANCE If any provision of this Agreement (or part of any provision) is found by any court or other authority of competent jurisdiction to be invalid, illegal or unenforceable, that provision or part-provision shall, to the extent required, be deemed not to form part of this Agreement, and the validity and enforceability of the other provisions of this Agreement shall not be affected. If a provision of this Agreement (or part of any provision) is found to be illegal, invalid or unenforceable, the provision shall apply with the minimum modification necessary to make it legal, valid and enforceable. CHANGES TO THE APPLICABLE LAW In case the applicable data protection and ancillary laws change in a way that the Agreement is no longer adequate for the purpose of governing lawful data sharing exercises, the Parties agree that they will negotiate in good faith to review the Agreement in light of the new legislation. Legal Basis for sharing and Personal data: Article 6(1) (c) legal duty and 6(1)(e) processing is Privacy notice requirements necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest . The Crime and Disorder Act 1998 gives each LA in England & Wales has the responsibility to formulate a strategy to reduce crime and disorder in their area and to work with police authorities to do this. Section 115 of the Act gives partners the power to share information for the purpose of reducing crime and disorder. Schedule 9 (5) of the Police and Justice Act strengthens this by introducing a new duty on the same agencies. The Children Act 1989 Under S.47 of the Children’s Act 1989, a Local Authority has a duty to investigate when informed that a child in their area is in police protection or the subject of a protection order. The Children Act 2004, as amended by the Children and Social Work Act , places duties on key agencies in a local area. Specifically, the police, clinical commissioning groups and the local authority are under a duty to make arrangements to work together, and with other partners locally, to safeguard and promote the welfare of all children in their area. The Statutory Guidance - Working Together to Safeguard Children (2018) and Information Sharing – Advice to Practitioners providing safeguarding services to Children, Young People, Parents, and Carers (July 2018) emphasise the need to share appropriately. Special Category Data: Art 9(g) Reasons of substantial public interest (with a basis in law) and (h) Health or social care (with a basis in law). For art 9(g) the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 conditions are para 6 (Statutory and government purposes) and para 18 (Safeguarding of children and of individuals at risk) with the underlying law being that identified in art 6 above; and for art 9(h) the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1 condition is (2)(2)(e) Health or social care purposes, the provision of social care. The underlying law is the same as for art 6. Criminal Offence Data the processing complies with Art 10, the art 6 condition is as noted above and the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 conditions are as noted above. Appendix 1 11 ) Introduction to the Sharing This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement will share personal data about Staff and service users to enable both Parties’ single service Public Health functions and the jointly delivered Public Health functions (described in Appendix 1) to be delivered. The Parties note there is an umbrella Memorandum of Understanding between them for Public Health functions, with this DSA covering the Data Protection requirements of the service. By signing this DSA the Parties agree to accept the conditions set out in this document, according to their statutory and professional responsibilities, and agree to adhere to the procedures described. This Agreement has been developed to: ● Define the specific purposes for which the Parties have agreed to share information. ● Outline the Personal and Special Category to be shared. ● Set out the lawful basis conditions under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared, including reference to the Human Rights Act 1998 ● Stipulate the roles and procedures that will support the processing/sharing of information between Parties. ● Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. ● Confirm the lead council for Joint Data Controller matters ● Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure that compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and Party-specific security requirements. ● Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. ● To illustrate the flow of information from referral through processing and outcome. Parties to this agreement cannot amend or add appendices unless agreed as part of a formal review. It is expected that each party will have procedures, processes and policies sitting underneath this agreement, for their respective organisations. These will, for example, describe the specific processes for secure transfer of data. . Responsibilities of Parties The Parties are registered with the ICO as Data Controllers. Each Party is a Data Controller for the data processed by each Party individually under this DSA. In respect of the jointly delivered work through shared posts described in Appendix 1 the Parties are Joint Data Controllers. It is agreed that for the jointly delivered work only, London Borough of Islington has primary responsibility for complying with UK GDPR obligations in respect of transparency obligations and individuals’ rights. For the other Public Health work, not jointly delivered, each Party will comply with its obligations around transparency and individuals’ rights. Both Parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: ● having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ● ensuring data quality. ● storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. ● having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including for managing data subject rights and complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ● ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality, and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. ● undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ, and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. ● having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Organisations and their staff must consult the organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian if they are unsure at any point in the processing and sharing of personal data. Each Partner must ensure that there are appropriate written contracts or agreements with employees, agency staff, volunteers etc. These must include requirements to ensure compliance with policies which include confidentiality. Each Partner must ensure that suitable vetting has taken place through standard employee checks and DBS checks as needed. In respect of data disclosed to either Party under this agreement the Parties agree that each Party is a Data Controller and therefore is responsible for onward sharing and other handling of such data in accordance with Data Protection laws. . Review and Termination of this DSA A review of this information sharing agreement will take place yearly, unless otherwise agreed by the Parties’ Data Protection Officers. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, the scope has not slipped, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. Changes in legislation and developments in the areas of public sector data sharing will be considered as and when they arise. In the event of termination of this agreement each party may continue to hold information originating from other parties for which they are Data Controller. Termination requires three month’s written Notice (email is acceptable) from the terminating Partner’s Director of Public Health to the other Partner’s Director of Public Health, with such Notice being copied to the both Partners’ DPOs at the contact emails in Section 5 below. . Purpose and Benefits . Purpose and Benefits This agreement covers the sharing of information by and between the listed parties for the purpose of delivering an effective Public Health service across both Boroughs. In respect of the jointly delivered Public Health functions (described in Appendix 1) the sharing will allow the service to be delivered effectively and efficiently, attaining the economies of scale intended by the shared function. In respect of data sharing for the functions delivered independently by each Party, the sharing will allow each Party to better deliver its Public Health functions to its residents resulting in better value for money, and shared expertise leading to higher quality outcomes for residents. The sharing will allow both partners to better deliver their statutory series and will allow more effective use of resources, giving more joined up working which increases efficiency. The public will benefit from this approach, as services will be delivered in a more streamlined way that utilises the information shared to provide better tailored and appropriate services. The benefits of this DSA are to: ● Cover the sharing of information for ● Sets parameters for sharing personal data and clearly identifies the responsibilities of organisations. ● Identify the correct lawful basis to share personal information. ● Ensure information is shared whenever there is a requirement to do so. ● Enables authorities to share data on performance, quality assurance, learning and impact analysis. . Lawful Basis The sharing of information must comply with the law relating to confidentiality, data protection and human rights. Having a legitimate purpose for sharing information is an important part of meeting those legal requirements. This is a complex area and each Partner must take their own decisions and seek advice from their organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian. Articles 6, 9 and 10 of the UK GDPR set out the acceptable conditions for the processing and sharing of personal, special category, and criminal data. The conditions relevant in the UK GDPR to data processed under this agreement are below. Local authorities engaged in the provision of Health and Social Care are required to do so under one or more of the following acts, and their amended or updated regulations: Care Act 2014 Children Act 2004 Health and Social Care Act 2012 National Health Service Act 2016 The Health and Social Care Act 2012 gives Local Authorities powers to perform public health functions, including commissioning and collaborating on a range of public health services to improve and protect the health of the local population and reduce health inequalities, and for advising the commissioners of local NHS services as well as the health and wellbeing boards on these matters. Local authorities engaged in Public Health provision are required to do so under one or more of the following regulations and their successors: Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 Statistics and Registration Service Act (2007) Section 42(4) Health and Social Care Act (2012) section 287 Health Service (Control of Patient Information) Regulations 2002 regulation 3 These acts create and delegate ministerial functions in the public interest, and the Data Protection Act section 8 specifically permits these as being purposes for Article 6 1(e) of UK GDPR – tasks in the public interest. Where the parties are to share personal information that relates to a person’s private or family life, the right to privacy in Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) will be applicable. Personal data: For the sharing of data between the Parties for general Public Health matters and for the shared service: Article 6(1) (c) legal duty and 6(1)(e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or for the parties’ official functions, and the task has a clear basis in law. For London Borough of Islington processing data on the behalf of London Borough of Camden for the shared service: Article 6(1) (c) legal duty and 6(1)(e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or for the parties’ official functions, and the task has a clear basis in law, and where the processing is providing a service direct to the public for which is consent is required, consent under article 6(1)(a). Special Category Data: For the sharing of data between the Parties for general Public Health matters and for the shared service: Art 9(g) Reasons of substantial public interest (with a basis in law), and permitted under the Data Protection Act 2018 Section 10 (Substantial Public Interest) as it meets the following conditions set out in Schedule 1 Part 2 para 6 (Statutory and government purposes) and para 18 (Safeguarding of children and of individuals at risk) Art 9(h) Health or social care (with a basis in law), and permitted under the Data Protection Act Schedule 1 Part 1 (2)(2) (d) the provision of health care or treatment, and (e) Health or social care purposes Art 9 (i) Public health (with a basis in law), and permitted under the Data Protection Act 2018 Section 10 the Data Protection Act 2018 (Public Health) as it meets the following conditions set out in Schedule 1 Part 1 (3) (a)(b) Public Health For London Borough of Islington processing data on the behalf of London Borough of Camden for the shared service: the same as above, plus where the processing is providing a service direct to the public for which is consent is required, explicit consent under article 9(a) . Consent Consent is not the lawful basis the public sector organisations use for processing information shared under this agreement, except where the Shared posts are providing health services directly to the public. It is noted that where consent is not the lawful basis for processing, consent does not need to be sought to share, and thus the concept of “overriding consent” is a misconception. Where consent is required the UK GDPR requirements for this will be met. . Proportionality and necessity Proportionality, data minimisation, necessity and not being excessive are factors to be taken into consideration when deciding whether to share personal information. In making the decision, employees must weigh up what might happen as a result of the information being shared against what might happen if it is not, and apply their professional judgement. It is for this reason professionals must ensure they comply with Article 5(1)(c) and share the adequate and relevant information, and limit that information to what is necessary for the achieving of the DSA aims. . Freedom of Information The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives all individuals the right to access official information held by a public authority (the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 also allow access to data. For ease of drafting, FOI is used to cover both legislation). Limited exemptions may apply and all public authorities must ensure they have recognised procedures in place for administering requests of this nature. All requests for FOI will be directed through the relevant organisations’ FOI processes. Each party will seek advice/opinion from the other parties where there is concern about that information being released and any impact it is likely to have. The final decision to disclose or not will lie with the party who received the request as the legal duty lies with them. In order to ensure that the authority in receipt of the FOIA request is able to respond within the statutory deadline, any request for assistance or information made to partner authorities should be made and processed within two working days, and any data exchange completed within seven working days. It is encouraged that all parties proactively publish this document. It may also be disclosed to the public under FOI. . Individuals Organisations processing personal data are required to begin with the ethos of Data Protection by Design and Default (also known as Privacy by Design (PbD)). This means that we must consider and uphold the privacy of an individual’s data before we begin and throughout the processing taking place. Each party agrees that they have undertaken a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment), where they feel the processing meets the legislative criteria for a DPIA. . Right to be informed – Privacy notices Where personal data is created or received by one of the parties, they are responsible, as required by law, for making the data subject(s) aware within a reasonable time frame that the organisation holds the data, what they will do with it, how long they will keep it, and who they will share it with (such as under this DSA). This is normally done through a privacy notice, whether written or verbal. Organisations agree that they will adhere to the transparency requirements of the UK GDPR and will issue appropriate notices which inform the data subject that the information will be shared with the parties under this agreement. For the Shared Service Posts, London Borough of Islington will act as the lead Data Controller for providing Privacy and Transparency information. . Data subject rights requests and complaints Each organisation must have in place appropriate policies and processes to handle data subject requests made in line with data protection law, to ensure they are responded to within deadline and in an appropriate manner. Requests include; right of access, right to rectification, right to erasure, right to restrict processing, right to data portability, right to object and rights related to automated decision making including profiling. If an individual successfully requests the erasure or limitation of use of their data (right to erasure, right to rectification, right to restrict processing, right to object), the party that has been informed by the data subject will communicate this to the other parties where relevant and appropriate. In each case each party is responsible for securely disposing of such information or limiting its processing. Each party must have clear, fair and objective complaint procedures. Any complaints from individuals how their data is being processed or shared will be handled under the policy and processes of the organisation concerned. For the Shared Service Posts, London Borough of Islington will act as the lead Data Controller for Data Subject Rights requests and complaints. . Data subjects The data subjects will be: Staff employed by either Partner Public Health service Members of the public engaging with the Shared Public Health functions Professionals involved with either of the above . Data . The data to be shared Data that will be shared includes (but is not limited to): ● name and contact details ● address ● age/date of birth ● Telephone number ● NHS Number ● Gender ● Race, Nationality and Religious or philosophical beliefs (to allow programme to be delivered in a culturally appropriate way) ● Special Educational Needs and Disabilities ● Health needs assessments ● Personal data relating to smoking cessation ● Births and deaths data ● Hospital episode statistics ● Sexual health data ● Opinion data of residents collected via focus groups, surveys and other forms of engagement ● Physical or mental health or condition (to allow risk assessments to be made and necessary actions taken) ● Linked health and social care datasets . Storing and handling information securely Information must be stored and shared lawfully and securely. Special category data may need a higher level of security. The employee/organisation sharing the information must choose the most appropriate secure method of transfer and be responsible for its safe delivery. Electronic records: Organisations may have different electronic methods for storing and sharing information securely. Some have local restrictions which block access to information shared using specific tools. Parties must make sure the chosen method is suitably secure and that access is only provided to those who need it, and only to the data needed. Unencrypted email (i.e. sent in plain text over the public internet) must not be used to share information under this DSA. Sharing methods that may be appropriate include: ● Email encryption tools where the email and attachments are encrypted from named sender to named recipient (e.g. Microsoft 365 Message Encryption; Egress Protect) ● Encryption via Transport Layer Security (TLS) where the email and attachments are encrypted in transit over the internet. Both the sender and recipient email domains must have TLS enabled. This can be checked using ● Secure corporately managed data repository and sharing platforms (e.g. MS Teams; Google Docs) ● Secure group email services (e.g. CJSM: ● Secure File Transfer Protocols ● Virtual Private Networks The above are examples, get advice from your organisation’s information security or IT teams on secure methods of sharing available at your organisation and document these in the organisation’s process documents. Phone/virtual meetings/face-to-face meetings: Information may be shared over the phone, in a virtual meeting, or at face to face meetings. Meeting attendance and distribution of content, e.g. meeting minutes or recordings, must be limited to those with a need to know. Sharing by telephone should be avoided unless the requirement is urgent and email is not practicable. Individuals should be aware of their surroundings and the presence of other individuals or voice recognition or ‘Internet of Things’ devices (e.g. virtual assistant apps like Alexa, Cortana, SIRI) to ensure they aren’t overheard by those that should not have access to the information discussed. Paper records: Printed paper records must always be kept to a minimum and kept secure whether in the office, home or during transit. Organisations must adopt an appropriate policy surrounding the use and transfer of paper records. Appropriate security methods must be applied when storing or disposing of paper records. . Access controls and security Both Parties will ensure that they have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place to guard against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, personal data. All personal data held by the Parties electronically will be stored in a secure network area with password protected entry and appropriate back-up functionality. The systems will be auditable so that it is possible for any auditor to establish who has accessed the system. All laptops, computers, and any other portable devices will be encrypted. Any individual no longer required to have access will promptly have such access revoked by the line manager and Human Resources related to the relevant employer. Both partners are NHS Digital’s Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSP ) compliant. There is an expectation that partner organisations will either be working toward ISO 27001, the International Standard for Information Security Management, or a similar standard of security such as Cyber Essentials or Cyber Essentials Plus. . Outside UK processing There is no intention to share data outside the EEA. Parties are responsible for ensuring that if information is processed or shared outside the EEA, that appropriate safeguards are in place and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. These are for example, a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies, binding corporate rules, and/or standard data protection contractual clauses. . Data quality Each partner is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and relevance of the personal data that it processes and shares and must have clear processes in place for managing data quality. Any party learning of the inaccuracy of personal data is responsible for informing the parties with whom that data has been shared. . Data breaches/incidents All parties must have a clear policy and procedure regarding the reporting and handling of data protection breaches or data loss incidents. This must include assessing the level of risk to the data subject(s), as well as to make a decision on notifying the ICO within the statutory time frame of 72 hours. If the incident may impact the processing of another party to this agreement, all relevant parties should be informed and appropriate coordination of the incident must take place. The decision to report the incident will lie with the data controller(s) of the information concerned. The parties agree to provide all reasonable and necessary assistance at their own expense to each other to facilitate the handling of any personal data breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. It is confirmed that security breaches (including misuse or unauthorised disclosure) are covered by the partner’s internal disciplinary procedures. If misuse is found there should be a mechanism to facilitate an investigation, including initiating criminal proceedings where necessary. . Appendices .
