It is required because local public services, most notably local authority children’s services, are increasingly finding it necessary to share personal sensitive data with one another and with suppliers in order to deliver on their statutory responsibilities. Hosting data within the London Data Platform and running analysis within its secure environment will allow for increased data security, as it drastically reduces the risk of data breaches associated with email transfers, data downloads or holding data locally. The architecture of the platform has been designed specifically with this use-case in mind and it holds data security as its core principle. This architecture is detailed in “Data security” below. Social Finance will act as architectural principal for this project and will thus be responsible for the role of primary security contact and specifier. Amazon Web Services will be the service provider. Details of the appropriate certifications are outlined in the sections below. Data flows The data shared by the CONTROLLER goes through the following steps: . Upload data . Prepare data for analysis . Analyse data . Share analysis These are expanded upon below and are represented in the data flow diagram (Figure 1). The flows in steps 1 and 2 above are the same for all data processing activities covered by this agreement. Therefore, they are described in this schedule only. The flows in steps 3 and 4 are specific to each processing activity (e.g. Pan-London Sufficiency Analysis involves different flows to Social Worker Workforce Analysis as they involve different organisations processing data). Therefore: Steps 3 and 4 are described in detail in the schedules created for each of those activities. The only material we provide here regarding steps 3 and 4 is a generic description (e.g. PROCESSOR does X rather than named organisation does X). . Upload data The CONTROLLER is given access to a private folder in the London Data Platform and uploads the data there. This folder is only accessible by authorised personnel from the CONTROLLER and the London Data Platform. . Prepare data for analysis i. Preparing the data of a single CONTROLLER The PROCESSOR runs scripts within the London Data Platform environment to: Degrade certain data fields to protect data subject anonymity, e.g. date of birth transformed into month of birth; postcode transformed into postcode sector Assess data quality (missing values, logically inconsistent values) At the end of this process, the data is pseudonymised. Identification of individuals would only be possible with access to the CONTROLLER’s case management system. The CONTROLLER’s processed dataset is deposited back in the CONTROLLER’s private folder; the CONTROLLER can download the processed dataset for analysis. ii. Merging all Borough’s data together An additional process within the London Data Platform environment merges the datasets from all CONTROLLERS into a single pan-London dataset. During this process, additional data minimisation and data degradation steps may occur to ensure that only the data required for pan-London analysis is accessible. These additional steps will be detailed in Schedules 3 onwards. The processed dataset is deposited into the PROCESSOR’s private folder (“LIIA Analysis folder”) in the London Data Platform. . Analyse data Typically, each specific analysis (e.g. Pan-London Sufficiency Analysis) requires only a subset of the full dataset. It may require: Fewer than the full set of data subjects (e.g. only children in care, rather than all children with a social worker) Fewer than the full set of fields describing each data subject (e.g. only information about the children’s demographics and the placement, rather than information about needs and disabilities) Data from a shorter period of time than is available in the full dataset (e.g. just the last 12m) Therefore, in line with the principle of privacy by design a specific dataset is created for each analysis which contains the minimum data required for that analysis. These are stored in the LIIA Analysis folder. Access to each of these datasets in the LIIA Analysis folder is restricted to named individuals at the PROCESSOR (or named sub-processor) with direct involvement in analyses of that dataset, as described in Schedules 3 onwards. The PROCESSOR accesses the dataset in the LIIA Analysis folder in one of two ways: Local download via a secure username/password combination. The dataset is then stored in a restricted area of the PROCESSOR’s data warehouse with access granted only to staff directly involved in its analysis. Remote access via a secure link, connecting directly from within analytical software (e.g. Power BI). The dataset is stored in the cache of the analytical software only, with access granted only to staff directly involved in its analysis. Analysis conducted on the processed dataset is described in the relevant Schedule below. . Share the analysis Aggregated analytical outputs are shared with all Boroughs via securely hosted software (e.g. Power BI). In all shared outputs, it is no longer possible to identify individual data points. Boroughs will be identifiable in these shared analyses, allowing benchmarking and comparison between boroughs. Where appropriate the LIIA d&i team will provide pan-London aggregate anonymous data for work commissioned or approved by ALDCS/LIIA or as agreed with partner organisations (where this data has already been collected through the LIIA CLD project) and so help reduce burdens on individual LA data & performance teams (relates to all use cases). Folder access rights on London Data Platform Access to any part of the platform requires individual access credentials (controlled through the platform identity and access management system and governed by appropriate security technologies i.e. single-sign on via major identity providers, password complexity and multi-factor authentication). Controller’s private folder - The CONTROLLER’s private folder on the London Data Platform is created manually by the London Data Platform admin. Several staff members from the CONTROLLER can be given access to the folder. The PROCESSOR will not be able to access the data hosted in the CONTROLLER’s private folder. Beyond staff at the CONTROLLER, only London Data Platform admin will be able to access this data to grant access rights and initiate data processing. LIIA Analysis folder - The LIIA Analysis folder on the London Data Platform is only accessible by authorised personnel from the PROCESSOR conducting the analysis and the London Data Platform admin and data engineer. Data retention Unless otherwise specified, data will be retained until six years have elapsed since data collection. Previous analysis finds that six years is the minimum for good quality journey analysis (an analytical approach we expect to employ), but that having more than six years’ data does not materially help to answer new questions or answer existing questions with greater certainty or granularity. Maintenance of this retention is implemented as part of the automated processing of data on the London Data Platform. On termination of this agreement, all data will be deleted from the CONTROLLER’s private folder and the LIIA Analysis folder. The CONTROLLER can request the deletion of data at any time before the termination date. London Data Platform infrastructure The application is architected to be secure by design. It follows National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) best practice for cloud applications and its use of Amazon Web Services for all core application components means that it is based on the most solid and robust of cloud platforms. Specifically, it adheres to the NCSC guiding principles as follows: Principle 1 - Data in transit protection The Data Platform will use the latest SSL certificates. Connections will be 128bit encrypted and authenticated using TLS 1.2. (data encrypted in transit) Principle 2 - Asset protection and resilience Data will be hosted on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in a UK availability zone and a UK data centre. The AWS data centre is secure and highly monitored (full list of procedures in place available here). Data tables will be stored in AWS S3 buckets protected by a private key/user password combination. (data encrypted at rest) AWS is certified ISO 27001 (full list of AWS certifications available here). Principle 3 - Separation between customers Robust use of Identity and Access Management (IAM) prevents users accessing or processing data or systems outside their own. Principle 4 - Operational security The platform will be subject to robust and well-defined operational processes Releases will be timely and well managed through a deployment management framework Incident management will have clear procedures and communication will be timely Principle 5 – Governance framework A governance framework will be established to clearly define feature extension signoff, administration oversight and eventual handoff of the system to a suitable long term owner as required. Principle 6 - Personnel security AWS personnel are subject to robust vetting and security checks. Access to systems from inside the London Data Platform will be limited to those identified in the data flows section above. Principle 7 –Secure development Engineering will follow software development best practices, including merge protections and code review Deployment will be automated and follow a test > release process across multiple environments before production Code will be subjected to multiple levels of automated and manual testing Principle 8 - Supply chain security Software dependencies will be tracked and vulnerabilities automatically reported Dependencies in code run on the processing environment will be subject to a robust and well managed allow-list Principles 9 and 10 - Secure user management/ Identity and authentication Uploads will be Private as default. Single-sign-on via major identity service providers (Microsoft Active Directory, Google Cloud Identity) will provide best in class password complexity enforcement and multi-factorauthentication requirements. A full audit log for user access and data movement will be recorded Principle 11 - External interface protection Exposed user interfaces will follow best practice for user facing application security – including cross-site scripting protection and cross-site request forgery protection The minimum required API will be exposed to reduce the available attack surface to the smallest possible Principle 12 – Secure Services Administration Administration of AWS services and infrastructure is carried out entirely through the AWS console and administration system which is subject to the resiliency and security principles laid down by Amazon themselves. Principle13 - Resilience and auditing The application will be fully penetration tested before production release is granted. Regular security audits by qualified third-party organisations will be carried out. Data protection from loss and lack of availability on AWS is covered by their business continuity and disaster recovery policy. Principle 14 – Security by Design and Default The design of the system is such that users are subject to guardrails which prevent accidental misuse. Code run on the platform will be sandboxed and airgapped from the wider internet Controls and role based access will prevent data leaking between users or clients Figure 1 – LIIA data flows diagram Schedule 5 (Pan-London sufficiency analysis) This schedule provides details of the data flow for care episode data for looked after children through the LIIA platform. The data submitted by the CONTROLLER is the Children Looked After return (SSDA903). Nature and purpose of analysis The analysis will support Local Authorities to develop a better understanding of their respective Looked After Children populations and help them to determine if there is a sufficiency of local provision. Undertaking this work at a regional level will enable Local Authorities to identify themes/trends that may not be possible to identify at a local level. The analysis will also support benchmarking between differently Local Authorities and geographies. The intention is that this analysis will support Local Authorities to meet their Sufficiency Duty in respect of Section 22G of the Children Act 1989. This Act places a duty on Local Authorities to take steps that secure, so far as is reasonably practicable, sufficient accommodation for looked after children within their local area. This Duty was further outlined in Statutory Guidance issued by the Department for Education in 2010 which made explicit the requirement for Local Authorities to act strategically to address gaps in provision by ensuring that plans to meet this Duty were included in relevant commissioning strategies. Details of analysis The analysis addresses many questions that are central to developing effective commissioning strategies such as: the distances children are placed from their homes, and any demographic factors that may lead to an increase in the likelihood that a young person is placed out of area how placement quality, as assessed by Ofsted, interacts with care episode stability the quality of outcomes for children from minority groups the utilisation of local provision and if there are specific gaps in supply Data to be shared The data submitted by the CONTROLLER will include personal data, including special category data, about children and young people who have, in the six years prior to the analysis, been: considered ‘looked-after’ within the meaning of the Children Act Personal data, including special category data to be processed: unique identifiers, including LA-issued identifiers demographic information, including gender, date of birth and ethnicity geographic identifiers, including home postcode, looked after placement postcode and Ofstedissued placement unique reference number Children’s Services episode information, including dates, need codes, legal status and outcomes, for care placement episodes Data minimisation In consideration of the data required to produce the analysis, we have minimised the scope of individuals whose data are shared to only include individuals who have been considered ‘looked-after’ under the meaning of the Children’s Act 1989, in the six years prior to analysis. Accordingly, in the course of data processing by the London DataStore (Step 2 in Schedule 2), all information is removed about: children of looked after children children who have been placed for adoption (who have not also been ‘looked-after’ in the same time period) adopters of children care leavers For data subjects who are in the scope of the analysis, we have evaluated whether any fields containing identifiers and personal, sensitive information are required to conduct the analysis. Accordingly, in the same process above, the following data minimisation occurs: Unique pupil number Date of birth degraded to month of birth (30x reduction in specificity) Postcodes (home and placement) degraded to postcode districts (~540x reduction in specificity) Details of data processing Data deposit by CONTROLLER and data processing on London DataStore occur as described in steps 1 & 2 of Schedule 2. Social Finance analysts created the code that processes the data on the London DataStore. The code is released to London DataStore as a PyPI package in a publicly accessible repository on GitHub. QA testing will be performed before it is deployed on the London DataStore. The sub-processor responsible for analysis and sharing of data, as described in steps 3 & 4 of Schedule , is London Borough of Ealing, and named sub-processors, detailed below and in Schedule 1. Data in the LIIA Analysis Folder is accessed through secure download to a MS Azure data warehouse hosted by Social Care Network (SCN). The warehouse is independent of any other data sources and maintained exclusively for London Borough of Ealing. Data stored in SCN’s data warehouse is encrypted using TLS 1.2, while in transit and at rest. All data is stored and backed up in the UK with access managed through 2-factor authentication. SCN are Cyber Essentials Plus certified. Full data security protocols employed by SCN can be found in Appendix 1 to this Schedule. Data joining Data in London Borough of Ealing’s data warehouse will be joined to data from Ofsted produced reports about placement providers, including data relating to placement cost and quality. This joining will be performed on information relating to care placements, and not on information relating to individual children. All joining will be performed in the Azure data warehouse hosted by SCN. The joining will take place using the following fields from the SSDA903: placement URN placement postcode (at postcode district level) The purpose for adding this additional data to the SSDA903 data is to allow analysis of the outcomes of episodes of care using child-level information from the SSDA903 alongside the quality and cost of placement providers using placement-level information from the Ofsted reports. Details of analysis The dataset is used to generate a Power BI report that will display analyses that aggregate above the level of the individual. Many different levels of aggregation will be presented, at the level of: number of children placed in Borough X from Borough Y number of children placed in postcode district X from Borough Y number of children placed at a list of placement providers in postcode district X from Borough Y All analyses created allow individual Boroughs to be identified. Risk of individual re-identification Users of the report will be able to filter visualisations in the report to sub-divide children by demographic variables, such as age, gender and ethnicity, as well as by additional dataset-specific variables, such as whether the child’s previous placement ended in ‘breakdown’. In visualisations that display the number of children from a Borough placed in a specific placement type in a selected postcode district, this has the potential to describe very small numbers of children, potentially as low as a single child. This is because the density of placements may be very low in less populated areas and the capacity of some placement types is also low. Though a single child may be described in this way, no directly identifiable data about that child, such as an identifier or date of birth, can be accessed by the user. This functionality does increase the risk, however, that a child becomes re-identifiable due to the circumstances of their Borough of origin, their demographic profile and their placement location. A way to mitigate against this would be to set a threshold for the minimum number of children that a visualisation will display data about. However, given the very low capacity (<= 4 beds) of some of the placement types of most interest to Commissioners in this kind of analysis, setting such a threshold would likely unacceptably reduce the value of the analysis. Therefore, no lower threshold is proposed for this analysis. Security of hosting The Power BI report is hosted by London Borough of Ealing. Only analysts directly involved in the project working for London Borough of Ealing, Social Care Network and Simpsons Associates can access the SCN Azure warehouse for this purpose. Access is maintained by London Borough of Ealing and provided via Azure Active Directory. All Simpson Associates consultants have Security Check (SC) clearance. Simpsons Associates hold ISO 270001 and ISO 9001, Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus certificates and regularly work with LAs, police forces and healthcare trusts. Sharing of analysis Commissioning Alliance share the Power BI report with named individuals only. Individuals with access to the report from each London Borough will be agreed by the London Borough and communicated to London Borough of Ealing. Access to the report is individually password protected, with sharing to new individuals only possible by London Borough of Ealing analysts. Existing links shared to individuals who do not have access will not provide access to the report. Dissemination of these aggregate analyses to individuals from organisations other than the London Boroughs, such as with placement providers, will be managed in line with Memoranda of Understanding between the ACDCS and LIIA Board. Such sharing is likely to greatly increase the value of the analyses produced, as it will enable communication of outputs to both the creators and suppliers of the demand for care placements. The test has proven more than satisfactory. Factor Authentication By default, SCN’s CHARMS application uses a 2-step process to authenticate users, involving a username/password combo followed by selected characters from a passphrase. These mimic the way banks in the UK allow access to online applications. Software Development Lifecycle SCN’s software is developed using C# and ASP.Net and runs on Windows Servers using Microsoft SQL Server as the data store. As code is written it is checked by VeraCode, a static code analysis tool which identifies any vulnerabilities that may have been written into the codebase by developers. Security Testing of beta releases are undertaken by the security Architect. Internal Pen Testing is undertaken at every major release by SCN. Defence in Depth SCN’s philosophy is defence in depth. All data is encrypted using TLS 1.2 to servers, a Web Application Firewall analyses the requests to reject any injection or client-side attacks, and IIS is set to implement the strongest security available. Code is scanned by VeraCode, ASP.Net security is enabled, all internal traffic is sent over HTTPS, and all the data in the database is encrypted, both in transit and at rest. Transparent Data Security, TDS, in SQL Server is used to achieve this. Backups Backups are taken every day and managed by the cloud provider. This ensures that there is no member of staff at SCN who could delete backups. Backups are available for 6 months. Transaction logging is used to enable any problems with data after the last backup and before the next. Multi-Tenanted Solution SCN’s applications are delivered as off the shelf, Software as a Service solutions, SAAS. Customers have their own Website and Database implementation on our infrastructure which is provided by UKFast. Data is stored in two datacentres, on either side of the city of Manchester, to ensure availability. All hardware infrastructure is mirrored in each datacentre. One datacentre acts as the failover - all activity in the prime datacentre is immediately updated to the failover datacentre in real time. Certifications SCN is Cyber Essentials Plus certified and is starting the ISO 27001 certification process. The infrastructure provider UKFAST is ISO 27001 certified and also ISO 27018, ISO 9001 and ISO 22301. Data Storage All data is stored in the UK and backed up in UK. LIIA Child Level Data DSAs This is the data sharing agreement. It has been signed electronically on a portal rather than a wet ink signature. This copy is published as the effective copy. The facts that it is unsigned and appears completed is simply because the signature is undertaken generically on an information sharing portal. Background The London Innovation and Improvement Alliance (LIIA) is a standing partnership of London Local Authorities, working together for the benefit of vulnerable children in the capital. Part of the LIIA project is a pan-London Sector-Led Improvement analysis team, hosted at Waltham Forest Borough Council, who produce pan-London analyses for the London Directors of Children's Services. A successful pilot phase ran in Jan-March 2021 with Enfield, Islington, Merton, Wandsworth, Richmond, and Kingston to create a process to safely, legally, and ethically take in individual-level data where appropriate, and create analyses based on it. Building on the learning from the pilot phase, this Agreement provides the basis to expand the project to cover all 32 London Boroughs and the City of London Corporation. This will create an infrastructure that has the legal and ethical framework to enable child-level data sharing and a secure & efficient data network that makes this practical and accessible for each LA in the LIIA without increasing burdens or cost unnecessarily or disproportionally. The infrastructure is designed to provide impact at scale, while maximising process efficiency and data security. It represents a key outcome of the Pan London Data Accelerator Programme. Data specialists Social Finance are advising, with a focus on ensuring that the process embeds the principles of privacy by design, that the processing remains proportionate to the benefits, and that the process can be set up with the minimum level of additional work for LA teams. Expanding the project to the whole of London requires a robust and secure data hosting infrastructure to facilitate the uploading, processing, and analysing of child-level data from multiple local authorities. The London Datastore, a data-sharing platform created by the London Greater Authority, provides such an infrastructure and will be the key partner for hosting and processing LA data. The overall framework will have LAs deposit data on the London Datastore, where it will be processed to create pan-London datasets, which will also be stored on the London Datastore. This Agreement will document and authorise this infrastructure. Access to pan-London datasets will be granted on a caseby-case basis to named individuals at 'analytical partners' (sub-processors as described by Clause 10.1) to conduct further data transformation and dissemination of analytical outputs. Authorisations for these analytical partners will be managed as additional Schedules to this Agreement. This technical and legal framework has the endorsement of the LIIA board and Information Governance for London. Q2 2023 amendments The LIIA Child Level Data Project has now launched, with all 33 London Boroughs signed up to share data and data from the SSDA903 shared by all Boroughs for one of the three starting use cases, PanLondon Sufficiency Analysis. Reporting from this use case has also gone live and has being shared with approx. 100 users across London Boroughs. Changes to the agreement are being proposed that will make amendments to the core data flows and to existing use cases, and will also add new use cases to the platform, following the approval of the LIIA Board. In line with the process established with Information Governance for London, these amendments will be scrutinised by one or more members of Information Governance for London, before being reviewed by the group in two monthly meetings. Only following endorsement by the body will each LA be asked to approve these changes through Information Sharing Gateway, making them live changes to the agreement. One of the changes is to the existing data flow structure, with the data ingress, processing and egress role previously played by GLA (the London DataStore) now taken on by Social Finance, who are building a novel data platform for this purpose. The reason for this change is that the London Data Store, while robust at dealing with open access data, lacks some of the primary security features necessary for handling data containing personally identifiable information. The full details of this will be described in an amended Schedule 2 of this agreement. As this is a significant change to the existing agreement, two members of Information Governance for London are taking an active role in the scoping and development of this platform to ensure that it meets the data security standards necessary for the data being shared. It is required because local public services, most notably local authority children’s services, are increasingly finding it necessary to share personal sensitive data with one another and with suppliers in order to deliver on their statutory responsibilities. Hosting data within the London Data Platform and running analysis within its secure environment will allow for increased data security, as it drastically reduces the risk of data breaches associated with email transfers, data downloads or holding data locally. The architecture of the platform has been designed specifically with this use-case in mind and it holds data security as its core principle. This architecture is detailed in “Data security” below. Social Finance will act as architectural principal for this project and will thus be responsible for the role of primary security contact and specifier. Amazon Web Services will be the service provider. Details of the appropriate certifications are outlined in the sections below. Data flows The data shared by the CONTROLLER goes through the following steps: . Upload data . Prepare data for analysis . Analyse data . Share analysis These are expanded upon below and are represented in the data flow diagram (Figure 1). The flows in steps 1 and 2 above are the same for all data processing activities covered by this agreement. Therefore, they are described in this schedule only. The flows in steps 3 and 4 are specific to each processing activity (e.g. Pan-London Sufficiency Analysis involves different flows to Social Worker Workforce Analysis as they involve different organisations processing data). Therefore: Steps 3 and 4 are described in detail in the schedules created for each of those activities. The only material we provide here regarding steps 3 and 4 is a generic description (e.g. PROCESSOR does X rather than named organisation does X). . Upload data The CONTROLLER is given access to a private folder in the London Data Platform and uploads the data there. This folder is only accessible by authorised personnel from the CONTROLLER and the London Data Platform. . Prepare data for analysis i. Preparing the data of a single CONTROLLER The PROCESSOR runs scripts within the London Data Platform environment to: Degrade certain data fields to protect data subject anonymity, e.g. date of birth transformed into month of birth; postcode transformed into postcode sector Assess data quality (missing values, logically inconsistent values) At the end of this process, the data is pseudonymised. Identification of individuals would only be possible with access to the CONTROLLER’s case management system. The CONTROLLER’s processed dataset is deposited back in the CONTROLLER’s private folder; the CONTROLLER can download the processed dataset for analysis. ii. Merging all Borough’s data together An additional process within the London Data Platform environment merges the datasets from all CONTROLLERS into a single pan-London dataset. During this process, additional data minimisation and data degradation steps may occur to ensure that only the data required for pan-London analysis is accessible. These additional steps will be detailed in Schedules 3 onwards. The processed dataset is deposited into the PROCESSOR’s private folder (“LIIA Analysis folder”) in the London Data Platform. . Analyse data Typically, each specific analysis (e.g. Pan-London Sufficiency Analysis) requires only a subset of the full dataset. It may require: Fewer than the full set of data subjects (e.g. only children in care, rather than all children with a social worker) Fewer than the full set of fields describing each data subject (e.g. only information about the children’s demographics and the placement, rather than information about needs and disabilities) Data from a shorter period of time than is available in the full dataset (e.g. just the last 12m) Therefore, in line with the principle of privacy by design a specific dataset is created for each analysis which contains the minimum data required for that analysis. These are stored in the LIIA Analysis folder. Access to each of these datasets in the LIIA Analysis folder is restricted to named individuals at the PROCESSOR (or named sub-processor) with direct involvement in analyses of that dataset, as described in Schedules 3 onwards. The PROCESSOR accesses the dataset in the LIIA Analysis folder in one of two ways: Local download via a secure username/password combination. The dataset is then stored in a restricted area of the PROCESSOR’s data warehouse with access granted only to staff directly involved in its analysis. Remote access via a secure link, connecting directly from within analytical software (e.g. Power BI). The dataset is stored in the cache of the analytical software only, with access granted only to staff directly involved in its analysis. Analysis conducted on the processed dataset is described in the relevant Schedule below. . Share the analysis Aggregated analytical outputs are shared with all Boroughs via securely hosted software (e.g. Power BI). In all shared outputs, it is no longer possible to identify individual data points. Boroughs will be identifiable in these shared analyses, allowing benchmarking and comparison between boroughs. Where appropriate the LIIA d&i team will provide pan-London aggregate anonymous data for work commissioned or approved by ALDCS/LIIA or as agreed with partner organisations (where this data has already been collected through the LIIA CLD project) and so help reduce burdens on individual LA data & performance teams (relates to all use cases). Folder access rights on London Data Platform Access to any part of the platform requires individual access credentials (controlled through the platform identity and access management system and governed by appropriate security technologies i.e. single-sign on via major identity providers, password complexity and multi-factor authentication). Controller’s private folder - The CONTROLLER’s private folder on the London Data Platform is created manually by the London Data Platform admin. Several staff members from the CONTROLLER can be given access to the folder. The PROCESSOR will not be able to access the data hosted in the CONTROLLER’s private folder. Beyond staff at the CONTROLLER, only London Data Platform admin will be able to access this data to grant access rights and initiate data processing. LIIA Analysis folder - The LIIA Analysis folder on the London Data Platform is only accessible by authorised personnel from the PROCESSOR conducting the analysis and the London Data Platform admin and data engineer. Data retention Unless otherwise specified, data will be retained until six years have elapsed since data collection. Previous analysis finds that six years is the minimum for good quality journey analysis (an analytical approach we expect to employ), but that having more than six years’ data does not materially help to answer new questions or answer existing questions with greater certainty or granularity. Maintenance of this retention is implemented as part of the automated processing of data on the London Data Platform. On termination of this agreement, all data will be deleted from the CONTROLLER’s private folder and the LIIA Analysis folder. The CONTROLLER can request the deletion of data at any time before the termination date. London Data Platform infrastructure The application is architected to be secure by design. It follows National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) best practice for cloud applications and its use of Amazon Web Services for all core application components means that it is based on the most solid and robust of cloud platforms. Specifically, it adheres to the NCSC guiding principles as follows: Principle 1 - Data in transit protection The Data Platform will use the latest SSL certificates. Connections will be 128bit encrypted and authenticated using TLS 1.2. (data encrypted in transit) Principle 2 - Asset protection and resilience Data will be hosted on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in a UK availability zone and a UK data centre. The AWS data centre is secure and highly monitored (full list of procedures in place available here). Data tables will be stored in AWS S3 buckets protected by a private key/user password combination. (data encrypted at rest) AWS is certified ISO 27001 (full list of AWS certifications available here). Principle 3 - Separation between customers Robust use of Identity and Access Management (IAM) prevents users accessing or processing data or systems outside their own. Principle 4 - Operational security The platform will be subject to robust and well-defined operational processes Releases will be timely and well managed through a deployment management framework Incident management will have clear procedures and communication will be timely Principle 5 – Governance framework A governance framework will be established to clearly define feature extension signoff, administration oversight and eventual handoff of the system to a suitable long term owner as required. Principle 6 - Personnel security AWS personnel are subject to robust vetting and security checks. Access to systems from inside the London Data Platform will be limited to those identified in the data flows section above. Principle 7 –Secure development Engineering will follow software development best practices, including merge protections and code review Deployment will be automated and follow a test > release process across multiple environments before production Code will be subjected to multiple levels of automated and manual testing Principle 8 - Supply chain security Software dependencies will be tracked and vulnerabilities automatically reported Dependencies in code run on the processing environment will be subject to a robust and well managed allow-list Principles 9 and 10 - Secure user management/ Identity and authentication Uploads will be Private as default. Single-sign-on via major identity service providers (Microsoft Active Directory, Google Cloud Identity) will provide best in class password complexity enforcement and multi-factorauthentication requirements. A full audit log for user access and data movement will be recorded Principle 11 - External interface protection Exposed user interfaces will follow best practice for user facing application security – including cross-site scripting protection and cross-site request forgery protection The minimum required API will be exposed to reduce the available attack surface to the smallest possible Principle 12 – Secure Services Administration Administration of AWS services and infrastructure is carried out entirely through the AWS console and administration system which is subject to the resiliency and security principles laid down by Amazon themselves. Principle13 - Resilience and auditing The application will be fully penetration tested before production release is granted. Regular security audits by qualified third-party organisations will be carried out. Data protection from loss and lack of availability on AWS is covered by their business continuity and disaster recovery policy. Principle 14 – Security by Design and Default The design of the system is such that users are subject to guardrails which prevent accidental misuse. Code run on the platform will be sandboxed and airgapped from the wider internet Controls and role based access will prevent data leaking between users or clients Figure 1 – LIIA data flows diagram Schedule 4 (Social Worker Workforce Analysis) Nature and purpose of analysis This schedule provides details of the data flow for Social Worker Workforce Census data through the LIIA platform. The data submitted by the CONTROLLER is the Children’s Social Work Workforce Census. The process will enable pan-London analysis to understand how the pan-London labour market for registered social workers is functioning for staff and employers. The purpose of the analysis is to collaborate with other authorities to improve the labour market for registered social workers e.g. by reducing reliance on agency staff, reducing staff turnover and ensuring equal opportunity for BAME staff. This will enable the CONTROLLER to meet its obligations: to establish steps to meet the needs of the social workforce, ‘the public sector equality duty’, created by Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 safeguarding children in need by improving the number of people working in order to accomplish their responsibilities, created by Section 17 of the Children’s Act 1989 to make arrangements to secure continuous improvement in the way in which its functions are exercised, having regard to a combination of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, ‘the duty of the best value’, created by Section 3 of the Local Government Act 1999 Data to be shared The data submitted by the CONTROLLER will include personal data, including special category data, about social workers registered with Social Work England providing services to children and young people under CONTROLLER's duty to them in the six years prior to the analysis. Personal data, including special category data to be processed: unique identifiers, including Social Work England registration number demographic information, including gender, date of birth and ethnicity Qualifications (e.g. qualification level, affiliation to fast track programmes) Contract information (e.g. start date, end date, role, FTE, agency/permanent status, length of assignment if agency) Number of Days work missed due to sickness absence in a given year Origin code (1-10) when arriving in post (e.g. newly qualified, arriving from another LA, arriving from agency) Destination code (1-9) and Reason for Leaving code (1-10) if leaving Data minimisation We have evaluated whether any fields containing identifiers and personal, sensitive information are required to conduct the analysis. Accordingly, in the course of data processing by the London DataStore (Step 2 in Schedule 2), the following degradation of sensitive data occurs: Registration number replaced with hash, to pseudonymise individual-level data Date of birth degraded to month of birth Details of data processing Data deposit by CONTROLLER and data processing on London DataStore occur as described in steps 1 & 2 of Schedule 2. Analysts at London Metropolitan University created the code that processes the data on the London Data Platform. The code is released to London Data Platform as a PyPI package in a publicly accessible repository on GitHub. QA testing will be performed before it is deployed on the London Data Platform. The parties responsible for analysis and sharing of data, as described in steps 3 & 4 of Schedule 2, are the PROCESSOR and London Borough of Waltham Forest (LBWF). Data in the LIIA Analysis Folder is accessed through a bearer token in Power BI. Data is stored in cache in a Power BI report, hosted by LBWF. Only analysts employed by the PROCESSOR or at LBWF who need to develop the Power BI report can access the data. The PROCESSOR will share the Power BI report with named individuals at 33 London Boroughs. Access to the report is individually password protected, with sharing to new individuals only possible by project staff at the PROCESSOR. All analyses shared are at an aggregate level at which individual Boroughs can be identified. Dissemination of these aggregate analyses to individuals from organisations other than the London Boroughs, such as with academic partners at London Metropolitan University and the North East London Social Work Teaching Partnership, will be managed in line with Memoranda of Understanding between the ACDCS and LIIA Board. Such sharing is likely to greatly increase the value of the analyses produced, as it will enable communication of outputs to the academic researchers who initiated this line of analysis. Their feedback on the analysis outputs will be valuable in identifying further productive lines of analysis. The contract between the PROCESSOR and LBWF will stipulate equivalent or greater information security to that described for the PROCESSOR, including the audit rights necessary to ensure that commitments are followed. Purpose This agreement sets out the framework for the sharing of Personal Data when one or more Controllers (the Data Disclosers) disclose Personal Data to the other parties in their capacity as Controllers (the Data Receivers). In this agreement the parties are also referred to as Data Sharers (without by that affecting their status as Controllers or Data Receivers pursuant to the Data Protection Legislation). The parties are also Joint Controllers of the uploaded data that they will be receiving and transmitting as a result of entering into this agreement. The parties are Independent Controllers when the details of the match are processed and then considered for use as part of an investigation by the relevant fraud hub member. Where this occurs fraud hub members should rely on part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 for law enforcement processing. This agreement also defines the principles and procedures that the parties shall adhere to and the responsibilities the parties owe to each other. Each party is a Public Authority and considers this Data Sharing initiative necessary in order to collaborate in relation to their participation in the London Borough Fraud Investigators Group (LBFIG). The aim of the data sharing initiative is to acquire information from third parties of the working practices of agency workers aimed at better understanding the corelation between hours worked and claimed and whether this reflects the data held by the third party employer. It will serve to benefit the signatories to this agreement in providing greater clarity on the work practices of agency staff and enable them to better deal with their respective agency staff as well as providing greater clarity and transparency in the provision of services to the public. The parties agree to only process Shared Personal Data, as described in sub-clauses 4.1 to 4.3 and as set out in Schedule 2, for the following purposes: (a) For fraud prevention purposes; (b) For protecting the relevant agency bodies’ legitimate interests and those of third parties it deals with in this case the relevant customer Councils as part of the London Boroughs Fraud Investigators Group (LBFIG). (c) Ensuring that public funds are properly accounted as well as discharging the parties’ statutory powers under schedule 9 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014. The parties shall not process Shared Personal Data in a way that is incompatible with the purposes described in this clause (Agreed Purposes). Each party shall appoint a single point of contact (SPoC) who will work together to reach an agreement with regards to any issues arising from the data sharing and to actively improve the effectiveness of the data sharing initiative. The points of contact for each of the parties are at Appendix : . Compliance with national data protection laws Each party must ensure compliance with applicable Data Protection Legislation at all times during the Term of this agreement as set out in clause 5. Each party has such valid registrations and or paid such fees as are required by the ICO which, by the time that the data sharing is expected to commence, covers the intended data sharing pursuant to this agreement, unless an exemption applies. . Lawful, fair and transparent processing Each party shall ensure that it processes the Shared Personal Data fairly and lawfully in accordance with sub-clause 5.2 during the Term of this agreement. Each party shall ensure that it has legitimate grounds under the Data Protection Legislation for the processing of Shared Personal Data. Where the legal basis is consent there must be written evidence of the terms of that consent, which is set out in Schedule 5 to this agreement. The lawful bases (and conditions or exceptions for processing of any Special Categories of Personal Data or Criminal Offence Data) and the legal power for data sharing are set out in Schedule 12. The Data Discloser shall, in respect of Shared Personal Data, ensure that it provides clear and sufficient information to the Data Subjects, in accordance with the Data Protection Legislation, of the purposes for which it will process their personal data, the legal basis for those purposes and such other information as is required by Article 13 of the UK GDPR including: (a) if Shared Personal Data will be transferred to a third party, that fact and sufficient information about that transfer and the purpose of that transfer to enable the Data Subject to understand the purpose and risks of that transfer; and (b) if Shared Personal Data will be transferred outside the UK pursuant to sub-clause 5.4(a) of this agreement, that fact and sufficient information about that transfer, the purpose of that transfer and the safeguards put in place by the Controller to enable the Data Subject to understand the purpose and risks of that transfer. The Data Receiver undertakes to inform the Data Subjects, in accordance with the Data Protection Legislation, of the purposes for which it will process their personal data, the legal basis for those purposes and such other information as is required by Article 14 of the UK GDPR including: (a) if Shared Personal Data will be transferred to a third party, that fact and sufficient information about that transfer and the purpose of that transfer to enable the Data Subject to understand the purpose and risks of that transfer; and (b) if Shared Personal Data will be transferred outside the UK pursuant to sub-clause 5.5(a) of this agreement, that fact and sufficient information about that transfer, the purpose of that transfer and the safeguards put in place by the Controller to enable the Data Subject to understand the purpose and risks of that transfer. If, for any reason, one party reasonably considers that the data sharing under this agreement is not lawful, fair or transparent, the SPoC of that first party shall immediately contact the SPoC of the other party or parties to notify them of that concern and consider what action, including suspending any future data sharing, needs to be taken. . Data quality The parties have developed a reliable means of converting Shared Personal Data to ensure compatibility with each party's respective datasets as set out in Schedule 6. The Data Discloser shall ensure that before the Commencement Date, Shared Personal Data is accurate and that it has appropriate internal procedures in place for the Data Receiver to sample Shared Personal Data before the Commencement Date and it will update the same if required before transferring the Shared Personal Data. Shared Personal Data must be limited to the Personal Data described in sub-clause 4.1 and Schedule of this agreement. . Data subjects' rights On receipt of a request from a Data Subject for Shared Personal Data, the party in receipt shall contact the other party or parties to this agreement through the SPoC to notify them of receipt of such a request. The party who receives the request shall have overall responsibility for responding to the request unless more than one party receives an identical or similar request from the same Data Subject. In those circumstances, the relevant SPoCs shall promptly discuss and implement the most effective way of discharging their responsibilities under the Data Protection Legislation to the Data Subject who has made the request(s). The parties each agree to provide such assistance as is reasonably required to enable the other party to comply with Subject Rights Requests within the time limits imposed by the Data Protection Legislation. The SPoC for each party is responsible for maintaining a record of Subject Rights Requests, the decisions made and any information that was exchanged. Records must include copies of the request for information, details of the data accessed and shared and where relevant, notes of any meeting, correspondence or phone calls relating to the request. The SPoC for each party is detailed in subclause 2.6. . Data retention and deletion The Data Receiver shall not retain or process Shared Personal Data for longer than is necessary to carry out the Agreed Purposes. Notwithstanding sub-clause 8.1, parties shall continue to retain Shared Personal Data in accordance with any statutory or regulatory retention periods applicable to them. The parties may put in place common rules for the retention and deletion of Shared Personal Data which shall be set out in Schedule 8. The Data Receiver shall ensure that any Shared Personal Data is returned to the Data Discloser or destroyed in accordance with the agreed Deletion Procedure set out in Schedule 8 in the following circumstances: (a) on termination of the agreement; (b) on expiry of the Term of the agreement; or (c) once processing of the Shared Personal Data is no longer necessary for the Agreed Purposes, as set out in sub-clause 5. Following the deletion of Shared Personal Data in accordance with sub-clause 8.3, the Data Receiver shall notify the Data Discloser that the Shared Personal Data in question has been deleted in accordance with the Deletion Procedure in Schedule 8 to this agreement. . Transfers For the purposes of this clause, transfers of Personal Data shall mean any sharing of Personal Data by the Data Receiver with a third party, and shall include, but is not limited to, the following: (a) subcontracting the processing of Shared Personal Data; and (b) granting a third party Controller access to the Shared Personal Data. If the Data Receiver appoints a third party Processor to process the Shared Personal Data it shall comply with Article 28 of the UK GDPR and shall remain liable to the Data Discloser for the acts and omissions of the Processor. The Data Receivers shall not disclose or transfer Shared Personal Data outside the UK. . Security and training The Data Discloser shall only provide the Shared Personal Data to the Data Receiver by using secure methods as agreed and set out in Schedule 9. The parties undertake to have in place throughout the Term appropriate technical and organisational security measures to: (a) prevent: (i) unauthorised or unlawful processing of the Shared Personal Data; and (ii) the accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, the Shared Personal Data; (b) ensure a level of security appropriate to: (i) the harm that might result from the unauthorised or unlawful processing or accidental loss, destruction or damage; and (ii) the nature of the Shared Personal Data to be protected. The level of technical and organisational measures agreed by the parties as appropriate as at the Commencement Date having regard to the state of technological development and the cost of implementing those measures is set out in Schedule 9. The parties shall keep those security measures under review and shall carry out those updates as they agree are appropriate throughout the Term. It is the responsibility of each party to ensure that its staff members are appropriately trained to handle and process the Shared Personal Data in accordance with the technical and organisational security measures set out in Schedule 9 together with any other applicable laws and guidance and that those staff members have entered into confidentiality agreements relating to the processing of Personal Data. The level, content and regularity of training referred to in sub-clause 10.4 shall be proportionate to the staff members' role, responsibility and frequency with respect to their handling and processing of the Shared Personal Data. . Personal data breaches and reporting procedures The parties shall each comply with its obligation to report a Personal Data Breach to the Information Commissioner and (where applicable) Data Subjects under Article 33 of the UK GDPR and shall each inform the other party of any Personal Data Breach irrespective of whether there is a requirement to notify the Information Commissioner or Data Subject(s). The parties agree to provide reasonable assistance as is necessary to each other to facilitate the handling of any Personal Data Breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. . Review and termination of agreement Any additional Data Receiver that wishes to be part of this data sharing initiative and agreement shall complete and submit a data sharing request form, as set out in Schedule 10. Each party must then complete and submit a data sharing decision form, as set out in Schedule 11. The consent of every party is required for the additional party to be included into this agreement. In the event that a party terminates the agreement or a new Data Receiver joins the agreement in accordance with sub-clause 12.1, an amended and updated version of this agreement will be drafted as soon as practicable and circulated to all other parties. The parties shall review the effectiveness of this data sharing initiative every six months and on the addition and removal of a party, having consideration to the aims and purposes set out in sub-clauses and 5. The parties shall continue, amend or terminate the agreement depending on the outcome of this review. The review of the effectiveness of the data sharing initiative will involve: (a) assessing whether the purposes for which the Shared Personal Data is being processed are still the ones listed in sub-clause 5 of and Schedule 2 to this agreement; (b) assessing whether the Shared Personal Data is still as listed in clause 4 of this agreement; (c) assessing whether the parties can continue to rely on a lawful basis or a condition or exception under Data Protection Legislation to lawfully share the Shared Personal Data; (d) assessing whether the legal framework governing data quality, retention, and Data Subjects' rights is being complied with; and (e) assessing whether Personal Data Breaches involving the Shared Personal Data have been handled in accordance with this agreement and the applicable legal framework; and (f) assessing whether there is a sufficient number of parties in the agreement to warrant continuing with the PoC. Each party reserves its rights to inspect the other party's arrangements for the processing of Shared Personal Data and to terminate the agreement where it considers that the other party is not processing the Shared Personal Data in accordance with this agreement. This Data Sharing Agreement will continue in force until terminated by the parties in accordance with clause 12. . Resolution of disputes with data subjects or the Supervisory Authority For the purposes of this clause, the parties are to be considered jointly liable. In the event of a dispute or claim brought by a Data Subject or the Information Commissioner concerning the processing of Shared Personal Data against either or several (including all) parties, the parties will inform each other about any such disputes or claims, and will co-operate with a view to settling them amicably and in a timely fashion. The parties agree to respond to any generally available non-binding mediation procedure initiated by a Data Subject or by the Information Commissioner. If they do participate in the proceedings, the parties may elect to do so remotely (such as by telephone or other electronic means). The parties also agree to consider participating in any other arbitration, mediation or other dispute resolution proceedings developed for data protection disputes. Each party shall abide by a decision of a competent court in the UK or of the Information Commissioner. . Language This agreement is drafted in the English language. Any notice given under or in connection with this agreement shall be in English. All other documents provided under or in connection with this agreement shall be in English, or accompanied by a certified English translation. The English language version of this agreement and any notice or other document relating to this agreement shall prevail if there is a conflict except where the document is a constitutional, statutory or other official document. .
