Between (1) Department of Health and Social Care for the purpose of the Independent Inquiry into the issues raised by the David Fuller case (‘the Inquiry’), and (2) London Borough of Camden (each a “Party” and together, the “Parties”) Concerning information sharing in respect of care of the deceased at mortuary and/or body store facilities provided by London Borough of Camden or provided by an external party with whom the local authority has an arrangement. Definitions See Annex A Background This DSA reflects the arrangements for the Local Authority to share information with the Inquiry. The information sharing will assist the Inquiry to fulfil its statutory and regulatory functions with regards to investigating care of the deceased This DSA explains how the Parties will comply with, and cooperate with one another in, their respective responsibilities under the Data Protection Legislation and respect Data Subjects’ rights when the Local Authority shares Personal Data with the Inquiry. Purpose and Objectives of the Information sharing The information to be shared under this DSA is set out at clause 6 and shall be shared for the purposes of an investigation by the Inquiry. The Inquiry was commissioned by the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, The Rt Hon Sajid Javid on 8 November 2021. The Terms of Reference of the Inquiry are published in Parliament and on the Inquiry website. Information sharing from the Local Authority to the Inquiry is necessary to assist the Inquiry to carry out its functions. Legal basis to receive, share and analyse data The Inquiry will process Personal Data fairly and lawfully in accordance with Data Protection Legislation and Article 6(1)(e) and Articles 9(2)(g) and (i) of the UK GDPR, and the Inquiry’s Privacy Notice (see section 9 below). This is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest and was commissioned by the Department of Health and Social Care. This should ensure high standards of quality and safety of health care are met, and that suitable and specific measures are in place to safeguard the rights and freedoms of the data subjects. Data Controller(s) The Inquiry will be the Data Controller for the information once disclosed to it by the Local Authority. The Inquiry is the Data Controller for the purposes of fulfilling its Terms of Reference. Data items to be processed The Local Authority will share Information that is relevant to the Inquiry in electronic form. No patient data will be required, but there may be occasions where the Inquiry requires personal data to be shared, such as names and roles. This will be requested on a case by case basis, with prior agreement on whether any of the information should be redacted beforehand. The Inquiry reserves the right to request and review unredacted copies of material in order to agree to any redactions applied. Information will be shared by the Local Authority with the Inquiry for the duration of the Inquiry in accordance with clause 11. The Inquiry will publish a report to fulfil the ToR, which may include data received from the Local Authority if it is considered necessary. Is there any interference with Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, Schedule 1 of the Human Rights Act 1998? of the European Convention on Human Rights by virtue of complying with this DSA is in accordance with the law, necessary in a democratic society in the interests for the protection of health or morals, and proportionate. How will the data sharing be carried out? Information will be shared by the Local Authority electronically via the secure webbased file sharing kahootz platform. This information will only be visible to the person(s) who uploaded it and the Inquiry team. The Inquiry will maintain appropriate security measures for the information held by it. The Parties will comply with Data Protection Legislation and take account of good practice and Codes of Practice issued by the Information Commissioner. The Local Authority shall provide a list of all material shared with the Inquiry. No data shall be processed outside of the EEA. Documents will not be destroyed if they are preserved for the public record, where an individual requests the return of an original document or where the Inquiry is required to share or keep a document to comply with any regulation or law. Annex B Inquiry Terms of Reference Background . David Fuller (DF), an electrical maintenance supervisor firstly at Kent and Sussex Hospital and then later at Tunbridge Wells Hospital, was arrested in December 2020 for the murders of two women in . When police searched his house, they found images and videos of him committing sexual offences on the bodies of at least 100 women and children at the Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust mortuary since 2008. . In January 2021, DF pleaded not guilty to the murders. He was later charged with the mortuary offences. In October 2021, he pleaded guilty to the mortuary offences. In November 2021, he pleaded guilty to the murders. . Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust began an investigation into the activities of DF overseen by an independent Chair, Sir Jonathan Michael. On 8 November 2021, the Right Honourable Sajid Javid MP, Secretary of State for Health and Social Care announced that this was to be replaced with an independent inquiry given the scale and nature of the offences. The Inquiry has not been set up under the Inquiries Act 2005 and will be adopting a non-judicial approach to its work. Terms of Reference . The Inquiry will be split into two phases: an initial report, on matters relating to Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust, reporting by the middle of 2022, and a final report, looking at the broader national picture and the wider lessons for the NHS and for other settings, reporting by the middle of 2023. . The Inquiry will review DF’s unlawful actions, how he was able to carry these out, why his actions went apparently unnoticed, and will make recommendations with the aim of preventing anything similar happening again. . An important part of the Inquiry is to afford the families who have been affected by DF’s offending an opportunity to be heard and for the Inquiry to be informed by this. The Inquiry will preserve the anonymity of families throughout the course of its work. Staff of the Trust and of DF’s private sector employers who have been affected by DF’s actions will also have an opportunity to share their experiences with the Inquiry. The Inquiry will make sure that families and others affected by the actions of DF can share their experiences and information with it in ways that are supportive and sensitive. . The Inquiry will also consider evidence and information from other interested parties, including, for example, Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust and its predecessors (‘the Trust’), relevant regulatory bodies and subject matter experts. All interested parties are required and expected to cooperate with the inquiry as is normal, professional practice. Findings and recommendations from previous relevant reports will also be considered in the work of the Inquiry. . The Inquiry will treat all information and personal data received in accordance with all relevant legal and regulatory requirements, including the UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). . The Inquiry will ensure that the families of victims are kept informed of progress. The Inquiry team will remain accessible throughout. The issues the Inquiry will consider in each phase, but is not limited to, are as follows Phase 1 To consider the process by which DF was recruited and employed by the NHS and by private sector facilities maintenance service providers during the period 1989 to 2020 and whether appropriate and adequate checks were carried out prior to and during his employment, whether the current checks are appropriate for individuals with access to mortuary facilities, and whether risks associated with those checks were managed. To determine what access DF was given to the mortuary and other areas of the Trust, and whether this was subject to usual or appropriate supervision, oversight and assurance, including analysis of swipe card activity and CCTV. To identify any evidence of other inappropriate or unlawful activities by DF elsewhere on Trust premises. To review any evidence of complaints, concerns or incidents concerning DF’s behaviour at the Trust, and how they were addressed by the Trust and his private sector employers. To consider whether the Trust’s arrangements for management of the mortuary, including security and access, to safeguard the bodies of the deceased, were in accordance with Human Tissue Authority (HTA) standards, any relevant guidance or regulatory requirements and any relevant recommendations from other inquiries. To consider whether arrangements for post-mortem examinations were satisfactory. To examine inspection reports of the mortuary by the HTA and any other regulator, and the associated assurance processes. To consider whether the Trust’s Board received sufficient assurance on the issues raised by the case of DF. To examine arrangements for transfer of the deceased between the Trust and other organisations, for example local funeral directors and to identify whether concerns were, or should have been raised. Phase 2 To consider whether procedures and practices in hospital settings, including in the private sector, where bodies of the deceased are kept, safeguard the security and dignity of the deceased, and would prevent a recurrence of matters raised by the case of DF. To consider whether procedures and practices (including the use of locum Anatomical Pathology Technologists) in non-hospital settings, including local authority mortuaries, funeral directors, the NHS ambulance service, medical schools, temporary mortuaries, direct funeral companies and hospices, where bodies of the deceased are kept, safeguard the security and dignity of the deceased and would prevent a recurrence of matters raised by the case of DF. To consider the role of regulators and their use of regulatory measures in assuring that mortuary practices safeguarded the security and dignity of the deceased in all settings, and hence consider the effectiveness of the national regulatory regime. To consider any other issues that arose during Phase 1 of the Inquiry. General . The Inquiry will Produce a Phase 1 report on its findings and recommendations on issues arising from its consideration of events at Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust and identify areas of concern for the wider NHS to be aware. Produce a final report which will provide an overview of the information it has reviewed, and which will set out the Inquiry’s findings and its recommendations. Publish anonymised accounts, setting out the experiences of the families affected by DF’s offending and inappropriate behaviour, and the impact this has had on them. Escalate any matters it comes across that require immediate attention to the relevant authorities. Report any instances of apparent collusion or other conduct of concern (including conduct that indicates the potential commission of criminal or disciplinary offences, or breach of professional codes of conduct) to the relevant employer(s), professional or quality regulator(s), and/or the police for their consideration. The Inquiry does not have the power to impose disciplinary sanctions or make findings as to criminal or civil liability. . The Inquiry will aim to make its initial report to the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care by the middle of 2022 and its final report with its findings and recommendations by the middle of 2023. The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care will make arrangements for their presentation to Parliament. . Although the Inquiry will be restricted to matters concerning mortuary practices in England, its findings and recommendations may have relevance across the United Kingdom. Addendum This is an addendum to the terms of reference that were published by the Inquiry on 23 February 2022. The addendum relates to points 4 and 11 of the terms of reference. New information has been provided to the Inquiry. The Inquiry will investigate this new information in line with its terms of reference which include assessment of the management of the mortuary, including the arrangements for security and access necessary to safeguard the bodies of the deceased. This further investigation means that the Inquiry will now be unable to publish its initial report on matters relating to Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust before the Autumn 2023. A final report, looking at the broader national picture and the wider lessons for the NHS and for other settings is planned for publication in 2024. The Inquiry will present the findings of both reports to the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, who will make arrangements for their presentation to Parliament.

Introduction to the Sharing This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement, London Borough of Camden and Imagineer will share personal data about children and their families at significant risk of needing residential placement and a project to put in place an enhanced package of support to avoid family breakdown. For simplicity, the Partner Organisation will be referred to as ‘Partner’. By signing this Agreement, the Parties agree to accept the conditions set out in this document, according to their statutory and professional responsibilities, and agree to adhere to the procedures described. This Agreement has been developed to: ● Define the specific purposes for which the signatory agencies have agreed to share information. ● Outline the Personal, Special Category and Criminal Data to be shared. ● Set out the lawful basis conditions under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared, including reference to the Human Rights Act 1998 ● Stipulate the roles and procedures that will support the processing/sharing of information between agencies. ● Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. ● Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure that compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and agency-specific security requirements. ● Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. ● To illustrate the flow of information from referral through processing and outcome. Parties to this agreement cannot amend or add appendices unless agreed as part of a formal review. It is expected that each party will have procedures, processes and policies sitting underneath this agreement, for their respective organisations. These will, for example, describe the specific processes for secure transfer of data. . Responsibilities of parties involved The Parties are registered Data Controllers under the Data Protection Act. All parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: ● having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ● ensuring data quality. ● storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. ● having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including for managing data subject rights and complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ● ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality, and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. ● undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ, and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. ● having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Organisations and their staff must consult the organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian if they are unsure at any point in the processing and sharing of personal data. . Confidentiality and vetting Each Partner must ensure that there are appropriate written contracts or agreements with employees, agency staff, volunteers etc. These must include requirements to ensure compliance with policies which include confidentiality. Each Partner must ensure that suitable vetting has taken place. This may be through standard employee checks and DBS checks. . Assessment and review and Termination of agreement A review of this information sharing agreement will take place yearly, unless otherwise agreed by the organisations’ Data Protection Officers. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, the scope has not slipped, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. Changes in legislation and developments in the areas of public sector data sharing will be considered as and when they arise, as will any changes to the signatory parties. In the event of termination of this agreement each Party may continue to hold information originating from other parties for which they are Data Controller. . Purpose and Benefits . Purpose This agreement covers the sharing of information by and between the listed parties for the purpose of the Closer to Camden pilot project. This pilot project aims to evidence that early prevention through implementing intensive local packages of care interventions could help prevent children from entering residential provision. Families being considered for this pilot project are on the Camden Dynamic Support Register - a register of children and young people where there are concerns that they are at risk of being admitted to an in-patient mental health unit or residential school placement. The families supported by the pilot project will receive a Personal Health Budget (PHB) from North Central London Integrated Care Board (NCL ICB) (in addition to their existing support from Social Care) if agreed by the ICB personal health budget panel. The PHB will enable families to receive care and support that best meets the current needs of their child and to enhance existing support being received. Imagineer, who have been appointed by NCL ICB will develop care plans with families and their child(ren) on how the integrated budget could help the family and how the family will be use the funds allocated. . Benefits The sharing will allow both partners to better deliver their statutory series and will allow more effective use of resources, giving more joined up working which increases efficiency. The public will benefit from this approach, as services will be delivered in a more streamlined way that utilises the information shared to provide better tailored and appropriate services. Families supported by the pilot project will receive a Personal Health Budget (in addition to their existing support from Social Care) to enable them to receive care and support that best meets the current needs of their child. This is to enhance existing support being received, and to reduce escalation of need and therefore avoid unnecessary inpatient setting admission. This would also help achieve better outcomes for the child and their families. The benefits of this DSA are to: ● Cover the sharing of information for Personal Care Plans to be developed including finding out more about the needs of the family and child, as well as access to the social care assessment and the social care recommendation for how the budgets can be used to support families based on assessed needs. ● Sets parameters for sharing personal data and clearly identifies the responsibilities of organisations. ● Identify the correct lawful basis to share personal information. ● Ensure information is shared whenever there is a requirement to do so. ● Enables authorities to share data on performance, quality assurance, learning and impact analysis. . Lawful Basis For the Council: Personal Data Processing: Article 6 (1) – (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller. Special Category Personal Data Processing: Article 9 (2) (b) social protection law - processing is necessary for the purposes of carrying out the obligations and exercising specific rights of the controller or of the data subject in the field of employment and social security and social protection law; 9 (2) (g) substantial public interest - processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest with the Data Protection Act Schedule 1, Part 2 condition is being para 6 Statutory etc., and government purposes For Imagineer: Personal Data Processing: Article 6 (1) – (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller. Special Category Personal Data Processing: Article 9 (2) (b) social protection law - processing is necessary for the purposes of carrying out the obligations and exercising specific rights of the controller or of the data subject in the field of employment and social security and social protection law; 9 (2) (g) substantial public interest - processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest with the Data Protection Act Schedule 1, Part 2 condition is being para 6 Statutory etc., and government purposes . Consent The parties will often work collaboratively with data subjects and aim for agreement with them on the actions to be taken. However, it is recognised that for a public authority this is different to using consent (Article 6 (a)) or explicit consent (Article 9 (a)) as the lawful basis conditions used for processing under this agreement. Consent is not generally the lawful basis the public sector organisations use for processing information shared under this agreement. It is noted that where consent is not the lawful basis for processing, consent does not need to be sought to share, and thus the concept of “overriding consent” is a misconception. It is possible that the other parties, such as voluntary groups, may use consent as a lawful basis for some personal data processing. Each party is responsible for managing consent where they use consent as the lawful basis condition. . Proportionality and necessity Proportionality, data minimization, necessity and not being excessive are factors to be taken into consideration when deciding whether to share personal information. In making the decision, employees must weigh up what might happen as a result of the information being shared against what might happen if it is not, and apply their professional judgement. It is for this reason professionals must ensure they comply with Article 5(1)(c) and share the adequate and relevant information, and limit that information to what is necessary for the achieving of the DSA aims. . Individuals Organisations processing personal data are required to begin with the ethos of Data Protection by Design and Default (also known as Privacy by Design (PbD)). This means that we must consider and uphold the privacy of an individual’s data before we begin and throughout the processing taking place. Each party agrees that they have undertaken a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment), where they feel the processing meets the legislative criteria for a DPIA. . Right to be informed – Privacy notices Where personal data is created or received by one of the parties, they are responsible, as required by law, for making the data subject(s) aware within a reasonable time frame that the organisation holds the data, what they will do with it, how long they will keep it, and who they will share it with (such as under this DSA). This is normally done through a privacy notice, whether written or verbal. Organisations agree that they will adhere to the transparency requirements of the UK GDPR and will issue appropriate notices which inform the data subject that the information will be shared with the parties under this agreement. . Data subject rights requests and complaints Each organisation must have in place appropriate policies and processes to handle data subject requests made in line with data protection law, to ensure they are responded to within deadline and in an appropriate manner. Requests include; right of access, right to rectification, right to erasure, right to restrict processing, right to data portability, right to object and rights related to automated decision making including profiling. If an individual successfully requests the erasure or limitation of use of their data (right to erasure, right to rectification, right to restrict processing, right to object), the party that has been informed by the data subject will communicate this to the other parties where relevant and appropriate. In each case each party is responsible for securely disposing of such information or limiting its processing. Each party must have clear, fair and objective complaint procedures. Any complaints from individuals how their data is being processed or shared will be handled under the policy and processes of the organisation concerned. . Data subjects The data subjects will be: children and their families at significant risk of needing residential placement, selected by a multi-disciplinary working group from the Dynamic Support Register. . Data . The data to be shared Data that will be shared includes: ● name and contact details ● address ● age/date of birth ● ethnicity, physical and mental health needs ● Information collected in their Social Care Plan, Care/Support Plan/ Short breaks review, and Child and Family Assessments ● Information about siblings ● Information about housing and benefits. . Storing and handling information securely Information must be stored and shared lawfully and securely. Special category data may need a higher level of security. The employee/organisation sharing the information must choose the most appropriate secure method of transfer and be responsible for its safe delivery. Electronic records: Organisations may have different electronic methods for storing and sharing information securely. Some have local restrictions which block access to information shared using specific tools. Parties must make sure the chosen method is suitably secure and that access is only provided to those who need it, and only to the data needed. Unencrypted email (i.e. sent in plain text over the public internet) must not be used to share information under this DSA. Sharing methods that may be appropriate include: ● Email encryption tools where the email and attachments are encrypted from named sender to named recipient (e.g. Microsoft 365 Message Encryption; Egress Protect) ● Secure corporately managed data repository and sharing platforms (e.g. MS Teams; ) ● Secure File Transfer Protocols ● Virtual Private Networks The above are examples, get advice from your organisation’s information security or IT teams on secure methods of sharing available at your organisation and document these in the organisation’s process documents. Phone/virtual meetings/face-to-face meetings: Information may be shared over the phone, in a virtual meeting, or at face to face meetings. Meeting attendance and distribution of content, e.g. meeting minutes or recordings, must be limited to those with a need to know. Sharing by telephone should be avoided unless the requirement is urgent and email is not practicable. Individuals should be aware of their surroundings and the presence of other individuals or voice recognition or ‘Internet of Things’ devices (e.g. virtual assistant apps like Alexa, Cortana, SIRI) to ensure they aren’t overheard by those that should not have access to the information discussed. Paper records: Printed paper records must always be kept to a minimum and kept secure whether in the office, home or during transit. Organisations must adopt an appropriate policy surrounding the use and transfer of paper records. Appropriate security methods must be applied when storing or disposing of paper records. . Access controls and security All parties will ensure that they have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place to guard against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, personal data. All personal data held by partner organisations electronically will be stored in a secure network area with password protected entry and appropriate back-up functionality. The systems will be auditable so that it is possible for any auditor to establish who has accessed the system. All laptops, computers, and any other portable devices will be encrypted. Any individual no longer required to have access will promptly have such access revoked by the line manager and Human Resources related to the relevant employer. . Outside UK processing Parties are responsible for ensuring that if information is processed or shared outside the UK, that appropriate safeguards are in place and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. These are for example, a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies, binding corporate rules, and/or standard data protection contractual clauses. . Data quality Each partner is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and relevance of the personal data that it processes and shares and must have clear processes in place for managing data quality. Any party learning of the inaccuracy of personal data is responsible for informing the parties with whom that data has been shared. . Data breaches/incidents All parties must have a clear policy and procedure regarding the reporting and handling of data protection breaches or data loss incidents. This must include assessing the level of risk to the data subject(s), as well as to make a decision on notifying the ICO within the statutory time frame of 72 hours. This complies with Articles 33 and 34 of UK GDPR. If the incident may impact the processing of another party to this agreement, all relevant parties should be informed and appropriate coordination of the incident must take place. The decision to report the incident will lie with the data controller(s) of the information concerned. The parties agree to provide all reasonable and necessary assistance at their own expense to each other to facilitate the handling of any personal data breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. It is confirmed that security breaches (including misuse or unauthorised disclosure) are covered by the partner’s internal disciplinary procedures. If misuse is found there should be a mechanism to facilitate an investigation, including initiating criminal proceedings where necessary. . Retention and Disposal Organisations are required by data protection legislation to document processing activities for personal data, such as what personal data is held, where it came from and with whom it has been shared. This Record of Processing Activity (ROPA) must include the retention period for the data. Information must not be retained for longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was obtained. Disposal or deletion of personal data once it is no longer required, must be done securely with appropriate safeguards, in accordance with that organisation’s disposal policies. Signatures . However, for the purpose of transparency and to monitor and audit compliance with our legal obligations under the Data Protection Legislation, the MOD require these agreements to be in writing setting out: i. Purpose, benefit, and nature of the data sharing agreement between the Parties. ii. The Parties’ lawful basis for the processing of the personal data. This requires the Parties to identify the legal grounds (as set out what under Article 6 of the UK GDPR and/or other applicable UK law (this includes common law)) that confer the legal powers or duties that requires and justifies the need to process the personal data in the manner proposed by the Parties. iii. The types and categories of Personal Data to be shared. iv. A brief description of the processing activities between the Parties. v. The transfer Mechanisms agreed between the Parties to be used to securely transfer the personal data. vi. Protective Measures to be adopted by the Parties such as access and storage controls once the data has been transferred. vii. Whether the Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) process has been followed. The Parties will need to confirm whether a full DPIA or pre-screening has been completed and signed off. Even if it is decided that a full DPIA is not required in line with current policy, the pre-screening risk assessment must be documented with clear audit trail of the review and authorisation of the risks and mitigations. Its completion must be recorded in the DUA. viii. The agreed data retention schedules. ix. How Freedom of Information Requests and/or Data Subject Requests will be managed and whether the Parties will notify the other Party before finalising any public response. x. The termination or escalation procedure for any disputes. ANNEX A –DATA USAGE AGREEMENT DATA USAGE AGREEMENT (DUA) BetweenTHE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE (MOD) AND Collectively referred to as Parties and individually referred to as a Party. This is a Data Usage Agreement (DUA) between the MOD and London Borough fof Camden for the processing of Personal Data for the resettlement of eligible persons (EPs) from Afghanistan to the United Kingdom as a result of the fall of Kabul in 2021; . The purpose of this DUA is to set out the terms of control of personal data of EPs who are due to be accommodated at MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA); or have transitioned through the MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA) prior to settling in longer-term accommodation. This will include a form summarising the services received during their stay at the sites. . For the purposes of this DUA, the Parties are acting as Independent Controllers and will process the personal data shared in compliance with all applicable data protection laws. Description Details Formalities This data sharing activity will run from November 2024 and will be reviewed annually until the Parties terminate this DUA once EPs are relocated Risk Assessment Data Protection Impact Assessments that cover the Processing of Personal Data for the processing activity have been completed: By MOD in June 2024 By London Borough of Camden in September 2024 Processing Activity Sharing of personal data related to EPs undergoing resettlement to the UK who are to be accommodated at MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA); or transitioned through the MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA) prior to settling in longer-term accommodation. For those transitioned through to a final location, this will include sharing a form summarising the services received during their stay at the TSFA/RSOM sites for LAs. Legal Gateway Legal Gateway for MoD As a Crown body, the MOD relies on its prerogative powers that emanate from Common Law. Legal Gateway for London Borough of Camden Care Act 2014, the Children Acts, Housing Acts, Homelessness Reduction Act 2017, Localism Act 2011, Equality Act 2010, Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 Lawful Basis for MOD Lawful Basis for processing Personal Data under Article 6 (1)(e) Processing “processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller”. It is in the public interest to ensure that EPs are granted with resettlement and supported with their initial orientation package to ensure a positive start to their integration in the UK The lawful bases under the Data Protection legislation that MOD relies on are: Article 6(1)(c) UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): “processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which controller is subject.” Article 6(1)(e) UK GDPR: “processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller”. It is in the public interest to ensure that eligible individuals are resettled and given the relevant medical and healthcare required. Article 9(2)(g) of UK GDPR: Special categories of personal data, such as health data or data that reveals their ethnic origin, will be processed as part of this data sharing arrangement. The lawful basis for processing is Article 9(2)(g) of UK GDPR: “processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest, on the basis of domestic law.” London Borough of Camden Lawful Basis for processing Personal Data Article 6(1)(c): Legal obligation: the processing is necessary for the Controller to comply with the law Article 6(1)(e): Public task: the processing is necessary for the Controller to perform a task in the public interest or for official functions, and the task or function has a clear basis in law. London Borough of Camden Lawful Basis for processing Special Category Personal Data Article 9 (2) (b): Employment, social security and social protection (if authorised by law) with the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1 condition being paras 1 and 2 Article 9(2)(g): Reasons of substantial public interest (with a basis in law) with the DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 condition being para 6 Article 9(2) (h) Health or social care (with a basis in law) with the Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 1 condition being paras 1 and 2 No criminal offence data is being processed. The London Borough of Camden is not undertaking Law Enforcement Processing under DPA Part 3 for this data. Duration of the Commencement date for this sharing activity is October 2024 and this is a processing regular/ ongoing processing activity to match for the purposes of EPs’ resettlement to the UK. The requirements and the type of data processing will be reviewed on an annual basis until the EPs are resettled to the UK. Nature and The MOD will share personal data to the Local Authority to facilitate at pace purposes of the the relocation of EPs into the UK. The MOD will provide EPs with temporary processing accommodation at MOD reception sits RSOM sites, for c. 6 weeks. Following this a settled property is identified for each family unit within a Local Authority. Sharing of personal data of EPs who are due to be accommodated at MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA); or have transitioned through the MOD reception sites (RSOM) and/or Transitional Service Family Accommodation (TSFA) prior to settling in longer-term accommodation. EPs matched to settled accommodation in a different Local Authority to their transitional accommodation, will have a summary of the services received during their stay at transitional accommodation that will be shared with the relevant Local Authority. The Local Authority will use this data to facilitate any required support for eligible persons and families housed in both transitional accommodation and settling into longer term accommodation in their Local Authority area. Mark information assets with the appropriate security classification and apply the appropriate baseline set of personnel, physical and information security controls that offer an appropriate level of protection against a typical threat profile. LEGAL STATUS OF THIS DUA This DUA may only be varied by written agreement of the Parties. This DUA is not intended to be legally binding, and no legal obligations or legal rights shall arise between the Parties from this DUA. The agreement between the Parties have been documented to ensure transparency for the personal data processing between the Parties. Nothing in this DUA is intended to, or shall be deemed to, establish any partnership or joint venture between the Parties, constitute either Party as the agent of the other Party, nor authorise either of the Parties to make or enter into any commitments for or on behalf of the other Party. The Parties may incorporate this DUA into other agreements by reference to cover off their requirements under the Data Protection legislation. . GOVERNING LAW AND JURISDICTION This DUA shall be governed by and construed in accordance with English law.

London Borough of Camden and London Borough of Camden Electoral Registration Officer Memorandum of Understanding For the purpose of data sharing Between Adult and Health Services and the Electoral Registration Officer The London Borough of Camden Electoral Registration Officer is legally a different Data Controller to the London Borough of Camden but is employed by the same organisation. This Memorandum is non-binding but constitutes a written agreement setting out the intentions of both data controllers to further the lawful purpose described below, aid appropriate information sharing, and safeguard the integrity and confidentiality of the data concerned. In the circumstances both data controllers agree that due to the close and intertwined nature of the relationships and processing, that a formal Data Sharing Agreement is disproportionate and that a MoU will suffice. This Memorandum of Understanding sets out the respective roles of the parties and the conditions under which the data sharing is permitted. It is intended to meet the requirements of regulation 35A (3) Representation of the People (England & Wales) Regulations 2001 which requires that a disclosure under that provision may be made only in accordance with a written agreement between the authority and the registration officer regulating the processing of the information, including its transfer, storage, destruction and security. Regulation 35A provides that the council permitted to disclose to the registration officer, for certain registration purposes, information contained in records held by the council. These are the purposes set out in paragraph 1A of Schedule 2 to the 1983 Act, except for the purpose of verifying information related to a person named in a relevant absent voting application. Paragraph 1A(1) of Schedule 2 to the Representation of the People 1983 Act enables provision to be made authorising or requiring a person to disclose information to another person for the purpose of assisting a registration officer (1) to verify information relating to a person who is registered or who is named in a registration application. (2) to ascertain the names and addresses of people who are not registered but who are entitled to be registered; or (3) to identify those people who are registered but who are not entitled to be registered. The Electoral Registration Officer confirms that the information requested comes within the scope of their legal powers in Regulation 35 (1) of the Representation of the People (England & Wales) Regulations 2001 which authorises a registration officer to inspect, for the purpose of their registration duties, records kept in any form by Camden. Purpose: The data is being accessed to allow the ERO to: maintain and manage the register of electors (including the public record of electors) meet any statutory requirements of the registration officer not listed above and to administer and enforce rules and regulations relating to electoral registration. Assistance with voting for persons with disabilities The personal data will include: Name Current address and previous address (where recorded or where applicable) Date of Birth National Insurance Number (where recorded) Nationality (where recorded) Details of disability and presence on the Sight Loss Register The data will be provided to the Electoral Registration Officer by provision of Sight Lost Register and other data if applicable via email in a.csv flat file in the format expected by the ERO system. Electoral registration staff will be able to request the information when required, although requests will not be so regular as to be unduly onerous to ASC, and the information will be provided within 5 working days of request. Retention and Deletion: The data files received will be destroyed once data has been entered into Democracy Counts. The statutory process of the Annual Canvass will check the information held on the register of electors and any potential electors who are identified as no longer being at the property will be archived in the EMS. Purpose Limitation and Information security. The ERO warrants that they have, will record and will maintain appropriate organisational measures to ensure that ERO staff do not use this data for any other purpose. Information Security for the ERO is provided by the council’s Information Security Team and DDS service and will be to the same standards as for other council assets. All those who will handle the disclosed data are bound by the employee code of conduct, have undergone appropriate employee checks as necessary for the role, will only use the information for purposes of their role and no other, will not share the information gained with other services or agencies (save where required to do so by law e.g. safeguarding duties, by court order or with the courts or as part of legal proceedings ). Breach of these conditions may result in disciplinary action for breach of the code of conduct. Agreement: Agreed: Name: Jamie Spencer Position Head of Insight, Quality & Financial Services and Caldicott Guardian for Adult Social Care Date: Agreed: Name: Jeanette Pegler Position: Electoral Services Manager Date: 28/03/25

Introduction to the Sharing This is a Data Sharing agreement between London Borough of Camden SEND and Inclusion Service and Central and North West London NHS Trust. This Data Sharing Agreement documents how the parties to this agreement, listed in Appendix A, will share personal data about Children and Young People, as well as parents who are referred to, or would benefit from, the London Borough of Camden SEND and Inclusion Service. By signing this Agreement, the named agencies agree to accept the conditions set out in this document, according to their statutory and professional responsibilities, and agree to adhere to the procedures described. This Agreement has been developed to: ● Define the specific purposes for which the signatory agencies have agreed to share information. ● Outline the Personal, Special Category and Criminal Data to be shared. ● Set out the lawful basis conditions under UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 through which the information is shared, including reference to the Human Rights Act 1998 ● Stipulate the roles and procedures that will support the processing/sharing of information between agencies. ● Describe how the rights of the data subject(s) will be protected as stipulated under the data protection legislation. ● Describe the security procedures necessary to ensure that compliance with responsibilities under data protection legislation and agency-specific security requirements. ● Describe how this arrangement will be monitored and reviewed. ● To illustrate the flow of information from referral through processing and outcome. Parties to this agreement cannot amend or add appendices unless agreed as part of a formal review. It is expected that each party will have procedures, processes and policies sitting underneath this agreement, for their respective organisations. These will, for example, describe the specific processes for secure transfer of data. . Responsibilities of parties involved The parties are Data Controllers. A list of signatories is at Appendix A. All parties confirm that they comply with data protection legislation by: having a lawful basis for processing and sharing personal data. ensuring data quality. storing and sharing information securely, with access management controls. having policies and procedures for compliance with data protection legislation including managing data subject rights and complaints, identifying and managing data breaches/incidents and retention & disposal. ensuring that mandatory training is undertaken regularly by their employees to ensure they are clear and up to date on their responsibilities. Every individual must uphold the principles of this agreement and overarching confidentiality and seek advice from the relevant Data Protection Officer when necessary. undertaking appropriate data protection due diligence checks with any contractors/data processors they employ and ensuring that a written agreement is in place with each data processor, and that all data processors will be bound by this agreement. having written processes for the processing of data to ensure employees use and share personal data in line with data protection law, the data protection principles, and this agreement. Organisations and their staff must consult the organisation’s Data Protection Officer/Information Governance Manager and/or Caldicott Guardian if they are unsure at any point in the processing and sharing of personal data. . Confidentiality and vetting Each Partner must ensure that there are appropriate written contracts or agreements with employees, agency staff, volunteers etc. These must include requirements to ensure compliance with policies which include confidentiality. Each Partner must ensure that suitable vetting has taken place. This may be through standard employee checks and DBS checks. . Review, Lifespan, Termination A review of this information sharing agreement will take place yearly, unless otherwise agreed by the organisations’ Data Protection Officers. The aim of the review will be to ensure the purposes are still relevant, the scope has not slipped, the benefits to the data subjects and organisations are being realised, and the procedures followed for information security are effective. Changes in legislation and developments in the areas of public sector data sharing will be considered as and when they arise, as will any changes to the signatory parties. This agreement will continue until terminated by one or both parties. The DSA may be terminated by agreement of the Parties’ Information Asset Owners, with such notice period as they agree, or by one Party giving written one month's notice to the other, by email Information Asset Owner to Information Asset Owner and copying in the respective DPOs. In the event of termination of this agreement each party may continue to hold information originating from other parties for which they are Data Controller. . Purpose and Benefits . Purpose This agreement covers the sharing of information by and between the listed parties for the purpose of the better coordination between the parties. The parties frequently hold information about the same child and family that is different in nature and purpose from each other, and a coordinated service offer that encapsulates both universal and targeted services will be facilitated by better information sharing. The sharing of information will enable the Services to maintain up-to-date records, identify the needs of relevant children as early as possible and provide tailored services. . Benefits The sharing will allow both partners to better deliver their statutory services and will allow more effective use of resources, enabling more joined-up working, which increases efficiency. The public will benefit from this approach, as services will be delivered in a more streamlined way that utilises the information shared to provide better tailored and appropriate services. The sharing of information between the parties will enable the identification of children and young people in common to support more detailed information about children’s development and progress. This would support the assessment processes in both services and inform service delivery and future planning. Furthermore, sharing of information between the parties would allow the identification of children with SEND who would benefit from targeted services provided by teams within the SEND and Inclusion service. The objectives aim to improve provision for families and young children, by better coordinating services so that those with the greatest need are identified as early as possible and provided with effective services that support their ability to thrive. The benefits of this DSA are to: Cover the sharing of information for staff within Service to be able to identify the needs of each family in Camden from a health, education, and social care view. Sets parameters for sharing personal data and clearly identifies the responsibilities of organisations. Identify the correct lawful basis to share personal information. Ensure information is shared whenever there is a requirement to do so. Enables authorities to share data on performance, quality assurance, learning and impact analysis. . Lawful Basis The sharing of information must comply with the law relating to confidentiality, data protection and human rights. Having a legitimate purpose for sharing information is an important part of meeting those legal requirements. Articles 6 and 9 of the UK GDPR set out the acceptable conditions for the processing and sharing of personal, special category data. The conditions relevant in the UK GDPR to data processed under this agreement are below. Personal data: Article 6 (1) (c) processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject; and (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller. Special category data: Article 9 (2)(g) processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest, on the basis of Union or Member State law which shall be proportionate to the aim pursued, respect the essence of the right to data protection and provide for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject; and (h) Processing is necessary for the purposes of preventative or occupational medicine, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment or management of health and social care systems. The underpinning laws are section 22(3) of the Children Act 1989 and the National Health Service Act which place legal duties on Local Authorities in respect to promoting cooperation between itself and relevant partner agencies to secure and advance the health and welfare of people and to improve the well-being of children in the local authority’s area. The Children Act 1989 places a duty on the local authority, each of the local authority’s relevant partners or other appropriate bodies or persons to make arrangements to promote co-operation between itself and relevant partner agencies to improve the well-being of children in the local authority’s area. National Health Service Act 2006 places a duty on the National Health Service and local authorities to cooperate with one another in order to secure and advance the health and welfare of people, which would indicate the requirement to share information. . Consent The parties will often work collaboratively with data subjects and aim for agreement with them on the actions to be taken. However, it is recognised that this is different to using consent (Article 6 (a)) or explicit consent (Article 9 (a)) as the lawful basis conditions used for processing under this agreement. Consent is not generally the lawful basis the public sector organisations use for processing information shared under this agreement. It is noted that where consent is not the lawful basis for processing, consent does not need to be sought to share, and thus the concept of “overriding consent” is a misconception. . Proportionality and necessity Proportionality, data minimization, necessity and not being excessive are factors to be taken into consideration when deciding whether to share personal information. In making the decision, employees must weigh up what might happen as a result of the information being shared against what might happen if it is not and apply their professional judgement. It is for this reason professionals must ensure they comply with Article 5(1)(c) and share the adequate and relevant information and limit that information to what is necessary for the achieving of the DSA aims. . Freedom of Information The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives all individuals the right to access official information held by a public authority (the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 also allow access to data. For ease of drafting, FOI is used to cover both legislation). Limited exemptions may apply and all public authorities must ensure they have recognised procedures in place for administering requests of this nature. All requests for FOI will be directed through the relevant organisations’ FOI processes. Each party will seek advice/opinion from the other parties where there is concern about that information being released and any impact it is likely to have. The final decision to disclose or not will lie with the party who received the request as the legal duty lies with them. In order to ensure that the authority in receipt of the FOIA request is able to respond within the statutory deadline, any request for assistance or information made to partner authorities should be made and processed within two working days, and any data exchange completed within seven working days. It is encouraged that all parties proactively publish this document. It may also be disclosed to the public under FOI. . Individuals Organisations processing personal data are required to begin with the ethos of Data Protection by Design and Default (also known as Privacy by Design (PbD)). This means that we must consider and uphold the privacy of an individual’s data before we begin and throughout the processing taking place. Each party agrees that they have undertaken a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment), where they feel the processing meets the legislative criteria for a DPIA. . Right to be informed – Privacy notices Where personal data is created or received by one of the parties, they are responsible, as required by law, for making the data subject(s) aware within a reasonable time frame that the organisation holds the data, what they will do with it, how long they will keep it, and who they will share it with (such as under this DSA). This is normally done through a privacy notice, whether written or verbal. Organisations agree that they will adhere to the transparency requirements of the UK GDPR and will issue appropriate notices which inform the data subject that the information will be shared with the parties under this agreement. In some cases, it may not be appropriate to let a person know that information about them is being processed and shared. Consideration should be given to whether notifying the individual may place someone at risk or prejudice a police or safeguarding investigation. In these circumstances, the parties need not inform individuals that the information is being processed/shared; but should record their reasons for sharing information without making the individual aware. . Data subject rights requests and complaints Each organisation must have in place appropriate policies and processes to handle data subject requests made in line with data protection law, to ensure they are responded to within deadline and in an appropriate manner. Requests include; right of access, right to rectification, right to erasure, right to restrict processing, right to data portability, right to object and rights related to automated decision making including profiling. If an individual successfully requests the erasure or limitation of use of their data (right to erasure, right to rectification, right to restrict processing, right to object), the party that has been informed by the data subject will communicate this to the other parties where relevant and appropriate. In each case each party is responsible for securely disposing of such information or limiting its processing. Each party must have clear, fair and objective complaint procedures. Any complaints from individuals how their data is being processed or shared will be handled under the policy and processes of the organisation concerned. . Data subjects The data subjects will be: Children and Young People referred to the SEND and Inclusion Service Children and Young People who would benefit from targeted services provided by teams within the SEND and Inclusion service. Parents of the above Many of the data subjects are vulnerable. Parties to this agreement are in positions of power over data subjects and data subjects have little or no control over why and how their data is processed. . Data . The data to be shared Data that will be shared includes: Name and contact details, Address Age/date of birth NHS number Gender, Race and Ethnicity Relevant Health records Information about why the Service User is (or is not) eligible for the Service Information about the child’s development and special educational needs, including observations, discussions held with parents/cares and nursery/school staff and assessment reports, advice, recordings, one page profiles, Individual education plans. Looked After Child Status Child In Need Status Early Help Access Names of persons with parental responsibility and contact details Name and contact details of GP Name of nursery/school/college the child or young person will attend/is attending . Storing and handling information securely Information must be stored and shared lawfully and securely. Special category data may need a higher level of security. The employee/organisation sharing the information must choose the most appropriate secure method of transfer and be responsible for its safe delivery. Electronic records: Organisations may have different electronic methods for storing and sharing information securely. Some have local restrictions which block access to information shared using specific tools. Parties must make sure the chosen method is suitably secure and that access is only provided to those who need it, and only to the data needed. Unencrypted email (i.e. sent in plain text over the public internet) must not be used to share information under this DSA. Sharing methods that may be appropriate include: ● Email encryption tools where the email and attachments are encrypted from named sender to named recipient (e.g. Microsoft 365 Message Encryption; Egress Protect) ● Encryption via Transport Layer Security (TLS) where the email and attachments are encrypted in transit over the internet. Both the sender and recipient email domains must have TLS enabled. This can be checked using ● Secure corporately managed data repository and sharing platforms (e.g. MS Teams; Google Docs) ● Secure group email services (e.g. CJSM: ● Secure File Transfer Protocols ● Virtual Private Networks The above are examples, get advice from your organisation’s information security or IT teams on secure methods of sharing available at your organisation and document these in the organisation’s process documents. Phone/virtual meetings/face-to-face meetings: Information may be shared over the phone, in a virtual meeting, or at face to face meetings. Meeting attendance and distribution of content, e.g. meeting minutes or recordings, must be limited to those with a need to know. Sharing by telephone should be avoided unless the requirement is urgent and email is not practicable. Individuals should be aware of their surroundings and the presence of other individuals or voice recognition or ‘Internet of Things’ devices (e.g. virtual assistant apps like Alexa, Cortana, SIRI) to ensure they aren’t overheard by those that should not have access to the information discussed. Paper records: Printed paper records must always be kept to a minimum and kept secure whether in the office, home or during transit. Organisations must adopt an appropriate policy surrounding the use and transfer of paper records. Appropriate security methods must be applied when storing or disposing of paper records. . Access controls and security All parties will ensure that they have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place to guard against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss or destruction of, or damage to, personal data. All personal data held by partner organisations electronically will be stored in a secure network area with password protected entry and appropriate back-up functionality. The systems will be auditable so that it is possible for any auditor to establish who has accessed the system. All laptops, computers, and any other portable devices will be encrypted. Any individual no longer required to have access will promptly have such access revoked by the line manager and Human Resources related to the relevant employer. There is an expectation that partner organisations will either be working toward ISO 27001, the International Standard for Information Security Management, or a similar standard of security such as NHS Digital’s Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSP) and Cyber Essentials or Cyber Essentials Plus. . Outside UK processing Parties are responsible for ensuring that if information is processed or shared outside the UK, that appropriate safeguards are in place and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. These are for example, a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies, binding corporate rules, and/or standard data protection contractual clauses. . Data quality Each partner is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and relevance of the personal data that it processes and shares and must have clear processes in place for managing data quality. Any party learning of the inaccuracy of personal data is responsible for informing the parties with whom that data has been shared. . Data breaches/incidents All parties must have a clear policy and procedure regarding the reporting and handling of data protection breaches or data loss incidents. This must include assessing the level of risk to the data subject(s), as well as to make a decision on notifying the ICO within the statutory time frame of 72 hours. This complies with Articles 33 and 34 of UK GDPR. If the incident may impact the processing of another party to this agreement, all relevant parties should be informed and appropriate coordination of the incident must take place. The decision to report the incident will lie with the data controller(s) of the information concerned. The parties agree to provide all reasonable and necessary assistance at their own expense to each other to facilitate the handling of any personal data breach in an expeditious and compliant manner. It is confirmed that security breaches (including misuse or unauthorised disclosure) are covered by the partner’s internal disciplinary procedures. If misuse is found there should be a mechanism to facilitate an investigation, including initiating criminal proceedings where necessary. . Retention and Disposal Organisations are required by data protection legislation to document processing activities for personal data, such as what personal data is held, where it came from and with whom it has been shared. This Record of Processing Activity (ROPA) must include the retention period for the data. Information must not be retained for longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was obtained. Disposal or deletion of personal data once it is no longer required, must be done securely with appropriate safeguards, in accordance with that organisation’s disposal policies. .
